chapters.title: Book 1 — The Good for Man
paragraphs: Every art and every systematic branch of knowledge, along with every action and deliberate choice, seems to aim at some good. This is why people often describe the highest good as "that at which all things aim."

But the ends aimed at clearly differ. In some cases the end is the activity itself; in others, it is some product beyond the activity. Wherever there are ends distinct from the activities that produce them, the products are by nature better than the activities. And since actions, arts, and sciences are many, their ends are also many. The end of medicine is health; of shipbuilding, a ship; of military strategy, victory; of household management, wealth.

Whenever several such arts fall under a single discipline — as bridle-making and other equipment-making fall under horsemanship, and horsemanship itself along with every military action falls under strategy — the ends of the master arts are more choice-worthy than the ends of the subordinate ones, since the subordinate arts are pursued for the sake of the master.
(It makes no difference here whether the activities themselves are the ends, or something further beyond them, as in the arts and sciences just mentioned.)

If then among all things we do there is some end we want for its own sake, and for whose sake we want everything else — since we do not choose everything for the sake of something further, because then desire would go on forever and come to nothing — this end must be the highest good, the best of all.

Surely the knowledge of this good carries great weight even for the conduct of life. Like archers with a target to aim at, we will be more likely to hit what is right. If so, we should try to describe at least in outline what it is, and to which of the sciences or capacities it belongs.

Naturally one would think it belongs to the most authoritative and comprehensive discipline. Political science fits this description. It determines which of the sciences should be studied in a community, which classes of people should learn them, and to what level. We also see that it governs the most highly regarded capacities — strategy, household management, rhetoric. Since political science makes use of all the other practical sciences and legislates what people should do and abstain from, its end must include the ends of the others. That end must therefore be the human good. Even if this good is the same for an individual and for a community, the good of the community is clearly greater and more perfect to secure. Achieving it for one person is worthwhile; achieving it for a nation or community is nobler and more godlike.

These, then, are the aims of the present inquiry, which is a kind of political science. I will have done enough if I clarify them as precisely as the subject allows. Exactness should not be demanded equally in all inquiries, any more than in all crafts. Notions of nobility and justice, which political science examines, admit so much variation and error that some think they exist only by convention, not by nature. Even what is commonly called good admits similar uncertainty, since many have been harmed by supposed goods — some destroyed by wealth, others by courage.

We must be content, then, in speaking of such things and from such data, to sketch the truth roughly and in outline. Since we are speaking of general matters and reasoning from general data, we can only draw general conclusions. Each person should receive what we say in that spirit. A well-educated person seeks precision in each subject only so far as the nature of the matter allows. It would be equally absurd to accept a mathematician who merely persuades without proving, or to demand rigorous demonstrations from a rhetorician.

Everyone judges well what he knows, and is a good judge of those things. So on any particular matter, someone trained in that subject is a good judge; and generally, a person of broad education is a good judge in general.

For this reason a young person is not a proper student of moral philosophy. He lacks experience of the actions of life, which are the subject matter. Moreover, since he tends to follow his passions, his listening will be pointless and unprofitable, because the aim is practice, not mere knowledge.

I make no distinction between young in age and youthful in temperament. The defect I am describing is not due to age itself, but to living at the mercy of passion and chasing each object as it arises. For such people, knowledge is useless, as it is for anyone who lacks self-control. But for those who form their desires and act according to reason, knowledge of these matters will be very valuable.
Let this suffice as a preface on three points: the student, the spirit in which our observations should be received, and the object we propose.

To pick up again where we began: since all knowledge and deliberate choice reaches for some good, what good is it that political science aims at? In other words, what is the highest of all the goods that are attainable by action?

In name, most people agree: both the general public and educated people call it happiness, and they think that living well and doing well are the same as being happy. But about what happiness actually is, they disagree, and the multitude's account differs from the wise. Some say happiness is one of the obvious and visible things — pleasure, wealth, or honor — though they disagree on which. Often the same person gives a different answer at different times: sick, he calls it health; poor, wealth. Aware of their own ignorance, people admire those who talk grandly beyond their understanding. Others have claimed happiness is something distinct from and beyond all these particular goods — something that gives them their goodness.
To sift through every opinion would probably be fruitless. It will be enough to examine the views that are most widely held, or that seem to have some reason behind them.

Here we must not forget the difference between reasoning from first principles and reasoning toward them. Plato was right to raise this question: does the right road run from first principles or toward them? It is like the track in a race course: from the judges to the far end, or the reverse.

We must begin with what is known. But what is known is of two kinds: what we know in itself, and what we know in relation to ourselves. Perhaps as individuals we must begin with what is known to us. This is why anyone who is to study profitably the principles of nobility, justice, and moral philosophy generally must have been well trained in habits. A principle is a matter of fact, and if the fact is sufficiently clear to a man, he needs no further reason for it. Someone who has been trained either has principles already, or can grasp them easily. As for the man who has neither and cannot receive them, let him hear his sentence from Hesiod:
"Best of all is he who grasps everything himself. Good again is he who follows a good suggestion. But the man who neither grasps it himself nor takes it to heart from another — he is useless."
But to return from this digression.

People seem to form their notions of the chief good — that is, of happiness — from the different lives they lead, which is natural enough. The many and the vulgar conceive happiness to be pleasure, and so they are content with the life of sensual enjoyment. Three lives stand out prominently: the one just mentioned, the life of politics, and the life of contemplation.

The many are clearly quite slavish, preferring a life fit for cattle. Yet they have some excuse, because many of the great share the tastes of Sardanapalus. The refined and the active, on the other hand, conceive happiness to be honor — since honor is more or less the end of the political life. But this seems too superficial to be what we are looking for. Honor depends more on those who bestow it than on the one who receives it, whereas we feel instinctively that the chief good must be something of our own, and not easily taken away.

Moreover, people seem to pursue honor in order to convince themselves they are good: they seek to be honored by the wise, by those who know them, and for virtue. So clearly, in their own view, virtue is higher than honor. One might well suppose virtue to be the end of the political life. But even this seems not quite final. It is conceivable for someone who possesses virtue to sleep or be inactive all through his life; or, as a third case, to suffer the greatest misfortunes. No one would call such a man happy — except for the sake of argument.
On these points, this is enough; they have been treated at sufficient length in my popular works.
A third kind of life is the contemplative, which we will examine in what follows.

As for the life of money-making, it is a constrained one, and wealth is clearly not the good we are looking for. Wealth is useful, that is, for the sake of something else. So one would sooner suppose that the ends already mentioned are the right ones, since they are chosen for their own sakes. But clearly they are not what we are looking for either, though much has been said about them. Enough, then, on these.

It would be better, perhaps, to examine the notion of a universal good — the same in all things — and to discuss what it means. This inquiry is uncomfortable, because it was friends of ours who introduced these Forms. Still, it seems better, perhaps, or rather it is our duty where truth is concerned, to give up even our own theories, especially because we are lovers of wisdom. Since both friends and truth are dear to us, we should prefer truth. Now those who introduced the doctrine of Forms did not posit Forms for things in which they spoke of priority and posteriority, and so they never posited a Form of numbers. But "good" is predicated in the categories of substance, quality, and relation. What exists in itself — substance — is prior in nature to what is relative, since the relative is an offshoot of what is. On their own principles, then, there cannot be a common Form in these cases.

Next, "good" is predicated in as many ways as there are modes of existence. It is predicated in the category of substance (as of God and intellect); of quality (as of the virtues); of quantity (as of the mean); of relation (as of the useful); of time (as of opportunity); of place (as of abode); and so on. So it cannot be something common, universal, and single. If it were, it would not be predicated in all the categories, but only in one.

Third, since everything that falls under a single Form falls under a single science, there would be, on their view, only one science of all goods taken together. But in fact there are many sciences even of goods falling under one category. Of opportunity (which is in the category of time), the science in war is strategy, in disease it is medicine. Of the mean (in the category of quantity), in food it is medicine, in training it is athletics. One might also reasonably ask what they mean by "very"-this or that, since, as they themselves would admit, the definition of humanity is the same in "very-Man" and in any individual man. Insofar as both are human, they will not differ at all. And if so, then "very-good" and any particular good will not differ either, insofar as both are good. Nor can one claim that the eternity of "very-good" makes it more good; what has been white a long time is no whiter than what has been white only a day.
The Pythagoreans give a more plausible account when they place "one" among the goods in their double list of goods and evils. Speusippus seems to have followed them in this.

But let these matters be discussed some other time. There is an obvious opening to object to what I have said: that the theory I am attacking is not applied by its advocates to all goods, but only to those that are pursued and rested in for their own sakes, which they say fall under one Form. Things that tend to produce or preserve these, or to prevent their opposites, are called good because of these others, and in a different sense. So clearly "goods" can be spoken of in two senses: some for their own sakes, others because of these.

Very well. Let us separate the independent goods from the instrumental ones, and see whether the independents are spoken of under one Form. What kind of things should we call independent goods? Those pursued even when separated from anything else — such as wisdom, sight, certain pleasures, and honors (which, though we also pursue them with further ends in view, one would still place among the independent goods)? Or does it come to this: that we can call nothing an independent good except the Form itself, so that the class of independent goods collapses to nothing?

If on the other hand these are independent goods, the account of their goodness must clearly be the same in all, just as the account of whiteness is the same in snow and in white lead. But in fact, of honor, wisdom, and pleasure, the accounts are distinct and different precisely insofar as they are good. The chief good, then, is not something common, answering to one Form.

Yet how is it that the name "good" is common to them? It cannot be a case of mere coincidence. Are different things called good because they come from one source, or because they all contribute to one end, or rather by analogy — as sight is to the body, so intellect is to the soul, and so on? Perhaps we should leave these questions for now, since an accurate investigation of them belongs to a different branch of philosophy. The same goes for the Form. Even if there is some one good predicated in common of all good things, or existing separately and independently, it clearly cannot be the object of human action or attainable by a human being; and we are now looking for something that is.

One might suppose it would be better to attain knowledge of the universal good with a view to the concrete goods that are attainable and practical — since, having such a model, we would better know which things are good for us as individuals, and so attain them.

This argument has some plausibility, but it is contradicted by the facts of the arts and sciences. All of them aim at some good and seek to supply what is missing, yet they do without this universal knowledge. It is not likely that every craftsman without exception should be ignorant of so great an aid, not even bothering to seek it. Nor is it easy to see how a weaver or carpenter will be helped in his craft by knowing "very-good," or how a man will be better at curing the sick or commanding an army for having seen the Form itself. The physician does not consider health in the abstract; he considers the health of a human being, or rather of this or that human being, since he has to heal individuals. So much for these points.

Let us return to the good we are looking for: what can it be? It is plainly different in different actions and arts. It is one thing in medicine, another in strategy, and so on. What, then, is the chief good in each case? Is it not the end for whose sake the other things are done? In medicine, health; in strategy, victory; in housebuilding, a house; in any other art, something else. In every action and deliberate choice, the end is what matters, because people do everything else with a view to it. So if there is some one end of all our actions, this must be the good achievable by action; and if more than one, then these.
So our discussion, after some wandering, has come back to the same point. This we must try to clarify further.

Since there are plainly many ends, and we choose some of them — wealth, musical instruments, tools generally — for the sake of others, clearly not all ends are final. But the chief good is plainly something final. So if there is only one final end, this must be what we are looking for; and if more than one, the most final of them.

What is pursued for its own sake we call more final than what is pursued for the sake of something else. What is never chosen for the sake of anything else is more final than what is chosen both for its own sake and for something further. So by "absolutely final" we mean what is always chosen for its own sake and never for the sake of anything else.

Happiness above all seems to be of this nature. We always choose it for its own sake and never for the sake of anything further. Honor, pleasure, intelligence, and every excellence we do choose for their own sakes — we would choose each even if no further result came of it — but we choose them also for the sake of happiness, believing that through them we shall be happy. No one chooses happiness for the sake of these, or for anything else at all.

The same conclusion seems to follow from considering self-sufficiency, which is thought to belong to the final good. By "sufficient for oneself" we do not mean sufficient for a solitary individual living alone, but sufficient also for parents, children, wife, and in general for friends and fellow citizens; since a human being is by nature adapted to social existence. Of course some limit must be set here, for if one extends it to parents, descendants, and friends of friends, there is no end to it. That point can be left for later. For now we define the self-sufficient as "that which taken alone makes life worth choosing and lacking in nothing." And this, we believe, is what happiness is. Further, we think it is the most choice-worthy of all things, not counted alongside other goods. For if it were counted alongside them, it is plain that with the addition of any good, however small, it would become more choice-worthy, since the larger good is always more choice-worthy.
So happiness is plainly something final and self-sufficient, the end of all action.

To say the chief good is happiness may seem a platitude, and what is wanted is a clearer account of its real nature. This can be reached once we discover the function of a human being. Just as with a flute player, a sculptor, or any craftsman — indeed anyone with a function or line of action — his good and excellence are thought to reside in his function, so it seems also to be with a human being, if he has a function.

Are we to suppose that carpenters and cobblers have certain functions and activities, while a human being as such has none, but is left by nature without a function? Or rather, just as each of his parts — eye, hand, foot — plainly has a function, should we not also suppose that a human being, over and above these, has some function of his own?

What, then, can this be? It cannot be mere life, because that is shared even with plants, and we are looking for what is peculiar to human beings. We must therefore set aside the life of mere nutrition and growth. Next comes the life of sensation, but this too is shared with horses, oxen, and every animal. There remains an active life of the rational part. This has two parts: one that is obedient to reason, and one that has and exercises reason. Since this life too is spoken of in two ways, we must take the sense involving actual activity, since this is thought more properly deserving of the name. If the function of a human being is an activity of the soul according to reason, or at least not without reason, and if we say that the function of any given thing and of a good thing of that kind are the same in kind (as, for example, the function of a harpist and of a good harpist — the one to play, the other to play well), then adding eminence in excellence to the function gives us the good. The function of a harpist is to play the harp; of a good harpist, to play it well. If this is so, and we take the function of a human being to be a certain kind of life — activity of the soul and actions with reason — and the function of a good human being to be doing these things well and nobly, since each thing is finished off well according to its own proper excellence; if all this holds, then the human good turns out to be activity of the soul in accordance with excellence. And if there is more than one excellence, then in accordance with the best and most complete.
We must add "in a complete life." For one swallow does not make a spring, nor does a single day; and in the same way, one day or a short time does not make someone blessed and happy.

Let this serve as a rough sketch of the chief good, since it is probably right to outline first and fill in afterwards. Any man can improve and fill out what has been sketched; time is a good discoverer and collaborator in such matters. This is how all improvements in the various arts have been brought about — anyone can fill in what is missing.

Remember what has already been said: we must not demand the same exactness in all matters, but in each according to the subject and as far as the subject properly allows. A carpenter and a geometer inquire into the right angle in different ways: the carpenter, insofar as it is useful for his work; the geometer, into its nature and properties, since he is concerned with the truth.
One must do the same in other matters, so that accessories do not outweigh the main business.

Nor must we demand the reason equally in all cases. In some it is enough that the fact has been well established, which is how it is with first principles. The fact is the starting point or principle.

Some first principles are grasped by induction, some by perception, some by habituation, others in other ways. We must try to follow each in its own way and take pains to define them well, because they have great influence on what follows. The principle is thought to be more than half the whole matter, and many of the points in question come into view along with it.

We must investigate happiness not only from our conclusion and the data our reasoning uses, but also from what is commonly said about it. All the evidence is in harmony with what is true, while what is false quickly jars with it.

Goods are commonly divided into three classes: external goods, and goods of the soul and of the body. Those belonging to the soul we call good most properly and pre-eminently. In our definition we set the actions and activities of the soul as what constitutes happiness, and these of course belong to the soul. So our account is a good one, at least by this ancient and widely accepted view. Rightly, too, certain actions and activities are said to be the end, since this places happiness among the goods of the soul and not among external goods. Agreeing also with our definition is the common view that a happy person lives well and does well; we have said happiness is pretty much a kind of living well and doing well.
Moreover, all the features we require in happiness turn up together in our account of it.

Some think happiness is virtue; others practical wisdom; others a kind of scientific wisdom. Others say it is these, or one of them, with the addition of pleasure, or at least not without pleasure. Others include external prosperity as well.

Some of these views rest on the authority of many people or of antiquity; others on the authority of a few, though distinguished. It is unlikely that either group is wholly wrong; probably each is right on some points, or even on most.
With those who say happiness is virtue, or a kind of virtue, our account agrees; for activity according to excellence belongs to excellence.

There is perhaps no small difference between conceiving of the chief good as a possession or as a use — that is, as a state or as an activity. The state or habit can exist in a subject without producing any good — in one asleep, for instance, or otherwise inactive. But the activity cannot fail to act, and to act well. Just as at the Olympic games it is not the finest and strongest who are crowned, but those who compete (for from these the prize-winners come); so also in life, it is those among the honorable and the good who act who rightly win the prizes.

Their life, too, is pleasant in itself. Pleasure is a state of mind; and each person finds pleasant what he is said to be fond of. A horse is pleasant to the horse-lover, a show to the show-goer; and likewise just acts to the lover of justice, and more generally things in accordance with virtue to the lover of virtue. Most people find pleasant things that clash with one another, because they are not pleasant by nature; but to the lovers of the noble, those things are pleasant that are so by nature. Acts according to virtue are of this kind, so they are pleasant to those lovers and in themselves.

Their life therefore has no need of pleasure as a sort of additional charm, but contains its pleasure in itself. Besides what I have said, a man is not even good if he does not take pleasure in noble actions. No one would call a man just who does not take pleasure in acting justly, or liberal who does not in liberal actions, and so on with the other virtues. If this is so, then actions in accordance with virtue must be pleasant in themselves. They are also good and noble, and each of these in the highest degree — if we take the judgment of the good man as correct, for he judges as we have said.
Happiness, then, is most excellent, most noble, and most pleasant. These qualities are not separated as in the Delian inscription:
"Most noble is what is most just; best is health; and most pleasant by nature is to win what one desires."
All these belong together to the best activities, and happiness we say consists in these — or in one, the best of them.

Yet happiness plainly does also need external goods added, as we have said. Without suitable resources it is impossible, or at least not easy, to do noble acts. Many things are done by means of friends, wealth, and political influence, as instruments. Lacking certain things mars blessedness — good birth, fine children, even personal beauty. Someone very ugly, or of low birth, or solitary and childless, is not really capable of happiness; still less, perhaps, if he has very bad children or friends, or has lost good ones by death. As I said, the addition of such prosperity does seem necessary to round out the idea of happiness. Hence some identify happiness with good fortune, others with virtue.
This raises the question whether happiness is something that can be learned, or acquired by habituation or other discipline, or whether it comes by divine dispensation, or even by chance.

If any gift of the gods to human beings exists, it is likely that happiness is one, and especially because it is the highest of human goods. But this may belong more properly to a different inquiry. It is clear that even if happiness is not sent directly from the gods, but comes to us through virtue and a certain kind of learning or discipline, it is still among the most godlike things. For the prize and end of virtue is plainly something supremely excellent, even divine and blessed.
On this view happiness will also be widely shared, since it can exist, through learning and diligence of a certain kind, in all who are not disabled in respect of virtue.

And if it is better that we should be happy this way than by chance, there is an argument in itself that it is so. What is in accord with nature, art, and every cause — especially the best cause — is by nature in the best way possible. To leave the greatest and noblest thing to chance would clash greatly with all this.

The question is also settled by our definition: happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with excellence or virtue of a certain kind. Of the other goods, some we must have to begin with, and the ones that cooperate with and serve this activity are given by nature as instruments.

This agrees with what we said at the start: that the end of political science is the highest. Political science takes the greatest care to make the members of the community of a certain character — good, that is, and disposed to do what is noble.

With good reason, then, we do not call any ox, horse, or other brute animal happy; none of them can take part in this kind of activity. For the same reason a child is not happy either, because his age prevents him from doing such actions. If the term is applied to a child, it is by way of anticipation.

For happiness, as we have said, requires complete virtue and a complete life. Many changes and chances of all kinds occur in a life. Someone most prosperous may fall into great misfortunes in old age, as in the old epics the tale is told of Priam. No one calls happy the man who has experienced such a fortune and died in misery.

Are we then to call no one happy while he is alive, and, as Solon would have us, look to the end? And if we maintain this, is a man happy when he is dead? Or is this a complete absurdity, especially for us who say happiness is an activity of a certain kind?

If on the other hand we do not claim the dead are happy, and this is not what Solon meant either, but only that at death one can safely pronounce a man happy since he is now beyond evils and misfortunes, this too is disputable. It is thought that the dead person has some share of good and evil — as one can when alive without being aware of the circumstances — for instance, honor and dishonor, and the good and bad fortune of children and descendants generally.

Yet this view has its own difficulties. After a man has lived in blessedness to old age and died accordingly, many changes may happen to his descendants. Some of them may be good and reach positions fitting their merits, others quite the opposite. Clearly, descendants at different generations may stand in all kinds of relations to their ancestors. It would be absurd if the dead man had to shift with them, becoming at one time happy, and then miserable. Yet it is also absurd that the fortunes of descendants should not affect their ancestors at all, for any time.
But we must return to the first difficulty; the present one will then be easily resolved.

If we must look to the end and only then pronounce a man blessed — not as being blessed now, but as having been so earlier — then surely it is absurd not to assert the truth about a man when he is happy, just because we are unwilling to call the living happy on account of their liability to change. Since we have conceived happiness as something stable and not easily changed, while good and bad fortune keep circling about the same people, it is clear that if we depend on their fortunes, we will often call the same man happy, then a little later miserable — presenting our happy man as,
"Chameleon-like, and built on rottenness."

Is not this the answer? It is wrong to let our judgment depend on the changes of fortune. Human welfare or misery does not consist in these, though human life needs them as accessories, as we have allowed. What determine happiness are the activities in accordance with virtue; and the opposite activities determine the opposite.

The present question, incidentally, bears witness to the truth of our account of happiness. Nothing among human affairs has so much stability as the activities in accordance with virtue. They are thought more lasting even than the sciences. And among these activities, the most precious are the most lasting, because the blessed live in them most and most continuously; which seems to be why they are not forgotten. The stability we are looking for, then, will belong to the happy man. He will be happy throughout his life, since he will always, or mostly, be doing and contemplating the things of virtue. He will bear the various chances of life most nobly, and always and in every way harmoniously, since he is the truly good man, or, in the phrase of our proverb, "foursquare beyond reproach."

Chance events are many and vary in size. Small pieces of good or bad fortune clearly do not tip the balance of life. But great and numerous ones, if they go well, will make life more blessed, since by their nature they add ornament and their use is noble and excellent. If they go badly, they bruise and mar blessedness; they bring real pain and hinder many activities. Even here, though, nobility shines through when a man bears with contentment many and great misfortunes — not from insensitivity to pain, but because he is noble and high-spirited.

If, as we have said, it is the activities that determine the character of life, no blessed man can ever become wretched. He will never do things that are hateful and mean. The man who is truly good and sensible bears all fortunes becomingly and always does what is noblest in the circumstances — just as a good general makes the best use of the forces he has, or a good cobbler makes the best shoe out of the leather given him, and so with all good craftsmen. If so, the happy man can never become wretched. I do not mean he will be blessed even if he meets the fortunes of Priam.

He will not be fickle or easily changed. He will not be shaken from his happiness by ordinary mischances, but only, if at all, by those that are great and numerous. After such misfortunes he cannot recover his happiness in a short time; he must do so, if at all, over a long and complete span, during which he has attained to great and noble things.

Why then should we not call happy the man who is active in accordance with complete virtue and is furnished with external goods sufficient to play his part in the drama of life — and this over no ordinary period, but over a complete life such as we have described?

Or must we add that he is to live so, and his death must be in keeping with such a life, since the future is dark to us and we assume happiness is in every way an end and complete? If so, we call blessed those among the living who have and will have the things we have specified — but blessed as humans.
Let this suffice on these points.
That the fortunes of descendants and friends contribute nothing at all to the condition of the dead seems a very heartless notion, and contrary to common opinions.

Since the things that happen are many and differ in all sorts of ways, with some touching us more closely and others less, to go into minute distinctions would be a long and endless task. It may be enough to speak in general outline.

If of the misfortunes that happen to a man himself, some carry weight and turn the balance of his life while others are, so to speak, lighter, and if the same holds for those befalling all his friends; and if further, whether the sufferer be alive or dead makes a much greater difference than it does in a tragedy whether crimes and horrors are presupposed or enacted on stage — then we must take this difference also into account. And still more, perhaps, the doubt whether the dead really partake of any good or evil. From all this it seems to follow that if anything does reach them, good or bad, it must be something slight — either in itself or to them — or at least of such a size and kind as neither to make happy those who are not, nor to deprive of their blessedness those who are.
The good or bad fortunes of their friends, then, do affect the dead somewhat — but in a kind and degree that neither makes the happy unhappy nor produces any other such effect.

Having settled these points, let us examine, in regard to happiness, whether it belongs to the class of things that are praiseworthy or to the class of things that are precious; it clearly does not belong to the class of mere capacities.

Everything praised is praised for being of a certain kind and bearing a certain relation to something else. We praise the just man, the brave man, and the good man generally, and virtue itself, because of the actions and results. We praise the strong man or the swift runner for being of a certain nature and standing in a certain relation to something good and excellent. This is shown by attempts to praise the gods: they come off looking ridiculous when measured by our standard, because all praise, as we have said, implies reference to a standard. If praise applies to such objects, then what applies to the best objects is not praise, but something higher and better. This is clear in fact: we call the gods blessed and happy, and among men we call blessed those most godlike. So also with goods: no one thinks of praising happiness as he does justice; rather, he calls it blessed, as being something more godlike and excellent.

Eudoxus too is thought to have given a good argument for pleasure's claim to the highest prize. He took it as a sign of pleasure's superiority to the things that are subjects of praise that, though it is among the good things, it is not itself praised. He attributed the same superiority to a god and to the chief good, on the ground that they are the standard to which everything else is referred. Praise belongs to virtue, because virtue makes men apt to do what is noble; encomia belong to definite achievements of body or soul.

To pursue this topic more exactly probably belongs to a treatise on encomia. For our purposes, it is enough that from what has been said it is clear happiness belongs to the class of things precious and final. It also seems so because it is a starting-point; it is with a view to happiness that we all do everything else. The starting-point and cause of good things we take to be something precious and divine.

Moreover, since happiness is a kind of activity of the soul in accordance with complete excellence, we must consider excellence. This will probably also give us a clearer view of happiness. The true statesman is generally thought to have taken the most pains about this; he wishes to make the citizens good and obedient to the laws. Examples are the lawgivers of the Cretans and Spartans, and any others there may have been. If this inquiry belongs to political science, then our investigation falls in line with our original plan.
We are to inquire about excellence — that is, human excellence — since it was the human good and human happiness we were investigating.
By human excellence we mean not the excellence of the body, but of the soul; for we call happiness an activity of the soul.

If this is so, it is plain that the statesman must have some knowledge of the nature of the soul — just as the eye doctor must know about the whole body, and all the more so since political science is more precious and higher than medicine. Indeed physicians of the higher class devote much time to knowledge of the body.

So the statesman must consider the nature of the soul, but with his own objects in view, and only so far as is sufficient for them. To go into greater exactness would be a task more laborious than belongs to his province.

The few statements on the subject in my popular treatises are enough, and we will use them here. The soul, it is said, has two parts: the irrational and the rational. (Whether these are actually separated like parts of the body, or are only conceptually two while naturally inseparable — like the convex and concave sides of a curve — does not matter for our present purpose.) Of the irrational, one part seems common to other living things and is vegetative: I mean the cause of nutrition and growth. One would assume such a faculty of the soul to be in everything that takes in nourishment, including embryos, and the same in them as in fully formed creatures (which is more likely than that it should be different).

The excellence of this vegetative part is clearly not peculiar to humans but common to other creatures. This part and its faculty seem most active in sleep, and the good and bad man are hardest to distinguish while asleep. Hence the common saying that for half of life there is no difference between the happy and the wretched. This accords with our view: sleep is an inactivity of the soul insofar as the soul is called good or bad — except that some movements find a way through the veil, so that good men come to have better dreams than ordinary men. But this is enough: we need not say more about the nutritive part, since by its nature it admits no excellence that is peculiarly human.

There seems to be another irrational part of the soul, which yet in a way partakes of reason. In the self-controlled man, and in the man who resolves to act well but fails, we praise the reason or rational part of the soul, because it exhorts rightly and to the best course. But clearly there is in them, besides the reason, another natural principle that fights against reason and strains against it. Just as paralyzed limbs of the body, when their owners try to move them to the right, are carried instead to the left, so it is with the soul. The impulses of those who cannot control their appetites pull in opposite directions. The difference is that in the body we see the aberrant motion, while in the soul we do not. We should still suppose, though, that in the soul too there is something besides reason, opposed to it and going against it. Exactly how it is different need not concern us here.

This other part evidently also partakes of reason, as we have said. In the self-controlled man it obeys reason; and in the man of perfected self-mastery, or the brave man, it is perhaps still more obedient — in them it agrees entirely with reason.

So the irrational is plainly twofold. The merely vegetative has no share of reason. But the appetitive, or the desiring part generally, does partake of reason in a sense, insofar as it is obedient to reason and capable of submitting to its rule. (In ordinary speech we talk of having "a word" of our father or friends — in a different sense from having "a word" of mathematics.)

That the irrational is in some way persuaded by reason is shown by admonition and every kind of rebuke and exhortation. If we are to say that this part also has reason, then the rational part, as well as the irrational, will be twofold: one having reason strictly and in itself; the other giving it a kind of filial regard.

Human excellence is divided along this distinction. We make two classes, calling one intellectual and the other moral. Pure science, intelligence, and practical wisdom are intellectual excellences; liberality and perfected self-mastery are moral excellences. In speaking of a man's moral character, we do not call him scientific or intelligent, but meek, or one of perfected self-mastery. We praise the man of science for his state of mind; and such states of mind as are praiseworthy we call excellences.

chapters.title: Book 2 — Moral Virtue
paragraphs: Human excellence, then, is of two kinds: intellectual and moral. Intellectual excellence is chiefly produced and increased by teaching, and so requires experience and time. Moral excellence, by contrast, comes from habit; the Greek word for it (ēthikē) is in fact only a slight variation on the word for custom (ethos).

From this it is plain that none of the moral virtues arises in us by nature. Nothing that exists by nature can be changed by habit. A stone, which by nature falls downward, cannot be trained by habit to rise, not even if you tossed it upward ten thousand times. Fire cannot be trained to descend. Nothing whose nature is in one way can by habit be brought to be in another. The virtues, then, do not come to us by nature, nor against nature; rather, we are equipped by nature with the capacity to receive them, and this capacity is perfected by habit.

Again, where we get capacities by nature, we possess the faculty first and perform the activities afterwards. The bodily senses are a clear example: it was not from having often seen or heard that we got these senses, but the reverse — we had them and then exercised them, not the other way around. But the virtues we get by first performing the actions. It is the same with the arts: what we have to learn to make, we learn to make by making. People become builders by building, harpists by playing the harp. In the same way, by doing just acts we become just, by doing acts of self-control we become self-controlled, and by doing brave acts we become brave.

This is confirmed by what happens in communities. Lawgivers make their citizens good by habituating them, and this is what every lawgiver intends; those who do not do it well miss their aim. And this is what separates a good constitution from a bad one.

Every virtue is both produced and destroyed by the same circumstances. So is every art. It is by playing the harp that both good and bad harpists are made, and similarly with builders and all the rest: by building well men become good builders, by building badly, bad ones. If this were not so, there would be no need of teachers; everyone would be naturally good or bad at his craft.

So too with the virtues. By our actions in dealings with other people, some of us become just, others unjust. By our actions in the face of danger, being habituated to feel fear or confidence, some become brave and others cowards.

It is the same with situations involving desire and anger. Some come to be self-controlled and even-tempered, others without self-control and hot-headed, according to how they behave in such situations. In a word, habits are produced from activities like them. Our task, then, is to give a certain character to these activities, since habits correspond to the differences in them.
Whether we are habituated in one way or another from childhood, then, makes not a small but a very great difference — or rather, it makes all the difference.

Since the aim of the present treatise is not mere speculation, as with some others (we are inquiring not just to know what virtue is but to become good; otherwise the study would be pointless), we must ask how to perform actions; for, as I just said, the quality of the resulting habits depends on this.

That we should act in accordance with right reason is a general maxim, and may be granted for the present. We will speak of it later — what right reason is, and how it is related to the other virtues.

But let this be understood between us from the start: everything said about moral action must be in outline, not with precision. As I remarked at the beginning, only the precision the subject allows should be expected. Matters of moral action and expediency have no more fixedness than matters of health. And if general statements are imprecise, even less can we be exact in applying them to particular cases. Particular cases fall under no art or fixed system of rules; in each case agents must look at the particulars themselves, just as in medicine or navigation. So though our subject is confessedly such, we must do what we can with it.

First, note this: it is the nature of such things to be spoiled by deficiency and by excess. We see this with health and strength (we must use visible examples to illustrate the invisible). Too much training ruins strength, and so does too little. Food and drink in too great or too small quantities ruin health; in due proportion they produce, increase, and preserve it.

So it is with the habits of self-mastery, courage, and the other virtues. The man who flees from and fears everything, standing up to nothing, becomes a coward. The man who fears nothing and goes at everything becomes rash. In the same way, one who tastes every pleasure and refrains from none loses all self-control, while one who avoids all pleasure, like the dull and boorish, becomes insensible. Self-mastery and courage are spoiled by excess and deficiency, but preserved by the mean.

Moreover, not only do habits originate, grow, and decay from and by the same circumstances; the activities they produce are also exercised on these same circumstances. So it is with strength, for instance: it comes by taking plenty of food and doing plenty of work, and the man who has attained strength is best able to do these very things. So with the virtues: by abstaining from pleasures we become self-controlled, and once we are so, we are best able to abstain from them. So with courage: by habituating ourselves to despise and face objects of fear we become brave, and once brave we are best able to face such objects.

As a test of whether the habits have been formed, we must take the pleasure or pain that follows the act. The self-controlled man not only abstains from bodily pleasures but is glad to do so; the man who abstains but is sorry to has no self-mastery. The brave man faces danger either with positive pleasure or at least without pain; the one who does it with pain is not brave.

Moral virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains. For because of pleasure we do what is bad, and because of pain we avoid what is right. This is why, as Plato observes, people should be trained from childhood to feel pleasure and pain at the proper objects; this is what right education is. Further: since the virtues have to do with actions and feelings, and every feeling and action is followed by pleasure or pain, here is another proof that virtue concerns pleasure and pain. The same is shown by the fact that punishments work through these; punishments are a kind of cure, and cures are by nature contraries of the ills they heal. To repeat what we said before: every habit of the soul, by its nature, bears on and exerts itself upon the same things by which it is naturally made better or worse. Such habits become vicious because of pleasures and pains — people pursuing or avoiding them when they should not, or at the wrong time, or in the wrong way. For this reason some define the virtues as states of impassivity and utter quietude; but they are wrong, because they speak without qualification, not adding "as one ought," "as one ought not," "when," and so on. Virtue, then, is a habit so related to pleasures and pains as to produce the best results, and vice is its contrary.

Consider the matter also in this way. There are principally three things that move us to choice and three to avoidance: the noble, the expedient, and the pleasant; and their three contraries: the base, the harmful, and the painful. The good man tends to go right, and the bad to go wrong, with respect to all of these — but especially with respect to pleasure. Pleasure is not only common to us and all animals; it is also a concomitant of everything that moves us to choice, since the noble and the expedient both give an impression of pleasure.
Moreover, pleasure grows up with us from infancy, so it is difficult to remove this feeling, engrained as it is into our very life.

We also adopt pleasure and pain (some of us more, some less) as the measure even of actions. All our work, therefore, must be with them; to receive right or wrong impressions of pleasure and pain is no small matter for conduct. Again, as Heraclitus says, it is harder to fight against pleasure than against anger. Art, and virtue too, arise in connection with what is more than usually difficult, since the good is of a higher order precisely where the task is hard. For this reason both virtue and moral philosophy in general must wholly occupy themselves with pleasures and pains; he who uses them well will be good, and he who uses them badly will be bad.

Let this, then, be our position: that virtue concerns pleasures and pains, and that the same circumstances (used differently) by which it is originally produced, also increase or mar it, and that its activity is exercised on the very circumstances out of which it came to be.

Now one might be perplexed by our claim that people become just by doing just acts and self-controlled by doing acts of self-control. One might say: if people are doing the actions, they must already have the virtues — just as people who do grammatical or musical acts are already grammarians or musicians. May we not reply that it is not quite so even in the case of those arts? A man may produce something grammatical either by chance or on someone else's suggestion. He will be a grammarian only when he not only produces something grammatical but does so in the manner of a grammarian — that is, in virtue of the grammatical knowledge he himself possesses.

Besides, the cases of the arts and the virtues are not parallel. Things produced by the arts have their excellence in themselves; it is enough that they turn out a certain way. But in the case of the virtues, the actions are not just of a certain kind (of justice, say, or of self-mastery); they must also be done by an agent who is in a certain state — first, knowing what he is doing; second, choosing the acts deliberately, and choosing them for their own sakes; and third, doing them from a stable and unchanging character. For the possession of an art, these requirements do not count, except the knowledge. For the possession of the virtues, knowledge counts for little or nothing; the other requirements count for much — in fact, are all in all — and they come from repeatedly doing acts of justice and self-mastery.

The acts are called just or self-controlled when they are such as a just or self-controlled man would do. But a man does not possess the virtues merely by doing these acts; he must do them in the way the just and self-controlled do them.

We are right, then, to say that these virtues are formed by doing the actions, and that without doing them a man will not even be on the way to being good. But most people do not perform these actions. They take refuge in talk and flatter themselves that they are philosophizing and will in this way become good — behaving much like sick people who listen attentively to the doctor but do none of what he prescribes. Just as those cannot get well in body under such treatment, these cannot get well in soul by such philosophizing.
Next, we must examine what virtue is. Since what comes to be in the soul is of three kinds — feelings, capacities, and states — virtue must belong to one of these three classes.

By feelings I mean such things as desire, anger, fear, confidence, envy, joy, love, hate, longing, emulation, pity — in short, all that are accompanied by pleasure or pain. By capacities I mean those in virtue of which we are said to be capable of these feelings: that is, of having become angry, or pained, or pitiful. By states I mean those in virtue of which we stand in some relation, well or badly, to the feelings mentioned. In relation to anger, for instance, we stand badly if we feel it too violently or too slackly, but well if we feel it in the mean. Similarly with the rest.
The virtues and vices are not feelings. We are not called good or bad in virtue of the feelings, but in virtue of the virtues and vices.

Again, we are neither praised nor blamed in virtue of the feelings — a man is not commended for being afraid or angry, nor blamed for being angry simply, but for being angry in a particular way. But in virtue of the virtues and vices we are praised or blamed.
Again, we feel anger and fear without deliberate choice, whereas the virtues are choices, or at any rate not independent of choice.
Moreover, with respect to the feelings we are said to be moved; with respect to the virtues and vices, not to be moved, but to be disposed in a certain way.
For these same reasons the virtues are not capacities either. We are not called good or bad simply because we are able to feel, nor are we praised or blamed for it.
Moreover, we have the capacities by nature, but we do not become good or bad by nature, as we said earlier.
Since the virtues are neither feelings nor capacities, it remains that they must be states.
We have now said what the genus of virtue is. But we must not merely say it is a state; we must also say what kind of state.

Observe, then, that every excellence both makes its possessor good and enables it to perform its function well. The excellence of the eye makes the eye good and makes it see well; the excellence of the horse makes the horse good — good at running, carrying its rider, and facing the enemy. If this holds universally, then the excellence of the human being — that is, virtue — must be a state that makes him good and enables him to perform his proper function well. How this happens has been said already, but it may also clarify things to consider the distinguishing nature of virtue.

In everything continuous or discrete, one can take a greater part, a smaller part, or an equal part — and these either with reference to the thing itself or relatively to us. The equal part is a mean between excess and deficiency. By the mean in the thing itself — the absolute mean — I mean what is equidistant from either extreme, which is one and the same for everyone. By the mean relative to us, I mean what is neither too much nor too little for the particular person — which is not one and the same for all. If ten is too much and two is too little, for example, people take six as the absolute mean; it exceeds the smaller by exactly as much as it is exceeded by the larger — an arithmetical proportion.

But the mean relative to us is not to be found in this way. If ten pounds of food is too much for someone and two too little, it does not follow that a trainer will order six pounds. That too may be too much or too little for the particular eater. For Milo it would be too little; for a man just beginning his training, too much. Likewise with exercises such as running or wrestling.
Every skilled person, then, avoids excess and deficiency and seeks out the mean — not the absolute mean, but the one relative to us.

If every skill does its work well by keeping its eye on the mean and bringing its product to this point (hence the common remark of well-made things: "one can neither add to them nor take away," since excess and deficiency destroy goodness while the mean preserves it), and if good craftsmen, as we say, work with their eye on this, and if excellence, like nature, is more exact and better than any art, then excellence must aim at the mean.

I mean moral excellence, of course — virtue. For it is virtue that is concerned with feelings and actions, and these admit of excess, deficiency, and the mean. For instance, one can feel fear, confidence, desire, anger, pity, and pleasure and pain generally, too much or too little, and both are wrong. To feel them when we ought, on the right occasions, toward the right people, for the right reasons, and in the right way — that is the mean, which is the best, and the property of virtue.

Likewise with actions there is excess, deficiency, and the mean. Virtue is concerned with feelings and actions in which excess is wrong and deficiency is blamed, while the mean is praised and correct. Both being praised and hitting the right course belong to virtue. Virtue, then, is in a sense a mean state, since it aims at the mean.

Further, one can go wrong in many different ways (since, as the Pythagoreans put it, evil belongs to the infinite, good to the finite), but one can go right in only one. So going wrong is easy, going right difficult; easy to miss the mark, hard to hit it. For these reasons too excess and deficiency belong to vice, and the mean to virtue. As the poet has it:
"Men may be bad in many ways, but good in one alone."
Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean relative to us, determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine it.

It is a mean between two vices — one of excess, one of deficiency. And it is so because vices fall short of or overshoot what is right in both feelings and actions, while virtue finds and chooses the mean.
So in respect of its essence and the account of its nature, virtue is a mean state; but in reference to the chief good and to excellence, it is the highest possible state.

But not every action or every feeling admits of a mean. Some are named in such a way as to convey badness already — spite, shamelessness, envy; and among actions, adultery, theft, murder. All of these and similar things are blamed because they are themselves bad, not because too much or too little of them is bad.

In these there is no going right; one is always wrong. Rightness or wrongness here does not depend on picking the right person, time, or manner — as with adultery, say; simply to do any such thing is to be wrong.

You might as well demand that there be a mean, an excess, and a deficiency with respect to acting unjustly, behaving as a coward, or giving up self-control entirely. At that rate there would be a mean of excess and deficiency, an excess of excess, and a deficiency of deficiency.

But just as there is no excess or deficiency of self-mastery or courage, because the mean is in one sense the highest state possible, so of those faulty states there can be no mean, no excess, and no deficiency. However done, they are wrong. In general: there can be no mean of excess and deficiency, nor any excess or deficiency of the mean.

It is not enough, however, to state this in general terms; we must also apply it to particular cases. In treatises on moral conduct, general statements have an air of vagueness, while detailed ones carry more conviction. Actions are always about particulars, and general statements must hold good in the particulars to be worth anything.
Let us take these details from the familiar table of virtues.
I. In respect of fears and confidence:

The mean state is courage. Men may exceed either in fearlessness or in positive confidence: the former has no name (as often), the latter is called rashness. The man who has too much fear and too little confidence is called a coward.
II. In respect of pleasures and pains (though not all of them, and perhaps fewer pains than pleasures):

The mean state is self-mastery; the excess, self-indulgence. As for deficiency with respect to pleasure, there are really no such people, so there is really no name for them. But as it is at least conceivable, let us call them insensible.
III. In respect of giving and taking wealth (a):

The mean state is liberality; the excess, prodigality; the deficiency, stinginess. Each extreme involves, in fact, an excess and a deficiency contrary to each other: the prodigal gives out too much and takes in too little, while the stingy man takes in too much and gives out too little. (Understand that we are giving only an outline and summary; we will draw the distinctions more precisely later.)
IV. In respect of wealth (b):

There are other dispositions besides these: a mean state called munificence (the munificent man differs from the liberal man, the former necessarily dealing with great wealth, the latter with small); the excess called either tastelessness or vulgar ostentation; and the deficiency, paltriness. These too differ from the extremes connected with liberality, and the manner of difference will be discussed later.
V. In respect of honor and dishonor (a):
The mean state is greatness of soul; the excess is what we may call vanity; the deficiency, smallness of soul.
VI. In respect of honor and dishonor (b):

There is also a state standing to greatness of soul as liberality stands to munificence: concerned with small honor, as greatness of soul is concerned with great honor. A man may grasp at honor either more or less than he should. The one who exceeds is called ambitious; the one who falls short, unambitious; the one in the mean has no proper name. Nor in fact do the states, except that the disposition of the ambitious man is called ambition. For this reason those at either extreme lay claim to the middle ground as a disputed territory, and we call the virtuous character sometimes ambitious, sometimes unambitious, and we commend sometimes one, sometimes the other. Why we do this will be discussed later; for now let us continue with the other virtues on the plan we have laid down.
VII. In respect of anger:

Here too there is excess, deficiency, and a mean state; but since these have no proper names, and we call the virtuous character meek, we will call the mean state meekness. Of the extremes, let the man who is excessive be called passionate and his state passionateness; the deficient man, spiritless, and his state spiritlessness.

There are also three other mean states, resembling each other somewhat but differing; they are alike in that they all concern intercourse of words and deeds, but they differ in that one has to do with truth, and the other two with what is pleasant — one in the form of relaxation and amusement, the other in all things encountered in daily life. We must say something about these also, so that we may see more clearly that in all cases the mean is praiseworthy, while the extremes are neither right nor worthy of praise but of blame.
Most of these have no proper names, but we must try, as in the other cases, to coin some for the sake of clarity and intelligibility.
I. In respect of truth:

The man in the mean state we will call truthful, and his state truthfulness. As for the disguise of truth: if in the direction of exaggeration, let us call it boastfulness and the man a boaster; if in the direction of understatement, reserve, and the man reserved.
II. In respect of what is pleasant in relaxation or amusement:

The mean state we will call easy-pleasantry, and the character accordingly a man of easy-pleasantry; the excess, buffoonery, and the man a buffoon; the man deficient in this, a boor, and his state boorishness.
III. In respect of what is pleasant in daily life:

The man who is as he should be may be called friendly, and his mean state friendliness. He who exceeds, if without any interested motive, is overly obliging; if with such a motive, a flatterer. He who is deficient, and in all cases unpleasant, is quarrelsome and cross.

There are mean states also in feelings and matters connected with them. Modesty, for instance, is not a virtue, yet a man is praised for being modest. For here too one person is said to be in the mean, another in the excess. The bashful man, who is overwhelmed with shame at every occasion, is in the excess; the man who has no shame at all is called shameless; the right character is modest.

Righteous indignation at undeserved success is a mean state between envy and malice. All three have to do with pleasure and pain at what befalls one's neighbor. The man who has this right feeling is pained by undeserved success of others; the envious man, exceeding him, is pained at all success of others; the malicious man falls so short of feeling any pain that he even rejoices — at the misfortunes of others.

But the discussion of these also belongs to another place, as does that of justice, because the word is used in more than one sense. After finishing this outline we will go into each in detail and say how they are mean states; and likewise with the intellectual excellences.

Since there are three states in each case — two faulty ones (excess and deficiency) and one right one, the mean — all are in a way opposed to one another. The extremes are opposed not only to the mean but to each other, and the mean is opposed to the extremes. Just as the half is greater than the smaller part and smaller than the greater, so the mean states, compared with the deficiencies, exceed, whether in feelings or actions; and the reverse when compared with the excesses. The brave man appears rash compared with the coward, and cowardly compared with the rash. The self-controlled man appears dissolute to the insensible, and insensible to the dissolute. The liberal man appears prodigal to the stingy, and stingy to the prodigal.

So the extreme characters push the man in the mean toward each other. The coward calls the brave man rash; the rash man calls him a coward; and so on. Given this mutual opposition, the contrariety between the extremes is greater than between either of them and the mean. They stand further from each other than from the mean, just as the greater and the smaller portions differ more from each other than either does from the exact half.

Again, in some cases an extreme bears a certain resemblance to the mean. Rashness, for instance, resembles courage; prodigality resembles liberality. But between the extremes themselves there is the greatest dissimilarity. Things furthest from one another are defined as contrary; so the further apart they are, the more contrary.

Further, of the two extremes, sometimes the excess is more opposed to the mean, and sometimes the deficiency. To courage, for instance, it is not rashness (the excess) but cowardice (the deficiency) that is most opposed. To self-mastery, it is not insensibility (the deficiency) but self-indulgence (the excess) that is most opposed.

Two reasons can be given for this. One is from the nature of the thing itself: because one extreme is nearer and more similar to the mean, we set against the mean not that one, but the other. Since rashness is thought nearer to courage and more like it than cowardice is, we oppose courage rather to cowardice; things further from the mean are thought more contrary to it. The second reason is from our own constitution: the extreme to which we individually have a natural bias seems more contrary to the mean in our own case. We have a natural bias toward pleasures, for which reason we are more inclined to lose all self-control than to practice self-discipline.
The states toward which we are biased, then, we call more contrary. For this reason too, total self-indulgence (the excess) is more contrary than insensibility (the deficiency) to self-mastery.

That moral virtue is a mean state, and how it is so, and that it lies between two faulty states — one of excess and one of deficiency — and that this is so because it aims at the mean in both feelings and actions: all this has now been fully and sufficiently set out.

And so it is hard to be good. It is hard in every instance to find the mean — just as finding the center of a circle is not something anyone can do, but only one who knows. So too, any man can get angry, give money, or spend lavishly — that is easy. But to do these to the right person, in due proportion, at the right time, for the right purpose, and in the right way — this is not something anyone can do, nor is it easy. That is why goodness is rare and praiseworthy and noble.
He who aims at the mean must first take care to steer clear of the extreme more contrary to it, just as Calypso in Homer advises Odysseus,
"Keep your ship clear of this smoke and surge."

Of the two extremes, one is always more erroneous, the other less so. Since it is difficult to hit exactly on the mean, we must take the least of the evils, as the safest plan; and this will be done by the method here described.

We should also take account of our own natural bias, which varies from person to person and can be known from the pleasures and pains that arise in us. We should force ourselves off in the contrary direction; for we shall reach the mean by removing ourselves far from the worse side, just as men straighten bent timber.
In all cases, we must guard most carefully against what is pleasant, against pleasure itself, because we are not impartial judges of it.
We ought to feel about pleasure as the elders of Troy felt about Helen, and pronounce a similar judgment in every case: by sending it away, we will err the less.
In brief, these are the precautions by which we shall best be able to attain the mean.

Still, it is a difficult matter, especially in particular cases. It is not easy, for instance, to determine exactly in what manner, with what persons, for what causes, and for how long one ought to feel anger. Sometimes we praise those deficient in this feeling and call them meek; at other times we call the hot-tempered manly and spirited.

Again, the man who makes a small deviation from what is right, either by excess or deficiency, is not blamed; only the one who makes a considerable one, since his deviation cannot be overlooked. But to what degree or kind a man must err to incur blame is not easy to determine in words, any more than any other matter of moral perception. Such questions belong to the particulars, and the decision rests with moral perception.

At any rate this much is plain: that the mean state is in all things praiseworthy; and that we must sometimes lean toward excess, sometimes toward deficiency, because this will be the easiest way to hit the mean — that is, what is right.

chapters.title: Book 3 — Moral Responsibility and Particular Virtues
paragraphs: Since virtue is concerned with the regulation of feelings and actions, and since praise and blame apply to what is voluntary while allowance, and sometimes pity, is made for the involuntary, it is perhaps a necessary task for anyone investigating virtue to draw the distinction between the voluntary and the involuntary. It is also useful for legislators in assigning honors and punishments.

Involuntary actions are thought to be of two kinds: those done under compulsion, and those done through ignorance. An action is properly compulsory when its origin lies outside the agent — such that the agent (or, better, the patient) contributes nothing — as when a wind carries you somewhere, or men who have you in their power do.

But when actions are done either from fear of greater evils, or from some noble motive — for instance, if a tyrant holding your parents or children ordered you to commit some shameful act, and compliance would save them while refusal would kill them — in such cases there is room to ask whether the actions are voluntary or involuntary.

A similar question arises with throwing goods overboard in a storm. In the abstract no one throws away his property willingly; but with a view to his own and his shipmates' safety, any sensible man would.

The truth is that such actions are mixed, but they are more like voluntary ones. They are worth choosing at the moment they are done; and the end of an action must be taken with reference to the actual occasion. Further, we must call an action voluntary or involuntary at the time it is done. In the given case the man acts voluntarily, because the origin of the motion of his limbs rests with him; and where the origin is in himself, it rests with him to do or not to do.
Such actions are voluntary, then, though in the abstract perhaps involuntary, since no one would choose any of them by itself.

For such actions men are sometimes even praised, when they endure some disgrace or pain for a great and noble equivalent. Conversely they are blamed; for it shows a base mind to endure things extremely disgraceful for no noble object, or for a trifling one.
For some acts no praise is given, but allowance is made — when a man does what he should not from things that overstrain human nature or pass the limits of human endurance.
Some acts, however, cannot be excused by compulsion; a man should rather suffer the worst and die. How absurd the pleas of compulsion with which Alcmaeon in Euripides' play excuses his matricide!

It is sometimes difficult to decide what sort of thing should be chosen in place of what, or endured in preference to what — and still more difficult to abide by one's decisions. The alternatives are generally painful and the actions required base, so praise or blame is awarded according to whether a person has been compelled or not.

What kind of actions, then, are to be called compulsory? We may say: simply and abstractedly, those whose cause is external and to which the agent contributes nothing. Where the acts in themselves are such as one would not wish but are worth choosing at the present moment and in preference to certain alternatives, and the origin rests with the agent, the actions are in themselves involuntary but, at the given time and in preference to those alternatives, voluntary. They are more like voluntary actions than involuntary, because actions consist in details, and these details are voluntary.
But what sort of things one ought to choose instead of what is not easy to settle, since there are many differences in particular cases.

Suppose someone said that pleasant and noble things exert a compelling force, since they are external and do compel us. At that rate every action would be on compulsion, since these are universal motives.
Besides, those who act on compulsion and against their will do so with pain, while those who act for the sake of what is pleasant or noble act with pleasure.

It is absurd to attribute one's actions to external things, rather than to one's own ready capacity to be captivated by them; or to take credit for one's noble actions while blaming pleasure for the base ones.
So what is compulsory seems to be whatever has its origin from outside, the compelled party contributing nothing.

Now every action done through ignorance is non-voluntary; but only that is involuntary which is attended with pain and regret. Someone who has done something through ignorance but is not distressed at his own action cannot be said to have done it with his will, because he did not know he was doing it; but neither against his will, because he is not sorry for it.

So within the class of those who act through ignorance, the one who feels regret afterwards is counted as an involuntary agent. The one who feels no regret we will call a non-voluntary agent, since he is genuinely different; where there is a real difference, it is better to have a proper name.

There also seems to be a difference between acting because of ignorance and acting with ignorance. We do not usually give ignorance as the cause of the actions of the drunken or angry man, but drunkenness or anger; yet he acts not knowingly, but with ignorance.
Moreover, every bad man is ignorant of what he ought to do and what to leave undone. Through such error men become unjust and generally evil.

We do not usually apply the term "involuntary" when a man is ignorant of his own true interest. Ignorance affecting moral choice constitutes depravity, not involuntariness. Nor does ignorance of principles count as involuntary (for men are blamed for such ignorance); it is ignorance of particular circumstances in which the action consists and with which it is concerned, where there is both pity and allowance, because he who acts in ignorance of these acts involuntarily in the proper sense.

It may be useful, then, to define these particular circumstances — what they are, and how many. Namely: who acts, what he is doing, with respect to what or in what, sometimes with what (as with what instrument), and with what result (for example, for preservation), and how (whether gently or violently).

No sane man could be ignorant of all these particulars in one and the same case — and clearly not of the agent, being himself. But he may be ignorant of what he is doing. Speakers sometimes say a thing slipped out unawares; or Aeschylus was supposed not to have realized it was unlawful to speak of the Mysteries; or the man in that recent catapult accident said he fired it merely to demonstrate it. One might suppose one's son to be an enemy, as Merope did; take a sharpened spear for a practice one; think a real stone was pumice; strike to save and kill instead; or strike thinking to give a demonstration, as in sham fighting.

Since ignorance is possible with respect to all these particulars that make up the action, one who acted in ignorance of any of them is thought to have acted involuntarily — most of all if he was ignorant of the most important, which are thought to be those in which the action consists, and the result.
Further, to make an action involuntary, the ignorance must be of this kind; and it must also be understood that the action is followed by pain and regret.

Since every involuntary action is either on compulsion or through ignorance, voluntary action would seem to be that whose origin is in the agent, the agent being aware of the particular circumstances in which the action consists.
It may not be right to call actions involuntary when they are done from anger or appetite.
