In the first place, if it were so, no other animal besides man could act voluntarily — nor even children. Next, are we to say we never act voluntarily when acting from appetite or anger? Or that we act voluntarily in doing what is right and involuntarily in doing what is disgraceful? The latter is absurd, since the cause is one and the same. As for the former, it is strange to call involuntary actions we are bound to reach for; there are occasions when anger is a duty, and things we are bound to desire (health, for instance, and learning).
Again, strictly involuntary actions are thought to be attended with pain, but actions done to gratify appetite are thought to be pleasant.

Further: what difference is there, in point of involuntariness, between wrong acts done from deliberate calculation and those done from anger? Both should be avoided. And the irrational feelings are thought no less natural to man than reason; so actions done from anger and appetite must equally belong to the individual. It is absurd, then, to class these actions among the involuntary.

Having drawn the distinction between voluntary and involuntary action, our next step is to examine the nature of moral choice. This seems more intimately connected with virtue, and a better test of character, than actions are.

Moral choice is clearly voluntary, but the two terms are not co-extensive; voluntary is the broader term. Children and other animals share in voluntary action but not in moral choice; and sudden actions we call voluntary but do not ascribe to moral choice.

Nor is moral choice the same as appetite, anger, wish, or any sort of opinion, as some have said. For in the first place, irrational animals have appetite and anger but not moral choice. Next, the man who fails in self-control acts from appetite, not moral choice; the self-controlled man from moral choice, not appetite. Again, appetite is often opposed to moral choice, but not to appetite itself.

Lastly, the object of appetite is the pleasant and the painful, but of moral choice neither. Still less can moral choice be anger, since actions done from anger are generally thought to be the least results of deliberate choice.

Nor is it wish, though wish seems closely related. For moral choice cannot have impossibilities as its objects; if a man said he chose them, he would be thought a fool. But wish may have impossibilities as objects — immortality, for instance.

Wish may also be directed at things one could do nothing to achieve oneself, such as the victory of a particular actor or athlete. But no one chooses such things, only those he believes he can himself help bring about.

Further, wish has the end rather as its object, while moral choice has the means to the end. We wish to be healthy, but we choose the means that will make us so. We wish to be happy — we commonly say so — but to say we choose happiness is not quite right; for moral choice seems to be concerned with what is in our own power.

Nor can it be opinion. Opinion is thought to range without limit, over eternal and impossible things as well as over what is in our own power. Opinion is divided logically into true and false, not into good and bad like moral choice.

No one perhaps maintains that moral choice is identical with opinion as such; but it is not even identical with opinion of any particular kind. For by choosing good or bad things we come to be of a certain character, but by having opinions about them we do not.
Again, we choose to take or avoid and the like; but we opine what a thing is, or what it is good for, or how — we do not opine to take or avoid.
Further, moral choice is praised more for having a right object than for being judicious, while opinion is praised for truth.
We choose things we know to be good, but we form opinions about what we do not know at all.
Choosing and opining well do not always go together. Some opine the better course, but through vice choose not what they should.
It may be urged that opinion always precedes or accompanies moral choice. Be that as it may; this is not the question. The question is whether moral choice is the same as any kind of opinion.

Since, then, it is none of these, what is it, or how is it characterized? It is plainly voluntary, but not everything voluntary is an object of moral choice. Can we not say it is the voluntary that has passed through previous deliberation? For moral choice is attended by reasoning and intellectual process. The etymology of the Greek word for it gives a hint: literally, "chosen in preference to something else."

Now, do men deliberate about everything, and is anything whatever an object of deliberation? Or are there matters about which there is none? (It may be better to say that by "object of deliberation" we mean what a sensible man would deliberate about, not what any fool or madman might.)
No one deliberates about eternal things — the universe, for example, or the incommensurability of the diagonal and side of a square.
Nor about things in motion that always happen in the same way, whether by necessity, by nature, or from some other cause — the solstices or sunrises, for instance.
Nor about things that vary, such as droughts and rains; nor about matters of chance, such as finding buried treasure.
Nor about all human affairs. No Spartan, for instance, deliberates about the best course for the Scythian government to adopt; we have no power over such results.
We deliberate about practical matters that are in our own power — what is left after all these exclusions.
I make this division because causes seem to be of four kinds: nature, necessity, chance, and also intellect and all human powers.
As humanity in general deliberates about what humanity in general can effect, so individuals deliberate about practical matters they can effect themselves.

We do not deliberate about arts or sciences that are exact and self-contained — for example, about written characters, since we have no doubt how they should be formed. But we do deliberate about things usually done through our own agency that do not invariably turn out in the same way: matters of medicine, say, or money-making. We deliberate more about navigation than about gymnastics, because it is less exactly determined; and more about arts than sciences, because we have more doubt about the former.

Deliberation takes place, then, in matters that fall under general rules yet are uncertain how they will turn out in a given case — that is, in matters with some indefiniteness. For important matters we call in associates in counsel, distrusting our ability to settle them alone.

Further, we deliberate not about ends, but about means to ends. No physician deliberates about whether to cure; no orator about whether to persuade; no statesman about whether to produce a good constitution; and no one in any function about his particular end. With a certain end set before them, they consider how and by what means it may be achieved. If there are several possible means, they go on to examine which is easiest and most creditable. If there is only one, they ask how it may be achieved through this one, and then by what means, until they arrive at the first cause — which will be the last found. A man deliberating seems to search and analyze, as if solving a geometrical problem. Not every search is deliberation (those in mathematics are not), but every deliberation is a search. The last step in the analysis is the first in the process of execution. If in the course of searching men come upon an impossibility, they give up; if money is needed but cannot be got, for instance. But if the thing appears possible, they attempt it.

By possible I mean what can be done through our own agency. What can be done through our friends is through our own agency in a certain sense, because the origin of action in such cases rests with us. The object of search is sometimes the necessary instruments, sometimes the method of using them; and in other cases sometimes the means, sometimes the procedure.

It seems, as has been said, that man is the originator of his actions; deliberation is concerned with whatever can be done through one's own agency, and the actions are for the sake of other things. So deliberation is not about the end but about the means to ends.

Nor is deliberation about matters of detail — whether this substance is bread, say, or whether it has been properly cooked; such things fall under sense perception. If a man is always to be deliberating, the process may go on endlessly.

The object of deliberation and of moral choice is exactly the same matter; but the object of moral choice is, from that moment on, separated off and definite. For the object of moral choice is what has been preferred to something else after deliberation. A man stops searching how he shall do something when he has traced the origin of action back to himself — to the governing principle in himself; for this is what makes the choice. A good illustration is found in the old kingly constitutions Homer drew on, in which kings would announce to the people what they had already decided.

Since the object of moral choice is something in our power, which is the object of deliberation and of reaching by the will, moral choice must be a reaching after something in our power, consequent on deliberation. After deliberating we decide, and then reach by our will in accordance with the result of deliberation.
Let this stand as a sketch of moral choice — its nature and the object it has, namely "means to ends."
That wish has the end as its object has already been said. There are two views on this: some think its object is the real good, others whatever appears good to the mind.

Those who hold that the object of wish is the real good face the difficulty that what is wished for by a man who chooses wrongly is not really an object of wish: on their theory, if it is wished, it must be good, but in the case supposed it is evil. Those who hold that whatever appears good to the mind is the proper object of wish face the objection that there is no object of wish by nature; to each individual, what seems good to him. But different people have different notions, possibly opposite ones.

If these views do not satisfy us, may we not say that, absolutely and as a matter of objective truth, the really good is the object of wish; but to each individual, whatever appears good. To the good man, what is truly good is the object of wish; to the bad man, anything at all may be. Just as in the body, what is wholesome to the healthy really is so, while other things are wholesome to the sick; and so with the bitter, sweet, hot, heavy, and the rest. The good man judges rightly in every case; in every case the impression conveyed to his mind is the true one.

For each state of character has its own proper noble and pleasant things, and these vary with the state. Perhaps the most distinguishing characteristic of the good man is that he sees the truth in every case; he is, as it were, the rule and measure in these matters.
Most people seem to be deceived because of pleasure. Though pleasure is not truly a good, it appears so to them; so they choose what is pleasant as good and avoid pain as evil.

Since the end is the object of wish, and the means to the end the object of deliberation and moral choice, actions concerning such means must be objects of moral choice, and so voluntary. The activities by which the virtues are built up are such actions. Therefore virtue is in our power.

So is vice. Wherever it is in our power to act, it is also in our power to refrain, and vice versa. So if acting (when noble) is in our power, so is refraining (which is in that case base); and conversely.
If it is in our power to do and to refrain from what is noble or base, and if doing or refraining in these cases is what constitutes being good or bad, then being good or vicious is in our power.

The familiar saying, "no man is voluntarily wicked nor involuntarily happy," is partly true and partly false. No one is happy against his will, of course, but wickedness is voluntary. Or must we dispute what has just been said and deny that a man is the originator and begetter of his actions as he is of his children?
If the facts are as described and we cannot trace our actions back to any origins other than those in our own power, then whatever has its origin in us is in our power, and is voluntary.

Testimony supports these positions, both from private individuals and from lawgivers. Lawgivers punish those who do wrong (unless they act on compulsion, or from an ignorance not self-caused), and honor those who act rightly, with a view to encouraging the latter and restraining the former. But what is not in our own power — not voluntary — no one thinks of encouraging. No one bothers to persuade us not to be hot, or to feel pain, or to be hungry, since we shall feel these things all the same.

What makes the case stronger is that lawgivers punish for the very fact of ignorance, when it is thought to be self-caused. For the drunken, penalties are doubled, because the origin lies in the man himself: he might have helped getting drunk, and this is the cause of his ignorance.

Again, those ignorant of legal regulations they are bound to know, and which are not hard to know, are punished. So too with other cases where neglect is thought to be the cause of ignorance, on the ground that it was in the agent's power to prevent his ignorance by paying attention.

Perhaps it will be said that a man is of such a character that he cannot attend to such things. But men are themselves the causes of becoming such characters, by living carelessly; and of being unjust or self-indulgent, by doing evil actions or spending their time in drinking and the like. In each case the particular activities form the corresponding character. This is clear from those who train for a contest or any course of action: they persevere in the activities.
As for the plea that a man did not know that habits are produced from particular actions — such ignorance is a mark of excessive stupidity.

And it is wholly beside the point to say that a man who acts unjustly or licentiously does not wish to form the habits of these vices. For if a man wittingly does the things by which he must become unjust, he is unjust voluntarily; he cannot by a wish cease to be unjust and become just. The analogous case: the sick man cannot by a wish be well again, yet in a supposable case he is voluntarily ill, because he produced his sickness by intemperate living and disregarding his doctor. There was a time when he could have helped being ill; but now, having let himself go, he cannot. Just as he who has let a stone out of his hand cannot recall it, yet it rested with him to aim and throw it — the origin was in his power. So the unjust man, or the man who has lost all self-control, might originally have helped becoming what he is; he is voluntarily what he is. But now that he is such, he cannot be otherwise.

Not only mental but bodily diseases can be voluntary in some men, whom we accordingly blame. No one blames those who are deformed by nature, only those who are so from lack of exercise and neglect; and likewise for weakness and maiming. No one would reproach a man who is blind from nature, disease, or accident — rather, he would be pitied. But anyone would blame him who was so from excess of wine or any other intemperance. With bodily ailments, then, those that depend on ourselves are censured, those that do not are not. If so, then in the case of mental disorders, the ones that are censured must depend on ourselves.

But suppose someone says: by our own admission, all men aim at what appears good to their minds; they have no control over this appearance; the end presents itself to each according to his individual character. If each is in some way cause of his own moral state, then he will also be cause of the impression he receives; but if not, no one is cause to himself of doing evil actions — he does them through ignorance of the true end, thinking he will secure the chief good through them. This aiming at the end, the objector says, is not a matter of choice; one must be born with a power of mental vision, so to speak, to judge well and choose what is truly good. He is blessed by nature who has this faculty well developed, since it is the most important and most noble thing, and one he cannot get or learn from another but has as nature has given it. For it to be so given well and finely would be excellence of nature in the highest and truest sense.

If all this is true, how will virtue be any more voluntary than vice? To both the good man and the bad, the end gives its impression and is fixed by nature (or however you wish to say). They act in light of it, referring everything else to that end.

Whether we suppose that the end presents itself to each man's mind not only by nature, but with some contribution from the man himself; or that the end is given by nature while virtue is voluntary because the good man does all the rest voluntarily — vice too must be equally voluntary. The bad man's own agency equally attaches to him in the actions, even if not in the selection of the end.

If then, as is commonly said, the virtues are voluntary (since we cooperate in producing our moral states, and we assume the end to be of a certain kind according as we are of certain characters), the vices must be voluntary too, since the cases are exactly parallel.

We have now stated in a general way about the moral virtues: their genus in outline, that they are mean states; that they are habits; how they are produced; that they act by their nature on the very circumstances out of which they were produced; that they are in our own power and voluntary; and that they are to be exercised as right reason directs.

But the particular actions and the habits are not voluntary in the same sense. Of the actions we are masters from beginning to end, supposing knowledge of the particulars; but of the habits we are masters only at the starting point. The gradual additions are imperceptible — as with diseases — yet the habits are still voluntary, because it rested with us to use our circumstances one way rather than another.

Let us now resume the particular discussion of the moral virtues: what each is, what its object-matter is, and how it is related to that object-matter. The number of them will become clear in the process.

First, then, courage. That it is a mean state with respect to fear and confidence has been said already. The objects of our fears are plainly fearful things, or in general evils; hence the common definition of fear as "expectation of evil."

We fear evils of all kinds: disgrace, poverty, disease, friendlessness, death. But not all of these are the brave man's object-matter, since there are things it is right and noble to fear, and not to fear them is base — disgrace, for example. The man who fears disgrace is good and has a sense of honor; the one who does not is shameless (though some call him brave by analogy, because he resembles the brave man in being free from fear). But poverty, or disease, or anything not proceeding from vice nor attributable to one's own fault, one ought not to fear. Still, being fearless in respect of these would not make a man brave in the proper sense.
Yet we do apply the term "brave" because of the similarity of cases. Some men, though timid in the dangers of war, are liberal and strong enough to face the loss of wealth.
A man is not a coward for fearing insult to his wife and children, or envy, or anything of that kind; nor is he a brave man for being bold when about to be flogged.

What kinds of fearful things, then, make up the brave man's object-matter? First of all, the greatest, since no man is more resolute in the face of what is dreadful. The greatest object of dread is death, since it is the end of all things, and the dead are thought no longer capable of good or evil. Even so, the brave man's object-matter is not death in every circumstance — on the sea, for instance, or in illness. In what circumstances, then? Surely in the most noble. And such is death in war, because it is death amid the greatest and most noble danger. This is confirmed by the honors awarded in communities, and by monarchs.
A man may most properly be called brave who is fearless in the face of a noble death, and of those sudden emergencies that threaten death — especially those arising in war.

Not that the brave man is not fearless on the sea (and in sickness) too, but not in the same way as sailors. They are hopeful from experience, while landsmen, though brave, give themselves up for lost and shudder at such a death. Courage is exercised in circumstances that admit of doing something to help oneself, or where death would be noble; neither of these conditions holds in death by drowning or by disease.

Fearful is a relative term; the same thing is not fearful to everyone. Some things are said in common speech to be so fearful as to be beyond human endurance; these, of course, would be fearful to every sensible man. But things within human capacity differ in magnitude and admit of degrees; so do the objects of confidence or boldness.

The brave man is not to be frightened out of his composure — so far as he is a man. He will fear such things, yes, but stand up against them as he ought and as reason directs, with a view to what is noble, since this is the end of the virtue.

One may fear such things too much, or too little, or fear what is not really fearful as if it were. So the errors are: a man fears when he ought not to fear at all; or fears in the wrong way; or at the wrong time; and so on. And similarly with things inspiring confidence. The brave man, then, withstands, fears, and is bold with respect to the right objects, from a right motive, in the right manner, and at the right times. He feels or acts as he ought, and as right reason directs.

The end of every activity is what accords with the corresponding habit. To the brave man, this is courage, which is noble. So this is also the end, since the character of each activity is determined by its end.
Thus honor is the motive from which the brave man withstands fearful things and performs acts of courage.

Of the characters on the side of excess, the man who exceeds in utter fearlessness has no proper name (as I noted before, many states do not); he would be a madman or insensitive to pain if he feared nothing — neither earthquake, nor the sea, as the story is told of the Celts.

The man who exceeds in confidence in the face of fearful things is rash. He is also a braggart who falsely claims the character of brave. He wishes to appear toward fearful things as the brave man really is, and imitates him where he can. For this reason most of them display a curious mixture of rashness and cowardice: pretending rashness in these circumstances, they do not hold up against what is really fearful.

The man who exceeds in feeling fear is a coward: he fears the wrong objects, in the wrong ways, and so on. He is also deficient in confidence, but he is most clearly seen to exceed in respect of pains. He is a faint-hearted kind of man, fearing everything. The brave man is his opposite: boldness belongs to the lighthearted and hopeful.

So the coward, the rash man, and the brave man have the same object-matter, but stand differently related to it. The first two exceed or fall short; the last is in a mean state and as he ought to be. The rash are also precipitate, eager before danger but falling away when it is upon them; while the brave are quick and sharp in action, but quiet and composed beforehand.

So, as has been said, courage is a mean state with respect to objects inspiring boldness or fear, in the circumstances described. The brave man chooses his course and withstands danger either because it is noble to do so or because it is base not to. But dying to escape poverty, or the pangs of love, or anything merely painful, is the act not of a brave man but of a coward. It is mere softness to flee what is toilsome; the suicide braves the terrors of death not because it is noble but to get out of the reach of evil.
Courage proper is something like what I have described, but five other dispositions are also called courage in common speech.

First, what most resembles true courage: citizen courage, so called because the motives thought to make members of a community face danger are the penalties and disgrace the laws hold out to cowardice, and the honors conferred on the brave. That is why the bravest peoples are those among whom cowards are disgraced and the brave are honored.
Such is the courage Homer exhibits in his characters — Diomedes and Hector, for example. Hector says,
"Polydamas will be the first to heap disgrace on me."
And Diomedes,
"For Hector surely will say one day, speaking in Troy, 'by my hand Tydides…'"

This most nearly resembles the courage spoken of before, because it arises from virtue — from a sense of shame and a desire for what is noble (that is, for honor), and from the avoidance of disgrace, which is base.

One might be inclined to place in the same rank those who act under compulsion from their commanders. But they are really lower; not a sense of honor but fear is their motive, and what they seek to avoid is not what is base but what is merely painful. Commanders do in fact compel their men; as Hector says (to quote Homer again),
"Whomever I shall find cowering apart from the fight, he shall by no means escape the teeth of dogs."

Commanders who station staunch troops by doubtful ones, or beat their men if they flinch, or line up troops with trenches or similar obstacles in their rear, do in effect the same as Hector — they all use compulsion.
But a man is to be brave not on compulsion, but from a sense of honor.
Second, experience and skill in particular circumstances is thought to be a kind of courage. Hence Socrates too thought courage was knowledge.

This quality is exhibited by different men in different circumstances. In matters of war, it is exhibited by professional soldiers ("the regulars"). There are many things in war of no real importance that they have been constantly used to seeing, so they have the look of courage because others do not see the real nature of these things. By their skill they are also better able than anyone else to inflict without suffering, since they can use their arms and have the ones most useful for attack and defense. Their case is parallel to armed men fighting unarmed men, or trained athletes fighting amateurs — in such contests, the best fighters are not the bravest but the strongest and the best conditioned.

In fact the regulars become cowards when the danger is greater than their means of meeting it — inferior numbers and resources, for instance. Then they are the first to flee, while militia stand and fall on the ground (as really happened at the Hermaeum). To the militia, flight was disgraceful, and death preferable to safety bought at such a price. The regulars, however, had entered the danger supposing themselves superior; on discovering their mistake, they fled, fearing death more than disgrace. This is not the feeling of the brave man.

Third, mere animal spirit is sometimes brought under the term courage. Those are thought brave who are carried on by spirit, as wild beasts against those who have wounded them. The truly brave also have much spirit; there is nothing like spirit for facing danger. Hence the frequent expressions in Homer: "infused strength into his spirit," "roused his strength and spirit," "keen strength in his nostrils," "his blood boiled." All of these seem to denote the arousing and impetuosity of animal spirit.

The truly brave act from a sense of honor, with spirit co-operating. But wild beasts act from pain, because they have been wounded or frightened; if they are quietly in their haunts, forest or marsh, they do not attack men. They are surely not brave for rushing into danger when goaded by pain and mere spirit, without any view of the danger. At that rate asses would be brave when they are hungry — beat them, and they will not leave their pasture. Licentious men too do many bold things from lust. We may conclude that those goaded on by pain and mere spirit are not brave. Still, this temper arising from animal spirit appears to be most natural, and would be courage in the true sense if moral choice and the right motive were added.

Men too feel pain at anger and take pleasure in revenge. But those who fight from these may be good fighters; they are not truly brave, since they do not act from a sense of honor or as reason directs, but from present feeling. Still, they bear some resemblance to the true character.

Fourth, the sanguine and hopeful are not therefore brave. Their boldness in danger arises from their frequent victories over many foes. The two characters are alike in both being confident — but the brave are so from the causes already mentioned, while these are so from a settled conviction of their superiority and that they will suffer nothing in return. (The drunk do much the same; they become hopeful when in that state.) But when the event disappoints their expectations, they run. It is the mark of a brave man, we said, to withstand things that are fearful to man or seem so, because it is noble to do so and the contrary disgraceful.

For this reason it is thought a greater proof of courage to be fearless and composed under sudden fear than under anticipated fear; courage in the former case comes more from a fixed habit, less from preparation. With foreseen dangers one may take one's line from calculation and reasoning; with sudden ones, one acts according to one's fixed habit of mind.

Fifth, those acting in ignorance have the look of courage, and are not very far from the hopeful. Still they are inferior because they have no estimate of themselves. The others do, and so hold their ground for a while; but the deceived flee the moment they know the facts are different from what they supposed. This is what the Argives experienced when they fell on the Spartans, thinking they were Sicyonians.
We have described, then, what kind of men the brave are, and those who are only reputed brave.

It must be noted that although courage has both boldness and fear as its object-matter, it does not have both equally. Its object-matter is the objects of fear much more than of boldness; the man who is undisturbed under the pressure of such things, and stands toward them as he ought, deserves the name of brave more than the man correctly disposed toward objects of confidence. Men are called brave for withstanding what is painful.
It follows that courage involves pain, and is justly praised; for it is harder to withstand painful things than to abstain from pleasant ones.

Not that the end and object of courage is not pleasant — it is, but is obscured by surrounding circumstances. The same is true in the gymnastic games: to boxers the end is pleasant (the crown and the honors), but the blows they receive are painful, and so is all the labor. Since the drawbacks are many and the goal small, the goal seems to offer no pleasure.

If we may say the same of courage: death and wounds must be painful to the brave man and against his will. Still he endures them because it is noble to do so, or disgraceful not to. The more complete his virtue and happiness, the more the thought of death will pain him; for such a man has most to lose by dying, and he is conscious of losing the greatest goods. This is a painful thought. But he is no less brave for feeling it so — rather, perhaps, he is shown to be more brave, since he chooses the honor to be reaped in war over the secure possession of these goods. Acting with pleasure does not attach to all the virtues, except so far as a man attains the end of his actions.

There is perhaps no reason why such men should not make the best soldiers — or rather, those less truly brave but with no other good to care for. They are ready to meet danger and will trade their lives for small gain.
Let this be enough on courage; its nature is not difficult to gather, at least in outline, from what has been said.
Next, self-mastery, which seems to come next to courage, since these two are the excellences of the irrational part of the soul.

That it is a mean state whose object-matter is pleasures has already been said. (Pains are its object-matter in a lesser degree and in a different way.) The state of utter self-indulgence has the same object-matter. The next step is to determine what kind of pleasures are in question.

Let pleasures be divided into mental and bodily. Examples of the mental are love of honor or of learning: plainly each man takes pleasure in what he has a tendency to like, his body being unaffected but his intellect engaged. Men are not called self-mastering or self-indulgent with respect to these pleasures, nor with respect to any that are not bodily. Those who love telling long stories, are prosy, and spend their days on random matters we call gossips, not self-indulgent; nor those who grieve at the loss of money or friends.

Self-mastery, then, has bodily pleasures as its object-matter, though not all even of these. Those who delight in objects of sight — colors, shapes, paintings — are not called self-mastering or self-indulgent. Yet one may take pleasure in these as one ought, or excessively, or too little.
So too with objects of hearing: no one applies these terms to those who take too much pleasure in musical tunes or acting, or to those who take such pleasure as they ought.

Nor to those whose pleasure arises from smell, except incidentally. We do not say men are self-indulgent for enjoying the scent of fruit, flowers, or incense — but rather those who enjoy the smells of perfumes and sauces. The self-indulgent take pleasure in these because they recall to their imagination the objects of their lusts. (You may see others, too, take pleasure in the smell of food when hungry.) Taking pleasure in such scents is a mark of the character in question, since these are objects of desire to him.

Nor do even animals receive pleasure through these senses, except incidentally. It is not the scent of hare's flesh but the eating it that a dog likes; the scent is only how perception of the pleasure arises. Likewise the lion does not like the lowing of the ox but the eating of him; he is made aware of the ox's nearness by the lowing, and so seems to take pleasure in it. Likewise he has no pleasure merely in seeing or finding a stag or wild goat, but in the prospect of a meal.

The habits of self-mastery and total self-indulgence have, then, as their object-matter such pleasures as animals also share — which is why they are plainly slavish and beastly. These are touch and taste.
Even taste men seem to use little or not at all. Taste belongs to distinguishing flavors, which is what men do who test the quality of wines or season rich dishes.

But men scarcely take pleasure in those things — at least, those we call self-indulgent do not — but only in the actual enjoyment, which arises entirely from touch: in eating, drinking, and grosser lusts. Hence the wish reported of a certain glutton: that his throat had been formed longer than a crane's neck, implying his pleasure came from touch.

The sense, then, with which self-indulgence is connected is the most common of all senses, and the vice is justly reproached, since it attaches to us not insofar as we are men but insofar as we are animals. It is beastly to take pleasure in such things and to like them best of all. The more respectable pleasures arising from touch have been set aside, such as those in gymnastic training from rubbing and the warm bath; the self-indulgent man's touch is not indifferently of any part of the body, but of particular parts.

Some desires are thought to be universal, others peculiar and acquired. The desire for food is natural, since everyone truly in need desires food, whether solid or liquid, or both (and, as Homer says, the man in the prime of youth needs and desires intercourse). But as for this or that particular kind of food, the desire is not universal, and in all men is not directed to the same things. Such specific desires clearly attach to us as individuals. Still there is something natural in it: different things are pleasant to different men, and the preference of some particular object to chance ones is universal. With the desires that are strictly and properly natural, few men go wrong, and all in one direction — that of excess. To eat and drink of whatever is on the table till overfilled is to exceed the natural limit; for natural desire is simply a supply of a real deficiency.
For this reason such men are called "belly-mad" — filling it beyond what they ought. It is slavish men who become of this character.

But with respect to peculiar pleasures many men go wrong, and in many ways. The term "fond of so-and-so" implies taking pleasure in wrong objects, or taking pleasure excessively, or like the mass of men, or in a wrong way. The utterly self-indulgent exceed in all these ways: they take pleasure in some things in which they should not (these being properly objects of detestation), and where taking pleasure is right, they do so more than they ought and like the mass of men.

That excess with respect to pleasures is self-indulgence, and is blameworthy, is plain. Looking at these habits on the side of pains, we find that a man is not said to have self-mastery for withstanding them (as in courage), nor to have the vice for not withstanding them. The self-indulgent man is such because he is pained more than he ought at not obtaining pleasant things — so his pleasure produces pain to him. The self-masterer is such by virtue of not being pained by their absence — that is, by having to abstain from what is pleasant.

The self-indulgent man desires either all pleasant things indiscriminately or those that are especially pleasant; his desire drives him to choose these in preference to anything else. This involves pain — not only when he misses his object, but in the very desiring, since all desire is accompanied by pain. It is a strange case: to be pained by reason of pleasure.

Men deficient on the side of pleasure, who take less pleasure in things than they ought, are almost imaginary. Such insensibility is not natural to man; even other animals distinguish between kinds of food, and like some and dislike others. If a man could be found who took no pleasure in anything and to whom all things were alike, he would be far from human; there is no name for such a character because it is simply imaginary.

The self-masterer is in the mean with respect to these things. He takes no pleasure in what delights the vicious man — indeed rather dislikes it — and none in improper objects. He takes no great pleasure in any object of this class; he is not pained at their absence; he does not desire them, or desires them only in moderation, neither more than he ought nor at improper times, and so on. Such pleasant things as are conducive to health and to good bodily condition he will reach for in moderation and as he ought, along with other pleasant things that do not hinder these objects and are not unseemly or beyond his means. Reaching for things outside these limits would be liking such pleasures more than is proper; but the self-masterer is not of that kind. He regulates his desires by the dictates of right reason.

Self-indulgence seems to be more truly voluntary than cowardice. Pleasure is the cause of the former, pain of the latter; pleasure is an object of choice, pain of avoidance. Pain deranges and spoils the disposition of its victim; pleasure has no such effect, and is more voluntary and therefore more justly open to reproach.

It is also easier to be trained by habit to resist objects of pleasure. There are many such things in life, and the process of habituation is unaccompanied by danger; whereas the case is the reverse with objects of fear.

Cowardice, as a settled habit, would seem to be voluntary in a different way from the particular instances that form it. It is itself painless; but its instances derange the man through pain, so that he throws away his arms and otherwise behaves disgracefully. For this reason some even think they exercise a compelling force.

With self-indulgence, by contrast, the particular instances are themselves fully voluntary, done with desire and direct willing; but the general result — the habit — is less voluntary, since no one desires to form the habit.

The Greek name for this vice (meaning literally "unchastened-ness") we apply also to the faults of children, there being a resemblance. Which is the primary and which the derivative application is not relevant here, but the later application clearly takes its name from the earlier. The metaphor is good. What grasps after base things and is liable to great increase ought to be chastened; and to this description desire and the child answer most truly, since children too live at the direction of desire, and grasping after what is pleasant is most prominent in them.

Unless the appetite is obedient and subject to the governing principle, it will grow very great. In the fool, the grasping after what is pleasant is insatiable and indiscriminate. Every activation of desire increases the corresponding habit; and if desires are great and violent in degree, they even drive out reason entirely. So they ought to be moderate and few, and in no respect opposed to reason. When the appetite is in such a state, we call it obedient and chastened.
In short, as the child ought to live in constant regard for the instructions of his educator, so the appetitive part ought to live in constant regard for those of reason.

So in the self-masterer the appetitive part must be in accord with reason, for what is right is the mark at which both aim. The self-masterer desires what he ought, in the right manner, and at the right times — which is exactly what reason directs. Let this be our account of self-mastery.

chapters.title: Book 4 — Further Moral Virtues
paragraphs: Next, liberality. This is thought to be a mean state with wealth as its object-matter. The liberal man is praised not in the context of war, nor in matters of self-mastery, nor in judicial decisions, but in respect of the giving and receiving of wealth — chiefly the giving. By wealth I mean all things whose worth is measured in money.

The states of excess and deficiency regarding wealth are prodigality and stinginess. Stinginess we always apply to those who care too much about wealth. Prodigality we sometimes apply with a more complex sense: we give the name to those who lack self-control and spend money on the unrestrained gratification of their passions. This is why they are thought the most base, because they combine many vices at once.

Still, this is not a strict and proper use of the term. Its natural etymological meaning refers to one particular evil — wasting one's substance. The prodigal (literally "unsaved") is wasting away by his own fault; and he may be said to be so, since the destruction of his substance is a kind of wasting of himself, these being the means of life. This, then, is our meaning of prodigality.

Whatever is for use may be used well or badly; and wealth is such a thing. He uses each thing best who has the virtue whose province it is. So he will use wealth best who has the virtue concerned with wealth — that is, the liberal man.

Expenditure and giving are thought to be the using of money; receiving and keeping are rather its possessing. So giving to the right people is more characteristic of the liberal man than receiving from the right quarters and abstaining from the wrong. Generally, doing well by others is more characteristic of virtue than being done well by, and doing positively noble things more than refraining from disgraceful ones. Anyone can see that doing well by others and doing things positively noble belong to the act of giving; to receiving belongs only being done well by or refraining from what is disgraceful.

Besides, thanks go to the giver, not to one who merely refrains from receiving, and praise even more. Also, refraining from receiving is easier than giving, since people are more often too little freehanded with their own than inclined to take what is not theirs.
And it is the givers who are called liberal; those who refrain from receiving are commended not for liberality but for just dealing, while for receiving men are not praised at all.
The liberal are liked almost best among virtuous characters, because they are useful to others; and their usefulness lies in their giving.

All actions in accordance with virtue are noble and done from the motive of honor. The liberal man will therefore give from this motive, and give rightly: to the right people, in right proportion, at the right times, and in whatever ways "right giving" requires. He will do this with positive pleasure, or at least without pain, since what is done in accordance with virtue is pleasant or at least not unpleasant, and certainly not painful.

But the man who gives to improper people, or not from a motive of honor but from some other cause, is to be called something other than liberal. Nor is he to be called liberal who gives with pain; that would show he would prefer his wealth to the noble action, which is no part of the liberal man's character. Nor will such a man receive from improper sources; receiving thus is not characteristic of one who does not value wealth. Nor will he be apt to ask favors, since one who does kindnesses does not usually receive them willingly. But he will receive from proper sources (his own property, for instance), doing so not as something noble but as necessary, so that he may have something to give. Nor will he be careless of his own, since his wish is to use it to help those in need. Nor will he give to chance persons, since he wants to have something to give to those he should, at the right times, and on occasions when it is noble to give.
It is a trait of the liberal man to go too far in giving, so that he leaves too little for himself; for not to think of oneself is characteristic of such a man.

Liberality is a term relative to a man's means; liberality depends not on the amount given but on the moral state of the giver, who gives in proportion to his means. There is no reason why the more liberal man should not be the one who gives a smaller amount, if he has less to give out of.
Those are thought more liberal who have inherited rather than acquired their means; for they have never experienced want, and besides, everyone loves best his own works, as parents and poets do.

It is not easy for the liberal man to be rich, since he is neither apt to receive nor to hold on to wealth, but to lavish it. He values wealth not for its own sake but for the sake of giving it away. Hence the common complaint to fortune that those who most deserve to be rich are least so. Yet this happens reasonably enough: it is impossible to be wealthy if one takes no trouble to be so, just as in any similar case.

Still the liberal man will not give to the wrong people, at the wrong times, or the like; he would then not be acting in accordance with liberality, and if he spent on such objects he would have nothing to spend where he ought. As I said, the liberal man spends in proportion to his means and on proper objects, while the one who does so in excess is prodigal. (We never call despots prodigal, because it does not seem easy for them by their gifts and expenditure to go beyond their immense possessions.)

To sum up: since liberality is a mean state with respect to giving and receiving wealth, the liberal man will give and spend on proper objects and in proper proportion, in great and small matters alike, and all this with pleasure to himself. He will also receive from right sources and in right proportion. Since the virtue is a mean state with respect to both, he will do both as he ought; proper giving is followed by a corresponding receiving, and improper receiving is contrary to it. (What follow one another co-exist in the same person; contraries clearly do not.)

Should it happen that he spends beyond what is needful or not well, he will be vexed — but only moderately and as he ought. Feeling pleasure and pain at the right objects and in the right way is a property of virtue.

The liberal man is a good partner in matters of wealth. He is easily wronged, since he does not value wealth, and he is more vexed by failing to spend where he should than by spending where he should not. He has no taste for the maxim of Simonides.
The prodigal goes wrong here too: he is neither pleased nor pained at the proper objects or in the proper way, as will become clearer.

We have said that prodigality and stinginess are states of excess and deficiency, and this in two things: giving and receiving. (Expenditure we class under giving.) Prodigality exceeds in giving and in not receiving, and is deficient in receiving; stinginess is deficient in giving and exceeds in receiving, though in small things.

The two sides of prodigality do not commonly go together; it is not easy to give to all while receiving from none, since private individuals who do this soon find their means run short. Such are in fact thought prodigal. A man who combines both these faults would seem considerably superior to the stingy man; he can easily be cured, both by advancing years and by lack of means, and so may come to the mean. He already has the facts of the liberal man about him: he gives and refrains from receiving, only not in a right manner or well. If he could be worked on by habituation in this respect, or change in any other way, he would be a true liberal man, since he will give to those he should and refrain from receiving where he should not. This is also why he is thought not of low moral character; exceeding in giving and in not receiving is no sign of badness or meanness, but only of folly.

The prodigal who acts in this fashion is thought far superior to the stingy man, for these reasons and also because he does good to many, while the stingy man does good to no one, not even himself. But most prodigals, as has been said, also receive from improper sources and on this point are stingy. They become grasping because they want to spend but cannot do so easily; their means run short, and they must get more from some other quarter. Then, since they care nothing for the noble, they receive recklessly from all sources indifferently; for they desire to give but care not how or whence.

For this reason their giving is not liberal, since it is neither noble, nor purely disinterested, nor done in a right way. They often make rich those who should be poor, and give nothing to respectable quiet people, but much to flatterers and those who serve their pleasures. Most prodigals, therefore, are also without self-restraint; being open-handed, they spend lavishly on the unrestrained gratification of their passions, and they turn aside to their pleasures because they do not live with reference to what is noble.
The prodigal, if unguided, slides into these faults; but with care he might come to the mean, and to what is right.

Stinginess, by contrast, is incurable. Old age and any kind of incapacity are thought to make people stingy, and it is more congenial to human nature than prodigality — most men are fond of money rather than apt to give. It also extends far and has many forms; the modes of stinginess are thought to be many. Since it consists of two things — deficiency in giving and excess in receiving — not everyone has it entire; sometimes it is divided. Some exceed in receiving, others are deficient in giving. Those called sparing, close-fisted, niggards, are all deficient in giving; but they neither desire nor want to receive other men's property, in some cases from genuine moderation and shrinking from what is base.

Some keep their property, as they either say or suppose, so as never to be driven to do anything disgraceful. To this class belongs the skinflint and every similar character, so named from the excess of not-giving. Others decline to receive what is their neighbor's from fear: their notion is that it is not easy to take other people's things without their taking yours. So they are content neither to give nor to receive.

The other class, stingy in receiving, exceeds in receiving anything from any source: such as those who work at disgraceful employments, brothel-keepers and the like, and usurers who lend small sums at high interest. All these receive from improper sources and in improper amounts. Their common feature is base gain; they all submit to disgrace for the sake of gain, and a small one at that. Those who receive great things from wrong sources and of the wrong kind, such as despots who sack cities and plunder temples, we call wicked, impious, and unjust — but not stingy.

The dicer, the bath-plunderer, and the robber belong to the class of the stingy; they too are given to base gain. Both the one sort and the other take trouble and submit to disgrace for the sake of gain — the former incurring the greatest dangers for their booty, the latter making gain of their friends to whom they ought to be giving.

So both classes, wishing to gain from improper sources, are given to base gain; and all such receivings are stingy. With good reason stinginess is called the contrary of liberality; it is a greater evil than prodigality, and men more often err in this direction than in that of prodigality proper.
Let this stand as our discussion of liberality and the contrary vices.

Next would seem to come a discussion of magnificence. Like liberality, this is a virtue whose object-matter is wealth; but unlike liberality, it does not extend to all transactions involving wealth, only to those that are expensive. In such matters it exceeds liberality in magnitude. Magnificence, as the Greek word hints, is fitting expense on a large scale. This is relative: the expense of equipping and commanding a trireme is not the same as that of giving a public spectacle. "Fitting," too, is relative to the individual, to the matter, and to what one is spending on. A man is not called magnificent for spending as he should in small or ordinary things, as in the line,
"Often to the wandering beggar did I give,"

but for doing so in great matters. The magnificent man is liberal, but the liberal man is not necessarily magnificent. The falling short of this state is called meanness; the exceeding it is vulgar profusion, tastelessness, and so on. These are faulty not because they are on an excessive scale with respect to right objects, but because they show off in improper objects, in improper ways. We will discuss these presently. The magnificent man is like a man of skill: he can see what is fitting and spend largely in good taste. As we said at the start, the confirmed habit is determined by its activities and its object-matter.

The magnificent man's expenses are great and fitting. So are his works; this ensures the expenditure is not merely great but befitting the work. The work must be proportionate to the expense, and the expense to the work, or even above it. The magnificent man will incur such expenses from the motive of honor (which is common to all virtues), and besides will do it with pleasure and lavishly; excessive accuracy of calculation is mean. He will consider rather how a thing may be done most beautifully and fittingly than how much it costs, or how it might be done most cheaply.

The magnificent man must therefore also be liberal, for the liberal man will also spend what he ought and in the right way. But it is the great — the large scale — that is distinctive of the magnificent man; the object-matter of liberality is the same, but without spending more money than another he will make the work more magnificent. The excellence of a possession and of a work are different: as a piece of property the most valuable thing is what is worth most, like gold; as a work it is what is great and beautiful, because the contemplation of such an object is admirable, and so is what is magnificent. The excellence of a work lies in magnificence on a large scale. Some expenditures we call honorable: dedicatory offerings to the gods, the furnishing of temples, sacrifices, and in general whatever has reference to the gods; and all such public matters as are objects of honorable ambition — as when one thinks it his duty to furnish a chorus splendidly for the stage, or fit out and maintain a trireme, or give a general public feast.

In all such cases, as I said, regard is to be paid to the rank and means of the person involved; they should be proportionate to these and befit not only the work but also the doer. For this reason a poor man cannot be magnificent; he has no means by which to spend largely and yet becomingly. If he attempts it, he is a fool, since he acts out of proportion and against propriety, whereas anything done in accordance with virtue must be done rightly.

Such expenditure is fitting also for those to whom such things already belong — whether in themselves, or through their ancestors, or through people connected with them — and for the highborn or people of high repute. For all these things imply greatness and reputation.

The magnificent man is pretty much as I have described him. Magnificence consists in such expenditures, because they are the greatest and most honorable. It also includes private expenditures that come once for all — such as marriage and things of that kind — and any occasion that engages the interest of the community or those in power, and the reception and sending off of strangers, and gifts and the repaying of gifts. The magnificent man is not apt to spend on himself but on the public good, and gifts are in much the same case as dedicatory offerings.

It is also characteristic of the magnificent man to furnish his house suitably to his wealth, for this too in its way reflects credit; and to spend rather on works of long duration, which are most honorable. And propriety in each case — the same things are not suitable to gods and to men, nor to a temple and a tomb. In each case the expenditure must be great of its kind; a great expense on a great object is the most magnificent, that being, in any particular case, what is great in those things.

Greatness of a work differs from greatness of expenditure. A very beautiful ball or cup is magnificent as a present to a child, though its price is small and almost mean. It is therefore characteristic of the magnificent man to do magnificently whatever he is about; for what is of this kind cannot easily be surpassed, and it bears a proper proportion to the expenditure.
Such, then, is the magnificent man.

The man in the state of excess, called vulgar profusion, is in excess because he spends improperly, as has been said. In cases calling for small expenditure he lavishes much and shows off tastelessly: giving his club a feast fit for a wedding, or, if he has to furnish a chorus for a comedy, dressing the actors in purple in the first scene, as the Megarians did. He does all such things not with a view to what is truly noble, but to display his wealth, and because he thinks he will be admired for them. He spends little where he ought to spend much, and much where he should spend little.

The mean man is deficient in every case. Even where he has spent the most, he will spoil the whole effect for want of some trifle; he is procrastinating in everything, contrives how to spend the least, and laments even that, thinking he does everything on a larger scale than he ought.
Both these states are faulty, but they do not involve disgrace, since they are neither hurtful to others nor very unseemly.

The name of greatness of soul implies that its object-matter is great things. Let us first settle what kind. It makes no difference whether we regard the moral state in the abstract or as exemplified in an individual.

He is thought to be great-souled who values himself highly, and does so justly; for a man who does this without grounds is a fool, and no virtuous character is foolish or senseless. The man I have described is great-souled. The man who estimates himself low, and does so justly, is modest; but not great-souled, since greatness of soul implies greatness, just as beauty implies large bodily conformation, while small people may be neat and well-made but not beautiful.

He who values himself highly without just grounds is vain — though the name need not be applied to every case of too high a self-estimate. He who values himself below his real worth is small-souled, whether his worth is great, moderate, or small; his own estimate falls below it. The strongest case of this error is the man of great worth, since what would he do if his worth were less?

The great-souled man, then, is at the summit in respect of greatness, but in respect of propriety he stands in the mean; he estimates himself at his true value, while the other characters are in excess and deficiency. Since he justly rates himself at a high or even the highest value, his character has special reference to one thing. "Value" here refers to external goods, and of these we should assume the greatest to be what we assign to the gods, what those in power especially desire, and the prize offered for the most honorable actions. All these descriptions fit honor; honor is the greatest of external goods. So the great-souled man bears himself as he ought in respect of honor and dishonor. Without need of words, the great-souled plainly have honor as their object-matter; it is what the great consider themselves specially worthy of, and on a certain scale.

The small-souled man falls short both in self-estimate and in comparison with the great-souled; the vain man exceeds in self-estimate, but does not exceed the great-souled. Now the great-souled man, being by hypothesis worthy of the greatest things, must be of the highest excellence. The better a man is, the more he is worth; the best is worth the most. So to be truly great-souled a man must be good; whatever is great in each virtue would seem to belong to the great-souled. It would not fit the character of the great-souled to flee with arms spread wide; nor to injure anyone. For with what object in view will a man, in whose eyes nothing is great, do what is base? In short, to go into particulars, the great-souled man would cut quite a ludicrous figure if he were not a good man; indeed he would not be deserving of honor if he were bad, since honor is the prize of virtue and given to the good.

This virtue, then, seems to be a kind of ornament of the other virtues; it makes them better and cannot exist without them. For this reason it is hard to be truly great-souled: the thing cannot exist without thorough goodness and nobility of character.

Honor and dishonor are especially the great-souled man's object-matter. At honor that is great and given by good men he will be pleased moderately, as getting his own — or perhaps a little less, since no honor can be quite adequate to perfect virtue. Still he will accept it because they have nothing higher to give him. Honor from ordinary people and on trifling grounds he will entirely despise; such does not come up to what he deserves. Likewise with dishonor: in his case there cannot be just ground for it.

Though honor is especially his object-matter, the great-souled man will also bear himself with moderation in respect of wealth and power and every kind of good or bad fortune, however it may fall out. He will not be overjoyed in prosperity nor unduly pained in adversity. He does not bear himself thus even toward honor, which is the greatest of such objects; it is the cause of power and wealth being choice-worthy, since those who have them desire to receive honor through them. If honor is a small thing to him, all other things will be so too. This is why such men are thought supercilious.

Pieces of good fortune also seem to contribute to this character. The well-born, the powerful, and the wealthy are considered entitled to honor, being in a position of eminence; what is eminent by good is more entitled to honor. So such circumstances dispose men toward greatness of soul, because they receive honor from some.

Truly and rightly, only the good man is entitled to honor. If he unites goodness with these external advantages, he is thought more entitled. But those who have these without virtue are not justified in their high self-estimate, nor are they rightly called great-souled; perfect virtue is one of the necessary conditions of such a character.

Such men become supercilious and insolent; it is not easy to bear prosperity well without goodness. Unable to bear it, and possessed with an idea of their superiority, they despise others and do whatever their fancy prompts. They mimic the great-souled without being like him, and they do this in the points they can. So, without doing the actions that flow only from real goodness, they still despise others. The great-souled man despises on good grounds (for he forms true opinions); the mass of men do it at random.

He is not a man to incur small risks, nor does he court danger, since there are few things he values. But he will incur great dangers; when he does venture, he is prodigal of his life, knowing that there are terms on which it is not worth his while to live. He is the sort of man to do kindnesses but is ashamed to receive them; the former puts a man in the position of superiority, the latter of inferiority. Accordingly he will greatly overpay any kindness done him, so that the original actor will be laid under obligation and be in the position of the recipient. Such men also remember those they have done kindnesses to, but not those from whom they have received them; the receiver is inferior to the giver, and our friend wishes to be superior. He is pleased to hear of his own kind acts but not of those done for him. That is why, in Homer, Thetis does not mention to Zeus the kindnesses she had done him, nor did the Spartans to the Athenians, but only the benefits they had received.

It is characteristic of the great-souled man to ask favors not at all, or very reluctantly, but to do a service very readily. He bears himself loftily toward the great and fortunate, but affably toward people of middle station. To outdo the former is difficult and a grand thing; to outdo the latter is easy. High bearing toward the great is not ignoble, but toward the humble it is low and vulgar — like parading one's strength against the weak.

He does not put himself in the way of honor, nor go where others are the chief men. He is remiss and slow, except for some great honor or work; he is concerned in few things, but those great and famous. He is open both in dislikes and likings, since concealment is a consequence of fear. He cares for reality rather than appearance, and speaks and acts openly. (His contempt for others makes him bold, and this is also why he is apt to speak the truth — except where reserve comes in.) But toward the generality of people he is reserved.

He cannot live with reference to anyone but a friend; to do so would be servile. That is why all flatterers are low, and men of low estate are flatterers. His admiration is not easily excited, since nothing is great in his eyes. He does not bear malice; remembering anything, and especially wrongs, is no part of greatness of soul — rather, overlooking them is. He does not talk of other men; he will not talk about himself or about another; he neither cares to be praised himself nor to have others blamed; nor does he praise freely. For the same reason he is not apt to speak ill even of his enemies, except to show contempt and insolence.

He is by no means given to lament about things that cannot be helped, or to request trivial things; for such dispositions belong only to those who are really anxious about those things. He is the kind of man to acquire what is beautiful and unproductive rather than what is productive and profitable; this is rather the part of an independent man.

Slow motion, a deep-toned voice, and a deliberate style of speech are thought characteristic of the great-souled man; for one who is earnest about few things is not likely to be in a hurry, and one who esteems nothing great is not likely to be intent. Sharp tones and quickness are consequences of the latter.

This is my idea of the great-souled man. The man in the deficiency is small-souled; the one in excess is vain. As with the last character discussed, these extremes are not considered exactly vicious, only mistaken, since they do no harm.

The small-souled man, being really worthy of good, deprives himself of his deserts. He seems to have something faulty about him from not estimating his own desert highly enough — from self-ignorance. But for this, he would have reached for what he was really entitled to, which is good. Still, such characters are not thought foolish, but rather laggards. Holding such a view of themselves seems to have a deteriorating effect on character; in all cases men's aims are regulated by their supposed desert, and these men, under a notion of their own lack of desert, hold aloof from honorable actions and courses, and likewise from external goods.

The vain are foolish and self-ignorant, and obviously so: they attempt honorable things as though they were worthy, and are then found out. They also set themselves off with dress, carriage, and the like; they desire their good circumstances to be seen, and talk about them under the notion of receiving honor in that way. Small-souledness, rather than vanity, is opposed to greatness of soul, since it is more commonly met with and is worse.

Greatness of soul, as we said, has great honor as its object. There seems also to be a virtue having honor as its object, as we said in the earlier book, which may seem to bear to greatness of soul the relation liberality bears to magnificence. Both of these virtues stand aloof from what is great and dispose us as we ought toward moderate and small matters. As in giving and receiving wealth there is a mean, an excess, and a deficiency, so too in reaching after honor there is more or less than is right, and also the reaching for it from right sources and in the right way.

We blame the lover of honor for aiming at honor more than he ought, and from wrong sources; and the man without love of honor for not choosing to be honored even for what is noble. Sometimes we praise the lover of honor as manly and loving what is noble, and the man without love of it as moderate and modest, as we noticed in the earlier discussion.

Clearly, since "lover of so and so" has several meanings, "lover of honor" does not always denote the same quality. When we use it to commend, we mean "more than most men are"; when to blame, "more than a man should be."

Since the mean state has no proper name, the extremes seem to dispute for it as unoccupied ground. But where there is excess and deficiency there must be a mean. In fact men do reach for honor more than they should, less, and sometimes just as they ought. The last is praised as a mean state regarding honor, though it has no proper name. Compared with what is called ambition it looks like lack of love for honor; compared with that, it looks like ambition; or compared with both, like both faults. Nor is this unusual among the virtues. Here the extreme characters appear opposed, because the mean has no name of its own.

Meekness is a mean state whose object-matter is anger. Since neither the mean character nor, one may almost say, the extremes have names, we give the name meekness (leaning rather toward the deficiency, which also has no name) to the character in the mean.

The excess may be called an over-aptness to anger; the passion is anger, and its producing causes are many and various. One who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and in the right manner, at the right time, and for the right length of time, is praised. This man will be meek, since meekness is praised. The notion represented by the word "meek" is that of being imperturbable, not led away by passion, but getting angry in the manner, at the things, and for the length of time that reason directs. But this character tends to err on the side of deficiency; he is not apt to take revenge, but rather to make allowances and forgive. The deficiency — call it spiritlessness or what you will — is blamed. Those not angry at what they ought to be are thought foolish; and so are those not angry in the right manner, at the right time, or with the right people. Such a man is thought to have no perception and no pain, and no tendency to defend himself; he feels no anger. To bear with insult in one's own person and patiently see one's friends suffer it is slavish.

The excess takes all forms: men are angry with those with whom they ought not, at things at which they ought not, more than they ought, too hastily, and for too long. These faults are not combined in any one person; that would be impossible, since the evil would destroy itself, and if developed in full force would become unbearable.

Those we call hot-tempered are soon angry, with the wrong people and at the wrong things, in excess — but they soon cool again, which is the best point about them. This comes from their not repressing their anger but repaying it (showing their feelings because of their vehemence); and then they have done with it.
The choleric are excessively vehement, angry at everything and on every occasion; hence their Greek name, meaning that their bile lies high.

The bitter-tempered are hard to reconcile and keep their anger long, because they repress the feeling; when they have revenged themselves, comes a lull, for the vengeance destroys their anger by producing pleasure in place of pain. Otherwise they keep the weight on their minds; since the feeling does not show itself, no one tries to reason it away, and digesting anger within oneself takes time. Such men are great nuisances to themselves and to their best friends.
We call cross-grained those angry at wrong objects, in excessive degree, for too long a time, and not appeased without vengeance or at least punishing the offender.

To meekness we oppose the excess rather than the deficiency, because it is more common: human nature is more disposed to take revenge than to forgo it. Also, the cross-grained are worse to live with than the too phlegmatic.

From what has been said, what was said earlier is also plain: it is not easy to define how, and with whom, and at what kinds of things, and for how long one ought to be angry, and up to what point a person is right or wrong. The man who transgresses the strict rule only a little, either on the side of excess or deficiency, is not blamed; sometimes we praise those deficient in the feeling and call them meek, sometimes we call the irritable spirited, as well qualified for command. So it is not easy to say in words what degree or kind of transgression makes a man blameable; the decision lies in particulars, and rests with moral perception. This much is plain: the mean state is praiseworthy, by which we are angry with the right people, at the right things, in the right manner, and so on; while the excesses and deficiencies are blameable, slightly so if slight, more so if great, and considerably so if considerable.
So the mean state is what we are to hold to.
Let this be our account of the moral states with anger as their object-matter.

Next, in social intercourse and exchange of words and deeds: some men are thought overly obliging, agreeing to everything and never opposing, with a view solely to giving pleasure and giving no pain to those they are thrown among. Others, taking exactly the opposite line, oppose in everything and care nothing whether they give pain; these are called cross and contentious.

These states are plainly blameable, and the mean between them praiseworthy, by virtue of which a man will let pass what he ought and as he ought, and will also object in like manner. But this state has no proper name. It is most like friendship; the man who exhibits it is just the sort we would call an amiable friend, with the addition of strong affection. That is the very point in which it differs from friendship — it is independent of any feeling or strong affection for those among whom the man mixes. He takes everything as he ought, not from love or hatred, but simply because his natural disposition leads him to do so. He will do this alike to those he knows and those he does not, to those he is intimate with and those he is not — only in each case as propriety requires, since it is not fitting to care alike for intimates and strangers, or to pain them alike.
In general, his social intercourse is regulated by propriety; his aim is to avoid giving pain and to contribute to pleasure, with a constant reference to what is noble and expedient.

His proper object-matter is the pleasures and pains arising from social intercourse. But where it is not noble, or where it is actually harmful to him, to contribute to pleasure, in these cases he will go against it and prefer to give pain.
If the thing involves unseemliness to the doer — and that not trifling — or any harm, while his opposition will cause some little pain, here he will not agree but will go against.

He will regulate his intercourse differently with great men and with ordinary men, and with all people according to his knowledge of them, and so taking in other differences. He gives to each his due, and in itself prefers to give pleasure and is cautious about giving pain. But still he is guided by the results — by what is noble and expedient, whichever preponderates.
He will inflict small pain with a view to a consequent pleasure.

The man of the mean character is pretty much as I have described him, but he has no proper name. Of those who try to give pleasure, the man who does so simply and disinterestedly is called overly obliging; the one who does so with a view to profit in wealth or what wealth can procure is a flatterer. The man who is always discontent is, as I said, cross and contentious. Here the extremes appear opposed to one another, because the mean has no proper name.

The mean state that avoids exaggeration has pretty much the same object-matter as the one just described, and likewise has no proper name. Still it may be well to go over these. By a particular discussion of each we shall be better acquainted with the general subject of moral character, and we shall be more convinced that the virtues are mean states on seeing that this holds universally.

In living in society, we have already spoken of those who carry on social intercourse with a view to pleasure and pain. Now let us speak of those who are true or false, both in words and deeds and in the claims they advance.

The exaggerator is thought to be apt to lay claim to things that reflect credit on him, both when they do not belong to him at all, and in greater degree than they really do. The reserved man, on the contrary, denies what really belongs to him or depreciates it. The mean character, a plain-matter-of-fact person, is truthful in life and word, admitting what really does belong to him and making it neither greater nor less than the truth.
