Each of these lines may be taken with or without some further motive; but in general men speak, act, and live each according to his particular character and disposition, unless he is acting from a special motive.

Since falsehood is in itself base and blameable, while truth is noble and praiseworthy, it follows that the truthful man (who is also in the mean) is praiseworthy, and the two who depart from strict truth are both blameable, but especially the exaggerator.

Let us speak of each, starting with the truthful man. I call him truthful — not meaning one who is true in his agreements or in matters that amount to justice or injustice (that would be another virtue). In matters not involving any such serious difference, the man we are describing is true in life and word simply because he is in a certain moral state.

Such a man must be judged good. For one who loves truth as such, and is guided by it in matters that are indifferent, will be all the more so in matters that are not indifferent; he will shrink from falsehood as base, since he shunned it even in itself. Such a character is praiseworthy, though he leans rather to the side of understatement, this being thought in better taste because exaggerations are hateful.

The man who lays claim to more than really belongs to him, without any special motive, is like a base man — otherwise he would not take pleasure in falsehood — but he shows as a fool rather than a knave. If he does it with a special motive — for honor or glory, as the braggart does — he is not too blameable; but if for pecuniary considerations, directly or indirectly, he is more unseemly.

The braggart is such not by his capacity but by his purpose; that is, by virtue of his moral state, and because he is a man of a certain kind. Some liars take pleasure in falsehood for its own sake; others lie from desire of glory or gain. Those who exaggerate for glory pretend to qualities followed by praise and the highest commendation; those who do it for gain assume qualities their neighbors can make use of and whose absence can be concealed — such as being a skilled soothsayer or physician. That is why most men pretend to such things and exaggerate in this direction; these faults are in them.

The reserved, who depreciate their own qualities, seem to be of more refined character, because they are not thought to speak from a view to gain but to avoid grandiosity. A very common trait in such characters is denying widely current opinions, as Socrates used to do. Some lay false claim to small things, the falsity of which is obvious; these are called factotums and are very contemptible.

This very reserve sometimes looks like exaggeration — take, for instance, the excessive plainness of dress affected by the Spartans. In fact, both excess and the extreme of deficiency partake of the nature of exaggeration. Those who practice reserve in moderation, in cases where the truth is not very obvious and plain, give an impression of refinement. Here it is the exaggerator (as the worse character) who appears opposed to the truthful man.

Next, since life has its pauses and admits of amusement and joking in them, it is thought there is a fitting kind of intercourse here too, and that rules can be prescribed as to what sorts of things one should say and how, and likewise what to listen to. (There will be a difference between saying and hearing such things.) Clearly in these matters too there will be excess, deficiency, and a mean.

Those who exceed in the ridiculous are judged to be buffoons and vulgar, grasping at it in any way and at any cost, and aiming rather at raising laughter than at saying what is seemly and avoiding pain to the object of their wit. Those who will not for the world make a joke themselves and are displeased at those who do are thought clownish and stern. Those jocular in good taste are denominated by a Greek word expressing ease of movement; such are thought to be, so to speak, motions of the moral character, and as bodies are judged by their motions so too are moral characters.

Since the ridiculous lies on the surface, and most men take more pleasure than they ought in joking, buffoons too get this name of easy pleasantry, as if refined and gentlemanly. But they differ from these, and considerably, as is plain from what has been said.

One quality belonging to the mean state is tact. It is characteristic of a man of tact to say and listen only to such things as befit a good man and a gentleman; for there are things it is becoming for such a one to say and hear in the way of joking, and there is a difference between a gentleman's jocularity and a vulgarian's, and between the educated man's and the uneducated man's. You may see this by comparing the Old and New Comedy: in the former, obscene talk made the fun; in the latter it is rather innuendo. The difference is not slight, as regards decency.

Are we to characterize the man who jests well by his saying what is becoming a gentleman, or by his avoiding pain to the object of his wit, or even by his giving the object pleasure? Any such definition is vague, since different things are hateful and pleasant to different men.

Be that as it may, whatever he says, such things too will he listen to — it is commonly held that a man will do what he will bear to hear. This must be qualified: a man will not do quite all he will hear, for jesting is a species of scurrility, and some scurrility is forbidden by law. It may be that certain kinds of jest should be forbidden too. The refined, gentlemanly man will bear himself in this as being a law to himself. Such is the mean character, whether denominated the man of tact or of easy pleasantry.

The buffoon cannot resist the ridiculous, sparing neither himself nor anyone else so long as he can raise a laugh, saying things no man of refinement would say, and some he would not even tolerate if said by others in his hearing.
The clownish man is wholly useless for such intercourse; contributing nothing jocose of his own, he is savage with all who do.
Yet some pause and amusement in life are generally judged indispensable.

The three mean states described do occur in life, and the object-matter of all is the exchange of words and deeds. They differ in that one concerns truth, and the other two concern the pleasurable; of these two, one is conversant with the jocularities of life, the other with all other points of social intercourse.

To speak of shame as a virtue is not correct; it is more like a feeling than a moral state. It is defined as "a kind of fear of disgrace," and its effects are similar to those of the fear of danger: those who feel shame blush, and those who fear death turn pale. Both are evidently in a way physical, which is thought a mark of a feeling rather than a moral state.

Moreover, shame is a feeling not suitable to every age, but only to youth. We think the young should be modest, since living at the beck and call of passion they do much that is wrong, and shame checks them. We praise young men who are modest, but no one would praise an old man for being given to shame, since we hold that he should do nothing shameful. Shame, since it arises at low, bad actions, does not belong at all to the good man, for such things should not be done at all. Nor does it matter to say that some things are disgraceful really, others only reputedly; neither should be done, so a man ought not to be in the position of feeling shame. In truth, to be the kind of man who does anything disgraceful is the part of a faulty character. And for a man to be such that he would feel shame if he did anything disgraceful, and to think this makes him a good man, is absurd; shame is felt only at voluntary actions, and the good man will never voluntarily do what is base.

Shame may indeed be good on a certain supposition — "if a man were to do such things, he would feel shame." But the virtues are good in themselves, not merely in supposed cases. And granted that shamelessness, not being ashamed to do disgraceful things, is base, it does not follow that it is good for a man to do such things and feel shame.
Nor is self-control properly a virtue, but a kind of mixed state. All this will be set forth in a later book.

chapters.title: Book 5 — Justice
paragraphs: The questions for our inquiry on justice and injustice are these: what kinds of actions are their object-matter, what kind of mean state justice is, and between what points the abstract principle — the just — is a mean. Let us conduct the inquiry by the method we have used in the earlier parts of this treatise.

By justice, all men mean a moral state by which men are capable of doing what is just, actually do it, and wish it. Similarly, by injustice a state by which men act unjustly and wish what is unjust. Let us take this as a rough starting sketch.

I mention wishing because states of mind and body are not like sciences or capacities. A capacity or science is thought to embrace contraries; a state does not. From health one does not do the contrary acts, only the healthy ones; we say a man walks healthily when he walks as the healthy man would.

Still, of two contrary states the one may often be known from the other, and often the states from their object-matter. If it is clear what a good bodily condition is, then it is also clear what a bad one is; and from what belongs to the good, the good itself is seen, and conversely. If the good state is firmness of flesh, then the bad state is flabbiness, and whatever causes firmness is connected with the good state.

In general, if of two contrary terms the one is used in many senses, the other will be too. So if "the just" is, then "the unjust" is. Now justice and injustice do seem to be used in many senses, but the line between these senses is so fine that it commonly escapes notice. It is not as plain as where the various senses of a word differ widely — as with the Greek kleis, which ambiguously denotes both the collarbone and the key used to lock a door.

Let us ascertain, then, in how many senses "unjust man" is used. The lawbreaker, the grasping man, and the unequal man are all thought unjust. So the just man must be the lawful man and the equal man. The just, then, is the lawful and the equal; the unjust is the unlawful and the unequal.

Since the unjust is also a grasping man, he will be so with respect to good things — but not all of them, only those that are the subject-matter of good and bad fortune, and are in themselves always good though not always so to the individual. Men pray for and pursue these things, though they should not; they should pray that what is good in the abstract may also be good for them, and choose what is good for themselves.

But the unjust man does not always choose the greater share; sometimes even the lesser, in the case of things that are simply evil. Still, since the lesser evil is thought in a way to be a good, and grasping is after good, he is in this case too thought to be a grasping man — that is, one who strives for more good than falls to his share. He is also an unequal man, this being an inclusive general term.

We said the lawbreaker is unjust and the law-keeper just. All lawful things are in a manner just, because what has been defined by the legislative power we call lawful, and each of these we say is just. The laws give directions on all matters, aiming either at the common good of all, or that of the best, or that of those in power (taking their standard from real goodness, or from some other criterion). So in one sense we mean by just the things that produce and preserve happiness and its ingredients for the community.

The law commands the actions of the brave man (not leaving the ranks, not fleeing, not throwing away one's arms), and those of the self-masterer (abstaining from adultery and wantonness), and those of the meek man (refraining from striking others or using abusive language). Similarly with the other virtues and vices, commanding some things and forbidding others, rightly if it is a good law, in a way somewhat inferior if it is one that has been extemporized.
Justice in this sense is in fact perfect virtue, not simply, but as exercised toward one's neighbor. For this reason justice is often thought the best of the virtues, and
"neither evening star nor morning star so worthy of our admiration,"
and in a proverb we express the same:
"All virtue is in justice comprehended."

It is perfect virtue in a special sense, because it is the exercise of perfect virtue. It is perfect because the man who has it can practice his virtue toward his neighbor and not merely on himself. Many can practice virtue in regulating their own personal conduct who cannot in their dealings with others. That is why Bias's saying is thought a good one:
"Office will show the man."

For the man who holds office is necessarily in contact with others — in a community. For this same reason justice alone of the virtues is thought to be a good to others, because it has immediate relation to another person: the just man does what is advantageous to another, whether his ruler or his fellow-subject. The worst man is he who practices vice not only in his own person but toward his friends also; the best is he who practices virtue not merely in himself but toward his neighbor, since this is somewhat difficult.

Justice in this sense is not a part of virtue but co-extensive with virtue; and the corresponding injustice is not a part of vice but co-extensive with vice. Wherein justice in this sense differs from virtue appears from what has been said: it is really the same, but the point of view differs. As it is related to one's neighbor, it is justice; as it is a certain moral state, it is simply virtue.

But the object of our inquiry is justice as a part of virtue (for there is such a thing, as we commonly say), and likewise particular injustice. That this exists is shown by the following. There are many vices by practicing which a man acts unjustly but does not grasp at more than his share of good. If, from cowardice, he throws away his shield; or from temper, uses abusive language; or from stinginess, refuses a friend monetary help. But whenever a man does a grasping action, it is often in the way of none of these vices, certainly not of all of them, but still in the way of some vice, and in the way of injustice. There is, then, some kind of injustice distinct from that co-extensive with vice and related to it as a part to a whole; and some "unjust" related as a part to a whole to the unjust co-extensive with violation of law.

Suppose one man seduces a married woman with a view to gain and actually profits, and another does the same from lust, at cost of money and damage to himself. The latter will be thought lacking in self-mastery rather than grasping, while the former is unjust and not lacking in self-mastery. Why? Clearly because of his gain.

All other acts of injustice we refer to some particular depravity: adultery to abandonment to passion, desertion of a comrade to cowardice, striking another to anger. But gaining by the act, we refer to no other vice than injustice.

Thus it is clear that there is a kind of injustice distinct from and besides the total injustice that includes all vice, but having the same name because its definition is in the same genus. Both have their force in dealings with others, but the one acts upon honor, wealth, safety — or whatever single name we can use to include all these — and is moved by the pleasure attendant on gain, while the other acts upon the whole sphere of the good man's action.

That there is more than one kind of justice, and one that is distinct from and besides the kind co-extensive with virtue, is now plain. We must next ascertain what it is and what its characteristics are.

The unjust has been divided into the unlawful and the unequal, and the just into the lawful and the equal. The injustice previously described is the unlawful kind. Just as the unequal and the more are not the same, but related as part to whole (all "more" is unequal, but not all unequal is "more"), the unjust and injustice we are now looking for are not the same as, but other than, those previously mentioned. They are the parts; those were the wholes. This particular injustice is a part of the injustice co-extensive with vice, and this particular justice is a part of the justice co-extensive with virtue. So what we must now discuss is the particular justice and injustice, and the particular just and unjust.

Let us set aside further consideration of the justice co-extensive with virtue (the practice of virtue in all its bearings toward others) and of the corresponding injustice (the practice of vice similarly). We must also separate off the just and unjust involved in these. One may fairly say that most lawful things are those that result naturally in action from virtue in its fullest sense, since the law enjoins living according to each virtue and forbids living according to each vice. The producing causes of virtue in all its bearings are the enactments about education for the community.

By the way, as to individual education — by which a man is simply good without reference to others — whether this is the province of political science or some other science must be determined later. It may be that being a good man and being a good citizen are not the same in every case.

Of particular justice and the corresponding just, one kind is concerned with the distribution of honor, wealth, or other things shareable among members of the community (here one man compared with another may have an equal or an unequal share); the other is the corrective kind, at work in various transactions between man and man.

This latter has two parts, since some transactions are voluntary and some involuntary. Voluntary ones include selling, buying, use, bail, borrowing, deposit, and hiring; they are called voluntary because the origin of these transactions is voluntary.

Involuntary transactions are either secret — theft, adultery, poisoning, pimping, kidnapping of slaves, assassination, false witness — or accompanied by open violence: insult, binding, death, plunder, maiming, foul language, slanderous abuse.

The unjust man, we have said, is unequal, and the abstract unjust is unequal. Clearly there is some mean of the unequal, namely the equal or exact half; in whatever admits of "greater" and "less," there is also the equal. If the unjust is unequal, the just is equal, which everyone will allow without proof; and as the equal is a mean, the just is a mean too. The equal implies at least two terms. So the just is both a mean and an equal; and these to certain persons — as a mean, between certain things (the greater and the less); as equal, between two; as just, to certain persons. The just then must imply four terms: two persons for whom it is just, and two terms representing the things.

There must be the same equality between the persons as between the things. As the things stand to one another, so must the persons; if the persons are not equal, they must not have equal shares. This is the source of all quarrels: when equals have and are given unequal shares, or when unequals have equal shares. The necessity of this equality of ratios is shown by the phrase "according to rate"; all agree that the just in distributions should be according to some rate, though they disagree on what rate: democrats say freedom, oligarchs wealth, others nobility of birth, the aristocratic party virtue.

The just, then, is a proportionate thing. Proportion is not merely of abstract number, but of number generally, since it is equality of ratios and implies at least four terms. (In discrete proportion this is plain; it is also true of continuous proportion, which uses one term as two and mentions it twice. Thus A:B:C expressed as A:B::B:C — B is named twice; if B is actually written twice, the proportionals become four.) The just likewise implies at least four terms, and the ratio between the two pairs is the same, because the persons and the things are divided similarly. So: A:B::C:D, and by alternation A:C::B:D. (With C and D representing the things,) A+C:B+D::A:B. The distribution consists in joining these terms; if they are joined so as to preserve this same ratio, the distribution joins them justly. The joining together of the first and third and of the second and fourth is the just in distribution; this just is the mean relative to what violates proportion, since proportion is a mean and the just is proportionate. Mathematicians call this geometrical proportion, because in geometrical proportion the whole is to the whole as each part to each part. Further, this proportion is not continuous, because one person-and-thing pairing does not make up one term.

The just, then, is this proportionate; and the unjust is what violates proportion. So one comes to have the greater, the other the less. This is indeed the case in actual transactions: the one who acts unjustly has the greater share, and the one treated unjustly has the less, of what is good. But with what is bad, this is reversed, since the lesser evil compared with the greater counts as good, being more choice-worthy, and what is choice-worthy is good — and the more so, the greater good.
This, then, is one species of the just.

The remaining one is the corrective, which arises in voluntary as well as involuntary transactions. This kind of just has a different form. What is concerned with distribution of common property always follows the proportion described: if the division is made from common property, the shares will bear the same proportion to one another as the original contributions did; and the unjust opposite to this just violates the proportionate.

But the just in transactions between men is equal in a certain sense, and the unjust is unequal — not according to that geometrical proportion, but according to arithmetical. It makes no difference whether a robbery is committed by a good man on a bad one or by a bad man on a good one, nor whether a good or a bad man has committed adultery. The law looks only at the difference created by the injury and treats the men as previously equal. Where one does and the other suffers injury, or one has done and the other suffered harm, this unjust — being unequal — the judge tries to reduce to equality again. When one has been wounded and the other has struck him, or one kills and the other dies, the suffering and the doing are divided into unequal shares. The judge tries to restore equality by penalty, taking from the gain.

"Gain" and "loss" are the terms applied in such cases, though they may not be strictly proper in every instance. "Gain" sits oddly with the man who gave a blow, and "loss" with the one who received it; still, once the suffering has been estimated, the one is called loss and the other gain.

The equal is a mean between the more and the less, which represent gain and loss in contrary ways. More of good and less of evil is gain; less of good and more of evil is loss; and between these the equal is the mean, which we call just. The corrective just, then, is the mean between loss and gain. That is why, in disputes, men have recourse to the judge: going to the judge is in fact going to the just, since the judge is meant to be the personification of the just. Men seek a judge as one in the mean; some even call judges middle-men, assuming that if they hit the mean, they hit the just. The just is a mean, then, since the judge is also.

So the judge's office is to make things equal. As if a line were unequally divided, he takes from the greater part the amount by which it exceeds the half, and adds it to the lesser. When the whole is divided into two exactly equal portions, men say they have their own, having received the equal. The equal is a mean between greater and less according to arithmetical equality.

This, by the way, accounts for the etymology of the Greek words for just and judge: dikaion is as if dichaion ("in two parts"), and dikastēs is as if dichastēs ("he who divides into two parts"). For when from one of two equal magnitudes something has been taken and added to the other, the latter exceeds the former by twice that portion; had it merely been taken from the former and not added to the latter, the latter would have exceeded the former by only that one portion. As it is, the greater exceeds the mean by one, and the mean exceeds by one that magnitude from which the portion was taken. This gives a rule for what to take from the one with the greater and what to add to the one with the lesser: the excess of the mean over the less must be added to the less, and the excess of the greater over the mean must be taken from the greater.

Let there be three straight lines of equal length. From one, cut off a portion; add it to another. The whole made by addition will exceed the remainder of the first line by twice the portion added, and will exceed the untouched line by that portion. The terms "loss" and "gain" come from voluntary exchange: having more than one's own is called gaining; having less than one's original stock, losing. This is seen in buying, selling, and other transactions guaranteed by law. When the result is neither more nor less, but exactly the same as before, people say they have their own, and neither lose nor gain.
The just we have been discussing, then, is a mean between loss and gain arising in involuntary transactions: having the same after the transaction as one had before it took place.

Some, following the Pythagoreans, think reciprocation is simply just; they defined the just without qualification as "that which reciprocates with another." But simple reciprocation fits neither the distributive just nor the corrective — though this is how they interpret Rhadamanthus' rule of the just,
"If a man should suffer what he has done, there would be straightforward justice."

Many differences arise: for example, if a magistrate has struck a man, he is not to be struck in return; if a man has struck a magistrate, he must not only be struck but also punished. Voluntariness or involuntariness also makes a great difference.

But in dealings of exchange, such a principle of justice as reciprocation forms the bond of union — only it must be reciprocation according to proportion and not exact equality. For by proportionate reciprocity of action the community is held together. Either reciprocity of evil is meant (and if not allowed, the condition seems servile), or reciprocity of good; and without this last there is no admission to participation, which is the very bond of union.

This is the moral of placing the Temple of the Graces (charites) in public thoroughfares: to impress the notion that there should be requital, this being the point of charis. One ought to requite with a good turn the man who has done one a favor, and then become the originator of another charis by doing him a favor.

Acts of mutual giving in due proportion may be represented by the diagonals of a parallelogram. At the four corners the two parties and their wares are placed, so that the side connecting the parties is opposite to that connecting the wares, and each party is connected by one side with his own ware, as in the diagram.

The builder is to receive from the shoemaker part of the shoemaker's ware and to give of his own. If there is first proportionate equality, and then reciprocation takes place, there will be the just result we are speaking of. Otherwise there is no equality and no lasting relation; there is no reason why the ware of one should not be better than the other's, and therefore before the exchange is made they must have been equalized. So it is in the other arts too; they would be destroyed entirely if there were not a correspondence in quantity and quality between producer and consumer. No dealing arises between two of the same kind — two physicians, say — but between a physician and a farmer, or more generally between those who are different and not equal; and these must have been equalized before exchange can occur.

Therefore all things to be exchanged must be capable of comparison. For this purpose money has come in, serving as a kind of medium, for it measures all things, including excess and defect — for instance, how many shoes are equal to a house or a given quantity of food. So many shoes must bear to a house (or food, if a farmer is exchanging with a shoemaker) the same ratio as the builder to the shoemaker; without this proportion there cannot be exchange or dealing, and the proportion cannot hold unless the terms are in some way equal. Hence the need, as said above, of some one measure of all things. This measure is really demand, which is the common bond of all such dealings. If the parties had no wants, or not similarly wanted one another's wares, either there would be no exchange, or not the same exchange.

By general agreement, money has come to be a representative of demand. The account of its Greek name nomisma is that it is what it is not by nature but by custom or law (nomos); it rests with us to change its value or make it wholly useless.

There will be reciprocation, then, when the terms have been equalized so as to stand in this proportion: farmer:shoemaker::wares of shoemaker:wares of farmer. They must be brought to this form of proportion when they exchange; otherwise one extreme will combine both deviations from the mean. When they have exactly their own, they are equal and have dealings, because the same equality can come to be in their case. Let A represent a farmer, C his food, B a shoemaker, D his wares equalized with A's. Then the proportion will be correct: A:B::C:D; now reciprocation will be practicable — without it there would have been no dealing.

That what connects men in such transactions is demand, as being some single thing, is shown by the fact that when either party does not want the other, or neither wants the other, they do not exchange at all; they do exchange when one wants what the other has — wine, for instance, in return for corn for export.

Further, money is a kind of security for exchange at a future time (supposing one wants nothing now, one will have it when one does); the theory of money being that whenever one brings it, one can receive commodities in exchange. Of course this too is liable to depreciation, since its purchasing power is not always the same, but still money is more permanent than the commodities it represents. This is why all things should have a price set on them: there may then be exchange at any time, and if exchange, dealing. So money, like a measure, makes all things commensurable and equalizes them. Without exchange there would be no dealing; without equality, no exchange; without commensurability, no equality. It is impossible that things so widely different should be really commensurate, but we can approximate sufficiently for all practical purposes by reference to demand. The common measure must be some one thing, and by agreement (for which reason it is called nomisma); this makes all things commensurable. All things, in fact, are measured by money. Let B be ten minas, A a house worth five minas (so, half B), C a bed worth 1/10 of B. It is clear how many beds equal one house — five.
Clearly exchange was conducted in this way before money existed; it makes no difference whether you give for a house five beds or the price of five beds.

We have now said what the abstract just and unjust are. Given these definitions, it is plain that acting justly is a mean between acting unjustly and being acted unjustly toward: the former is equivalent to having more, the latter to having less.
Justice, we should note, is a mean state — not in the same manner as the virtues already mentioned, but because it aims at producing the mean, while injustice occupies both extremes.

Justice is the moral state in virtue of which the just man is said to be able to practice what is just by moral choice, and to make just division — between himself and another, or between two others — not giving himself the greater and his neighbor the lesser share of what is choice-worthy (and the reverse of what is hurtful), but giving what is proportionately equal; and similarly when adjudging the rights of two others.

Injustice is all this with respect to the unjust. Since the unjust is excess or deficiency of what is good or hurtful respectively, in violation of proportion, injustice is both excess and deficiency, because it aims at producing excess and deficiency. In a man's own case, it aims at excess of what is simply advantageous and deficiency of what is hurtful; in the case of other men, likewise (speaking generally), only that the proportionate is violated not always in one direction, but in whichever way happens in the given case. Of the unjust act, the lesser form is being unjustly dealt with, and the greater is acting unjustly toward others.
Let this description of the nature of justice and injustice, and of the just and unjust in general, be sufficient.

Since a man may do unjust acts and yet not have formed an unjust character, the question arises whether a man is unjust in each particular form — a thief, an adulterer, a robber — by merely doing acts of that character.

The answer is that this alone does not make the difference. A man may have had relations with another's wife, knowing with whom he was sinning, but have done it not by deliberate choice but under impulse of passion. He acts unjustly, but has not necessarily formed an unjust character; he may have stolen but not be a thief; committed adultery but not be an adulterer, and so on.

We have already spoken of the relation of reciprocation to the just. We should now note that the just we are investigating is both the just in the abstract and as exhibited in social relations. The latter arises between those who live together with a view to self-sufficiency, who are free and equal — either proportionately or numerically.

Those not in such a position do not have the social just among themselves, though some just of a kind, resembling social just. Just implies mutually acknowledged law, and law the possibility of injustice, for adjudication is the act of distinguishing between the just and the unjust.

Among those for whom injustice is possible, acting unjustly is possible; but it does not hold conversely that injustice attaches wherever acting unjustly is possible. By injustice in this strong sense we mean assigning oneself the larger share of what is abstractly good and the lesser of what is abstractly evil.

This is why we do not allow a man to rule, but principle; a man rules for himself and becomes a despot. A ruler's office is to be guardian of the just and therefore of the equal. Since the just man takes no special personal advantage — he does not allot himself the larger share of abstract good unless it falls to him proportionately — he really rules for others. That is why men say justice is a good not to oneself so much as to others, as mentioned earlier. Therefore some compensation must be given the ruler, as there actually is in the form of honor and privilege; where these are not adequate, rulers turn into despots.

But the just arising in the relations of master and father is not identical with this, only similar. There is no possibility of injustice toward what is absolutely one's own; a slave or a child (while still at an age not separated into an independent being) is, as it were, part of oneself, and no one chooses to hurt himself. Hence there cannot be injustice toward oneself. Therefore there is no social unjust or just, which was said to exist in accordance with law, among those for whom law naturally exists — those among whom there is equality of ruling and being ruled.
Hence the just applies rather between a man and his wife than between a man and his children or slaves; this is the just arising in domestic relations. And this is different from the social just.

The social just is of two kinds, natural and conventional. Natural has the same force everywhere and does not depend on our accepting it or not. Conventional is what, before enactment, might be this way or that indifferently, but is fixed afterwards — the price of ransom being fixed at a mina, or sacrificing a goat instead of two sheep, and all matters of special enactment, such as sacrificing to Brasidas as a hero; in short, all matters of special decree.

Some think all justs are of this latter kind, on the ground that whatever exists by nature is unchangeable and has everywhere the same force (fire, for instance, burns not here only but in Persia as well), while the justs they see changed in various places.

This is not really so, but is so in a way — though among the gods perhaps not at all. Among us, at least, there is something existing by nature; even granting that everything is subject to change, there is that which exists by nature and that which does not.

More: it is practically clear what, among things that can be otherwise, does exist by nature and what does not but depends on enactment and convention — even granting that both are subject to change. The same distinctive illustration applies here as elsewhere: the right hand is by nature the stronger, yet some men may become equally strong in both.

A parallel can be drawn between justs that depend on convention and expedience, and measures. Wine and corn measures are not equal in all places; they are larger where men buy, smaller where these same men sell. Likewise justs that are not natural but human inventions are not everywhere the same, for not even forms of government are; yet there is only one that by nature would be best everywhere.

Of justs and lawfuls, each bears to the acts that embody it the relation of universal to particular: the acts are many, but each principle is only singular because it is a universal. Hence there is a difference between an unjust act and the abstract unjust, and between a just act and the abstract just. A thing is unjust in itself, by nature or ordinance; when this has been embodied in act, there is an unjust act — not until then, only some unjust thing. Likewise of a just act. (Perhaps dikaiopragēma is the more correct generic term for just act, while the word dikaiōma, which I have been using, properly means an act corrective of an unjust act.) As to each of these, what kinds there are, how many, and what their object-matter is, we must examine later.

For now we say this: the justs and unjusts being as described, a man is said to act unjustly or justly when he embodies these abstracts in voluntary actions. When he does so involuntarily, he acts neither unjustly nor justly except accidentally; being just or unjust is only accidental to such agents.

So both unjust and just actions are defined by being voluntary or otherwise. When the unjust is embodied voluntarily, it is blamed and is also an unjust action; if voluntariness is absent, there is a thing in itself unjust but not yet an unjust action.

By voluntary, I mean, as before, whatever a man does with things in his own power, with knowledge, and without ignorance of the person to whom, the instrument with which, or the result with which he does it (for instance, whom he strikes, with what, and with what probable result), and each of these not accidentally nor under compulsion. Suppose someone were to seize his hand and strike a third person with it; the owner of the hand does not act voluntarily, since it did not rest with him to do or leave undone. Again, the person struck may be his father, and he may know he is striking a man, or even one of the present company, without knowing it is his father. Similar distinctions apply to the result and in fact to the whole of any action. In short, involuntary is what is done through ignorance, or what, though not from ignorance, is not in the agent's control or is done under compulsion.
I mention these cases because many natural things we do and suffer knowingly are neither voluntary nor involuntary — growing old, or dying, for instance.

Accidentality can also attach to unjust acts just as to just ones. A man may have restored a deposit, but against his will, from fear of the consequences of refusal; we must not say he does what is just, or acts justly, except accidentally. Similarly, the man who under compulsion and against his will fails to restore a deposit acts unjustly, or does what is unjust, accidentally only.

Again, voluntary actions we do either from deliberate choice or without it — from it when we act from previous deliberation, without it when we do not. Since the harms done in transactions between men are threefold, the mistakes attended with ignorance are these: a man does a thing not to the man he intended, not the thing he intended, not with the instrument he intended, or not with the intended result. He did not think he would hit him at all, or not with this, or this was not the man he thought he would hit, or he did not think this would be the result — as when he did it not to wound but merely to prick, or it is not the man whom, or the way in which, he meant.

When the harm has come about contrary to all reasonable expectation, it is a misadventure; when not contrary to expectation but without viciousness, it is a mistake (a mistake being when the origin rests with the agent himself; a misadventure when it is external to him). When a man acts knowingly but without previous deliberation, it is an unjust action — for example, what is done from anger or other passions that are necessary or natural. In doing these harms or making these mistakes, men act unjustly and their actions are unjust, but they are not yet confirmed unjust or wicked persons on this account, since the harm did not arise from depravity in the doer. But when the harm arises from deliberate choice, then the doer is a confirmed unjust and depraved man.

On this principle, acts done from anger are fairly judged not to be done with malice aforethought; the person really in the wrong is not the one who acts in wrath but the one who caused his wrath. And the dispute is not over the fact, but over the justice of the case — the occasion of anger being a sense of injury. They do not dispute the fact, as in questions of contract (where one party must be a knave, unless real forgetfulness can be pleaded); rather, admitting the fact, they dispute on which side the justice lies. The one who plotted against the other — the real aggressor — cannot be ignorant, and so the one thinks there is injustice, the other does not.

A man acts unjustly, then, if he has hurt another of deliberate purpose; one who commits such acts of injustice is by that very fact a man of unjust character when they are in violation of the proportionate or the equal. Likewise a man is of just character when he acts justly of deliberate purpose; and he does act justly if he acts voluntarily.

As for involuntary acts of harm, they are either excusable or not. Excusable: errors done not merely in ignorance but from ignorance. Inexcusable: those done not from ignorance but in ignorance caused by some passion that is neither natural nor fairly attributable to human infirmity.
A question may be raised: have we spoken with sufficient distinctness about being unjustly dealt with, and about dealing unjustly toward others?
First: is the case possible that Euripides puts, saying somewhat strangely,
"My mother he hath slain; the tale is short — either he willingly did slay her willing, or else with her will but against his own"?

Is it really possible for a person to be unjustly dealt with with his own consent, or must every case of being unjustly dealt with be against the sufferer's will, just as every act of unjust dealing is voluntary?
Next, are cases of being unjustly dealt with to be ruled all one way, as every act of unjust dealing is voluntary? Or may we say some are voluntary and some involuntary?

Similarly with being justly dealt with: all just action is voluntary, so it is fair to expect that being dealt with unjustly or justly must be correspondingly opposed — either voluntary or involuntary.

The claim that every case of being justly dealt with is voluntary is strange, since some are certainly dealt with justly against their will. A man may also fairly raise this question: does he who suffers what is unjust always suffer it unjustly, or is the case in suffering the same as in acting — in both it is possible to participate in what is just only accidentally? Clearly the case of what is unjust is similar: doing things in themselves unjust is not identical with acting unjustly, nor is suffering them the same as being unjustly dealt with. So too of acting justly and being justly dealt with; for it is impossible to be unjustly dealt with unless someone else acts unjustly, or to be justly dealt with unless someone else acts justly.

If acting unjustly is simply "hurting another voluntarily" (by which I mean knowing whom you are hurting, and with what, and how), and if the man who lacks self-control voluntarily hurts himself, then this would be a case of being voluntarily dealt with unjustly, and it would be possible for a man to deal unjustly with himself. (This is one of the questions raised: can a man deal unjustly with himself?) Or a man may, through lack of self-control, be hurt by another man acting voluntarily — another case of being unjustly dealt with voluntarily.

The solution, I think, is this: the definition of being unjustly dealt with is not quite right; we must add, to the hurting with knowledge of person, instrument, and manner, the fact that it is against the wish of the man hurt.

So a man may be hurt and suffer what is in itself unjust voluntarily, but no man can be unjustly dealt with voluntarily: no one wishes to be hurt, not even he who lacks self-control, who in fact acts contrary to his wish; no one wishes for what he does not think to be good, and the man who lacks self-control does not do what he thinks he ought to do.

And he who gives away his own property (as Homer says Glaucus gave to Diomedes, "armor of gold for bronze, armor worth a hundred oxen for that worth but nine") is not unjustly dealt with; the giving rests entirely with himself. Being unjustly dealt with requires that someone else deal unjustly toward him.
So it is clear that being unjustly dealt with is not voluntary.

Two points we set out to discuss still remain. First: is he chargeable with an unjust act who in a distribution has given the larger share to another in contravention of proper ratio, or is it the one who has the larger share? Second: can a man deal unjustly with himself?

On the first, if the distributor acts unjustly and not the one who has the larger share, then if a person knowingly and willingly gives another more than himself, here is a case of a man dealing unjustly with himself — which moderate men are in fact thought to do, since it is characteristic of the fair-minded man to take less than his due.

Is not this the answer? The case is not quite fairly stated. In the supposed case, through some other good — credit, say, or the abstractly honorable — the man did get the larger share. And the difficulty is solved by referring to the definition of unjust dealing: the man suffers nothing contrary to his wish, so on this score he is not unjustly dealt with — only hurt, if anything.

It is also evident that it is the distributor who acts unjustly, not the one with the greater share. The mere fact that the abstract unjust attaches to what a man does does not constitute unjust action; the action must be voluntary. Voluntariness attaches where the origin of the action is, and this is clearly in the distributor, not in the receiver. And the term "doing" is used in several senses; in one, inanimate objects kill, or the hand, or the slave by his master's bidding; so the receiver does not act unjustly but does things which are in themselves unjust.

Suppose a man has made a wrongful award in ignorance. In the eye of the law he does not act unjustly, nor is his award unjust; yet in a certain sense it is, since the just according to law and the primary or natural just do not coincide. But if he knowingly decided unjustly, then he himself, like the receiver, got the larger share — either of favor from the receiver or of private revenge against the other party. The man who decided unjustly from these motives got a larger share, in exactly the sense in which one does who receives part of the actual matter of the unjust action; in this case the man who wrongly adjudged, say, a field, got not land but money by his unjust decision.

Men suppose that acting unjustly rests entirely with themselves, and conclude that acting justly is therefore also easy. But this is not so. To have relations with a neighbor's wife, or strike a neighbor, or hand over money, is indeed easy and rests with oneself; but doing these acts with certain inner dispositions is neither easy nor entirely within one's power. Similarly, men think that knowing what is just and what unjust is no great instance of wisdom, because it is not hard to grasp what the laws speak of. They forget that these are not just actions except accidentally; to be just, such actions must be done and distributed in a certain way — a more difficult task than knowing what is wholesome. In medicine it is easy to know honey, wine, hellebore, cautery, or the use of the knife; but to know how to administer these with a view to health, and to whom and when, amounts in fact to being a physician.

From the same mistake they also suppose that acting unjustly is equally in the power of the just man — since the just man no less, nay even more, than the unjust may be able to do the particular acts: he may have relations with a woman or strike a man; or the brave man may throw down his shield and turn his back and run. True. But the mere doing of these things does not constitute acts of cowardice or injustice (except accidentally); what does is doing them with certain inner dispositions. Just as it is not the mere using or not using of the knife, or administering or not administering certain drugs, that constitutes medical treatment or curing, but doing these things in a particular way.

Further, the abstract principles of justice have their province among those who partake of what is abstractly good, and can have too much or too little of it. Some beings cannot have too much of it — perhaps the gods. Others find no use in any part of it — those incurably wicked, to whom all things are hurtful. Others find them useful to a certain degree. For this reason the province of justice is among human beings.

Next we must discuss equity and the equitable — their relation to justice and the just. On examination the two do not appear identical, yet not different in kind. Sometimes we commend the equitable and the man who embodies it, so that by way of praise we commonly transfer the term to other acts instead of "good," showing that the more equitable a thing is the better it is. At other times, following a certain train of reasoning, we arrive at a difficulty, in that the equitable though distinct from the just is yet praiseworthy; it seems to follow that either the just is not good, or the equitable is not just (since by hypothesis they are different); or else, if both are good, they are identical.

This is a fair statement of the difficulty that arises on these grounds about the equitable. But all these views can be reconciled and involve no contradiction. The equitable is just, being also better than one form of just; but it is not better than the just as if different from it in kind. The just and the equitable are identical, and, both being good, the equitable is the better.

What causes the difficulty is that the equitable is just — but not the just according to written law; it is in fact a correction of that kind of just. The reason is that every law is necessarily universal, while some things cannot be stated rightly in any general formula. Where there is a necessity for general statement, and a general statement cannot apply rightly to all cases, the law takes the generality of cases, fully aware of the error thus involved; and rightly too, since the fault lies not in the law nor in the lawgiver but in the nature of the thing, because the matter of action is necessarily such.

When the law has spoken in general terms and a case of exception to the rule arises, it is proper — insofar as the lawgiver omits the case and is wrong through his universality of statement — to set the omission right by deciding as the lawgiver himself would have decided were he present, and would have provided by law had he foreseen the case. So the equitable is just, but better than one form of just: not better than the abstract just, but better than the error that arises from universality of statement. This is the nature of the equitable: a correction of law where it is defective by reason of its universality.

This is also why not everything is according to law; for some things it is impossible to lay down a law, and so special enactments are needed for particular cases. To speak generally, the measure of the undefined must itself be undefined — as the Lesbian rule is made of lead, shifting to the shape of each stone; so the special enactment shifts to the facts of the particular case.

It is clear then what the equitable is: it is just but better than one form of just. From this it also appears who the equitable man is: one with a tendency to choose and carry out these principles, not apt to press the letter of the law on the worse side, content to waive his strict claims even though backed by the law. This moral state is equity — a species of justice, not a different moral state from justice.
The answer to the second question raised above — whether a man can deal unjustly with himself — is obvious from what has been said.

First: one class of justs is those enforced by law in accordance with virtue in the widest sense. For instance, the law does not bid a man kill himself; whatever it does not bid, it forbids. Whenever a man voluntarily hurts another contrary to the law (unless by way of requital), knowing whom he hurts and with what, he acts unjustly. One who in a rage kills himself voluntarily does this contrary to right reason, which the law does not permit. He therefore acts unjustly — but toward whom? Toward the community, not toward himself (since he suffers with his own consent, and no one can be unjustly dealt with with his own consent). For this reason the community punishes him; a certain infamy attaches to the suicide, as to one who acts unjustly toward the community.

Next, a man cannot deal unjustly with himself in the sense in which a man is unjust who only does unjust acts without being entirely bad. These two are different; the unjust man is in a way bad, as the coward is, not as though he were chargeable with badness in the full extent of the term; so he does not act unjustly in this sense. If self-injustice were possible, it would imply that the same thing could be taken away from and added to the same person — but this is impossible, the just and the unjust always implying more than one person.

An unjust action must be voluntary, done from deliberate purpose, and aggressive (for the man who hurts because he has first suffered and merely requites is not thought to act unjustly); but here the man does to himself and suffers the same things at the same time.
Further, it would imply the possibility of being unjustly dealt with with one's own consent.
And besides, a man cannot act unjustly without his act falling under some particular crime; but a man cannot seduce his own wife, burgle his own premises, or steal his own property.
The general answer to the question is to cite what was settled earlier about being unjustly dealt with with one's own consent.

It is also obvious that being unjustly dealt with and dealing unjustly with others are both wrong. The one is having less, the other having more than the mean, parallel to the health in medicine and the good condition in athletic training. But dealing unjustly with others is the worse, since it involves wickedness and is blameworthy — wickedness wholly, or nearly so (not all voluntary wrong implies injustice); being unjustly dealt with does not involve wickedness or injustice.

In itself, then, being unjustly dealt with is the less bad; but accidentally it may be the greater evil. Scientific statement cannot take in such cases. A pleurisy is called a greater physical evil than a bruise, yet the bruise may be the greater accidentally — a bruise from a fall may cause one to be captured by the enemy and killed.

Further, just may exist metaphorically between certain parts of a man's nature (I do not say between a man and himself exactly), but not every kind of just — only that belonging to the relation of master and slave, or of head of a family. Throughout this treatise the rational part of the soul has been viewed as distinct from the irrational.

Taking these into consideration, there is thought to be a possibility of injustice toward oneself, since in this sphere one can suffer something in contradiction to impulses really one's own. So there is thought to be a just of a certain kind between these parts mutually, as between ruler and ruled.
Let this be accepted as our account of the distinctions we recognize regarding justice and the rest of the moral virtues.

chapters.title: Book 6 — Intellectual Virtue
paragraphs: Having said earlier that men should choose the mean instead of excess or deficiency, and that the mean is according to the dictates of right reason, we will now explain this term.

In all the habits we have explicitly mentioned, as in all the others, there is, so to speak, a mark; the man who has reason, with his eye fixed on it, tightens or slackens the rope. There is a certain limit to the mean states we say accord with right reason, lying between excess on one side and deficiency on the other.

To speak this way is true enough, but it conveys no very definite meaning. In all other pursuits that demand attention and diligence, where skill and science are brought to bear, it is equally true to say that one must neither labor nor relax too much or too little, but in moderation, as right reason directs. Yet a man who had only this would not be much the wiser — as if, asked what are proper applications to the body, he were told, "Oh, whatever the science of medicine and the physician direct."
In respect of the mental states, then, it is not enough to say what has already been said. We must further spell out what right reason is and what its definition is.

In dividing the excellences of the soul we said there were two classes, the moral and the intellectual. We have already covered the moral. We will now speak of the intellectual, premising a few words on the soul itself. As stated before, the soul consists of two parts, the rational and the irrational. We must now make a similar division of the rational.

Let us take it that there are two parts of the soul possessed of reason: one by which we grasp things whose principles cannot be otherwise than they are, and one by which we grasp things that can be otherwise. (To things generically different, there must correspond generically different parts of the soul, naturally adapted to each, since these parts of the soul possess their knowledge in virtue of a certain resemblance and appropriateness to their objects.) Let us call the former the "scientific" part, and the latter the "calculative" (since deliberating and calculating are the same, and no one ever deliberates about things that cannot be otherwise). The calculative, then, is one part of the rational faculty of the soul.
We must discover the best state of each of these, since this will be the excellence of each; and this again is relative to the work each has to do.

There are in the soul three functions on which depend moral action and truth: sense, intellect, and appetition (whether vague desire or definite will). Sense is the originating cause of no moral action, as is seen from the fact that animals have sense but in no way partake of moral action.

Intellect and will are connected thus: what in intellect is affirmation and negation, in will is pursuit and avoidance. Since moral virtue is a state apt to exercise moral choice, and moral choice is will consequent on deliberation, reason must be true and will right for good moral choice; what reason affirms, the will must pursue.

This intellectual operation and this truth bear on moral action. Truth and falsehood are the good and bad of intellectual operation that is purely speculative, not concerned with action or production; for this is the work of every intellectual faculty. The work of the faculty that is a mix of practical and intellectual is the truth that, as described above, corresponds to the right movement of the will.

The starting point of moral action is moral choice (I mean what actually sets it in motion, not its final cause); and of moral choice, appetition and reason directed to a certain result. Moral choice is thus neither independent of intellect, that is, of intellectual operation, nor of a certain moral state; right or wrong action cannot arise independently of intellect and of moral character.

But operation of the intellect by itself moves nothing; only when directed to a certain result — when exercised in moral action. (I say nothing here of its being exercised in production, for this function is originated by moral action; every one who makes, makes with a view to something further; what is or may be made is not an end in itself but only relative to something else, and belongs to some one. What is done, by contrast, is an end in itself; acting well is itself an end, and this is the object of will.) So moral choice is either intellect put in a position of willing, or appetition subjected to an intellectual process. Such a cause is man.

Nothing done and past can be the object of moral choice; no man chooses to have sacked Troy, for no one ever deliberates about what is past, only about what is future and therefore can still be influenced — the past cannot be undone. Agathon is right to say,
"Of this alone is deity bereft — to make undone whatever has been done."
Truth, then, is the work of both intellectual parts of the soul. The excellences of each are those states in which each will best attain truth.

Starting from the point just made, we will now speak of these excellences again. Let the faculties by which the soul attains truth in affirmation or negation be assumed to be five: art, scientific knowledge, practical wisdom, philosophic wisdom, and intuition. (Supposition and opinion I do not include, since with these one may go wrong.)

What scientific knowledge is, is plain from the following considerations, speaking strictly rather than being led away by resemblances. We all conceive that what we strictly know cannot be otherwise than it is. For as to things that can be otherwise, the moment they are out of our actual observation, we are uncertain whether they are or are not.

So whatever comes within the range of scientific knowledge is necessary, and therefore eternal (since all things that exist necessarily are so), and all eternal things are without beginning and indestructible.

Again, all scientific knowledge is thought to be teachable, and what comes within its range to be learnable. All teaching is based on previous knowledge (as stated also in the Analytics), for there are two ways of teaching: by syllogism and by induction. Induction is the source of universal propositions, and syllogism reasons from these universals. So syllogism may reason from principles that cannot themselves be proved syllogistically, and these must be grasped by induction.

So scientific knowledge is "a state or mental faculty apt to demonstrate syllogistically," and so on as in the Analytics. A man knows strictly and properly when he establishes his conclusion in a certain way and the principles are known to him. If the principles are not better known to him than the conclusion, whatever knowledge he has will be merely accidental.
Let this be our definition of scientific knowledge.

Matter that may exist otherwise than it actually does in any given case (commonly called contingent) is of two kinds: that which is the object of making, and that which is the object of doing. Making and doing are distinct (as we show in the exoteric treatise), so that state of mind, conjoined with reason, apt to do, is distinct from that also conjoined with reason, apt to make; neither includes the other — doing is not making, nor making doing. Architecture is an art and is the same as "a certain state of mind, conjoined with reason, apt to make," and there is no art that is not such a state, nor any such state that is not an art. Art in its strict and proper sense, then, must be "a state of mind, conjoined with true reason, apt to make."
All art has to do with production and contrivance — seeing how anything may be produced that may either be or not be, whose origination rests with the maker and not with the thing made.

So neither things that exist or come into being necessarily, nor things in the way of nature, come under the province of art; these are self-originating. Since making and doing are distinct, art is concerned with the former and not the latter. In a certain sense art and fortune are concerned with the same things, as Agathon says by the way,
"Art loves fortune, and by fortune is beloved."
Art, then, is "a certain state of mind, apt to make, conjoined with true reason." Its absence is the same state conjoined with false reason, and both are employed upon contingent matter.
As for practical wisdom, we shall ascertain its nature by examining to what kind of persons we in common speech ascribe it.

It is thought to be the mark of the practically wise man to be able to deliberate well about what is good and expedient for himself — not in any definite line, such as what conduces to health or strength, but what conduces to living well. A proof is that we call men wise in this or that when they calculate well toward some good end where there is no definite rule. In a general way the man who is good at deliberation will be practically wise. No one deliberates about things that cannot be otherwise, nor about things not within his own action. Since scientific knowledge requires strict demonstrative reasoning (which contingent matter does not admit — and all matters of deliberation must be contingent, since one cannot deliberate about what is necessary), practical wisdom cannot be scientific knowledge or art. Not scientific knowledge, since what falls under doing must be contingent; not art, since doing and making differ in kind.

It remains, then, that practical wisdom must be "a true state of mind, conjoined with reason, apt to do, having as its object those things good or bad for a human being." For of making, some end beyond itself is always the object; of doing, this cannot be, since well-doing is itself an end.

This is why we think Pericles and men of that stamp practically wise: they can see what is good for themselves and for men in general. We also think those skilled in household management or civil government to be such. This is why the Greek name for self-mastery (sōphrosynē) etymologically signifies "that which preserves practical wisdom": what it preserves is the notion I have mentioned — of one's own true interest.

For it is not every kind of notion that the pleasant and the painful corrupt and pervert — not, for instance, that the three angles of every rectilinear triangle are equal to two right angles — but only those bearing on moral action.

The principles of moral action are its final causes. To the man corrupted by pleasure or pain the principle is at once obscured, nor does he see that it is his duty to choose and act in each case with a view to this final cause and for its sake; viciousness has a tendency to destroy the moral principle. Practical wisdom, then, must be "a state conjoined with reason, true, having human good as its object, and apt to do."

Again, art admits of degrees of excellence, but practical wisdom does not. In art, one who goes wrong on purpose is preferable to one who does so unwittingly; in practical wisdom or the other virtues this is not so. Plainly, then, practical wisdom is an excellence of a certain kind, not an art.

Since there are two parts of the soul that have reason, practical wisdom must be the excellence of the opinionative (formerly called calculative or deliberative), since both opinion and practical wisdom are exercised on contingent matter. Further, practical wisdom is not simply a state conjoined with reason; this is proved by the fact that such a state may be forgotten and thus lost, while practical wisdom cannot.

Scientific knowledge is a conception concerning universals and necessary matter, and there are certain first principles in all trains of demonstrative reasoning (that is, of all scientific knowledge, since this is connected with reasoning). The faculty that grasps the first principles of what falls within the range of scientific knowledge cannot be scientific knowledge, or art, or practical wisdom. Not scientific knowledge, since the object of scientific knowledge must be derived from demonstrative reasoning; not either of the other two, since they are exercised on contingent matter only. Nor can philosophic wisdom grasp these first principles, since the philosophic man must in some cases depend on demonstrative reasoning.

It comes, then, to this. The faculties by which we always attain truth and are never deceived, whether with necessary or contingent matter, are scientific knowledge, practical wisdom, philosophic wisdom, and intuition; and the faculty that grasps first principles cannot be any of the first three. So it must be intuition that performs this function.

Philosophic wisdom we use principally in two meanings. In the arts, we ascribe it to those who carry their arts to the highest accuracy; Phidias we call a wise sculptor; Polyclitus, a wise statuary; meaning here nothing else by wisdom than excellence in art. In the other sense, we call some men wise in a general way, not in any particular line or thing — as Homer says of a man in his Margites: "Him the gods made neither a digger of the ground, nor a plowman, nor in any other way wise."

Philosophic wisdom, then, must mean the most accurate of all knowledge. The wise man must know not only the deductions from first principles but also possess truth about the first principles. So philosophic wisdom is the union of intuition and scientific knowledge — knowledge of the most precious objects, so to speak, with a head on.

I say of the most precious things, because it is absurd to suppose political science, or practical wisdom, to be the highest, unless it can be shown that man is the most excellent of all that exists in the universe. If "healthy" and "good" are relative terms — differing as applied to men or fish — but "white" and "straight" are always the same, then one must allow that "philosophically wise" is always the same while "practically wise" varies. For people apply the term practically wise to whatever provides well for itself, and commit its affairs to it; this is why they call some animals practically wise — those that plainly have a faculty of foresight about their own subsistence.

It is plain that philosophic wisdom and political science cannot be identical. If we call the faculty exercised on what is expedient for oneself philosophic wisdom, there will be many rather than one, since there is not one and the same faculty for the good of all animals collectively, except in the sense in which one speaks of one art of healing for all living things.

If it is urged that man is superior to all other animals, this makes no difference; there are many other things more godlike in nature than man, as most obviously the elements of which the universe is composed.

It is plain, then, that philosophic wisdom is the union of scientific knowledge and intuition, and has for its objects the things most precious by nature. Accordingly people call Anaxagoras, Thales, and men of that stamp philosophically wise, but not practically wise, when they see them ignorant of what concerns themselves. They say what they know is out of the common run, certainly, and wonderful, and hard, and fine — but still useless, because they do not seek what is good for them as men.

Practical wisdom is exercised on human matters, and on things that can be deliberated about. To deliberate well is most peculiarly the work of the man who possesses this wisdom; no one deliberates about things that cannot be otherwise, nor about any save those having some definite end, that end being a good resulting from moral action. The man to whom, simply and without qualification, we should give the name of good in counsel is he who by calculation has a capacity for attaining the best of the practical goods for man.

Practical wisdom does not consist in knowledge of general principles only; one must also know the particular details, since it is apt to act, and action is concerned with particulars. Hence some without much general knowledge are more practical than others who have it — among them, those who draw all they know from actual experience. Suppose a man knows that light meats are easy of digestion and wholesome, but not which meats are light; he will not produce a healthy state. A man who knows that the flesh of birds is light and wholesome will have a much better chance. Since practical wisdom is apt to act, one ought to have both kinds of knowledge; or, if only one, the knowledge of particulars rather than of principles. So in practical wisdom there will be a distinction of supreme and subordinate.
Further, political science and practical wisdom are the same mental state, but the point of view differs.

Of practical wisdom exercised on a community, the supreme is the faculty of legislation; the subordinate, concerned with particulars, usually bears the common name "political science," and its functions are action and deliberation. (The particular enactment is a matter of action, being the ultimate issue of this branch of practical wisdom; and this is why people commonly say only these men are really engaged in governing, because they alone act — standing to legislators as workmen to a master builder.)

That form is thought to be practical wisdom in the most proper sense which has the interest of the individual as its object; this usually appropriates the common name. The others are called household management, legislation, and executive government, the last divided into deliberative and judicial. Knowledge for oneself is one kind of knowledge, but it admits of many shades. The common notion is that the man who knows and attends to his own concerns only is the man of practical wisdom, while those who extend their concern to society at large are considered meddlesome.

Euripides puts this sentiment in a character: "How foolish am I, who, when I might have shared equally, idly numbered among the multitude of the army *** for those that are busy and meddlesome, Zeus hates." Most men seek their own good and hold that this is their proper business. From this opinion the notion has arisen that such men are the practically wise. Yet the good of the individual may be unattainable apart from a family or a community; and how a man should manage his own affairs is sometimes not plain, and must be inquired into.

A corroboration is this: the young come to be geometricians, mathematicians, and wise in such matters, but are not thought able to possess practical wisdom. The reason is that practical wisdom has for its object particular facts, which come to be known from experience; a young man does not have this, since experience takes time.

One might ask why a boy may become a mathematician but not a philosopher or natural scientist. The reason, surely, is that mathematics is grasped by abstraction, while the principles of philosophy and natural science must be gained by experience. The young talk of the latter but do not realize them, while the nature of mathematics is plain and clear.

In matters of practice, error attaches either to the general rule in the process of deliberation, or to the particular fact. A general rule, for instance: "All water of a certain gravity is bad." The particular fact: "this water is of that gravity."
Practical wisdom is not scientific knowledge, plainly, since it has to do with the ultimate issue, as has been said; every object of action is of this nature.

It is opposed to intuition, which grasps principles that cannot be proved by reasoning, while practical wisdom is concerned with the ultimate particular fact — grasped not by scientific knowledge but by perception. I do not mean one of the five senses, but the same perception by which we grasp the mathematical fact that no rectilinear figure can be contained by fewer than three lines — that a triangle is the ultimate figure, which is also a stopping point.
This, however, is perception rather than practical wisdom, which is of another kind.

Inquiring and deliberating differ, though deliberating is a kind of inquiring. We ought to consider also what good deliberation is — whether a kind of scientific knowledge, or opinion, or happy conjecture, or some other faculty. It is obviously not scientific knowledge; men do not inquire about what they know, and good deliberation is a kind of deliberation, and the deliberator is inquiring and calculating.

Nor is it happy conjecture, which is independent of reasoning and rapid; but men deliberate at length, and it is a common saying that one should execute swiftly what one has resolved on through deliberation, but deliberate slowly.
Quick perception of causes is a different faculty from good counsel; it is a species of happy conjecture. Nor is good counsel any kind of opinion.

Since he who deliberates badly goes wrong and he who deliberates well is right, clearly good counsel is rightness of some kind — but not of scientific knowledge or of opinion. Scientific knowledge cannot be called right, since it cannot be wrong; and rightness of opinion is truth, and everything that is the object of opinion is already definitely fixed.

Still, good counsel is not independent of reason. It must, then, be a rightness of intellectual operation simply, which does not amount to an assertion. The objection to opinion was that it is not a process of inquiry but already a definite assertion; whereas the deliberator, well or ill, is engaged in inquiry and calculation.

Good counsel, then, is a rightness of deliberation. The first question concerns the nature and objects of deliberation. Rightness is an equivocal term; we plainly do not mean rightness of any kind whatever. The man lacking self-control, or a bad man, will obtain by his calculation what he sets before him as an object; he may be said to have deliberated rightly in one sense, but will have attained a great evil. To have deliberated well is thought to be a good, because good counsel is rightness of deliberation of such a kind as is apt to attain good.

But even this may be reached by false reasoning; one may hit on the right outcome by wrong means, with a fallacious middle term. This will still not be good counsel, which gets what it ought but not through proper means.
