Again, one man may hit on a thing after long deliberation, another quickly. Neither of these by itself is good counsel; rightness must be with reference to what is expedient, with a proper end in view, pursued by right means and at the right time.

One may deliberate well generally or toward some particular end. Good counsel in general, then, is rightness toward what is the end in a general way; particular good counsel is rightness toward a particular end.
Since deliberating well belongs to the practically wise, good counsel must be "rightness in respect of what conduces to a given end, of which practical wisdom is the true conception."
There is also the faculty of judiciousness (synesis), and its absence, in virtue of which we call men judicious or the contrary.

Judiciousness is not entirely identical with scientific knowledge or opinion (or everyone would be judicious), nor is it any particular science — like medicine (whose object is things wholesome) or geometry (whose object is magnitude). It does not have as its object things that always exist and are immutable, nor things that happen to come into being, but matters one might doubt and deliberate about.

So its object-matter is the same as practical wisdom's; yet the two faculties are not identical. Practical wisdom has the capacity for commanding and taking the initiative; its end is what one should do or not do. But judiciousness is apt only to decide on suggestions. (Though Greek adds "well" to the faculty and its concrete noun, these really mean the same thing as the plain words.) Judiciousness is neither the having nor the attaining of practical wisdom. Just as learning is called syniénai when a man uses his knowledge, so judiciousness consists in employing the opinionative faculty in judging matters within the province of practical wisdom, when another states them — and not judging merely, but judging well. (For "well" and "nobly" mean the same here.) The Greek word for this faculty derives from the use of syniénai in learning (manthanein and syniénai being often used as synonyms).

The faculty called gnōmē, in virtue of which we call men eugnōmones (having good gnōmē), is "the right judgment of the equitable man." This is shown by the fact that we most commonly say the equitable man has a tendency to make allowance, and making allowance in certain cases is equitable. Syngnōmē (the word for allowance or pardon) is right gnōmē, having the capacity to make equitable decisions. By "right" I mean that of the truthful man.

All these mental states tend toward the same object, as common language leads us to expect. We speak of gnōmē, judiciousness, practical wisdom, and practical intuition, attributing gnōmē and practical intuition to the same individuals we call practically wise and judicious, because all these faculties are exercised on the extremes — on particular details. By his aptitude for deciding on matters within the province of the practically wise, a man is judicious and has good gnōmē; he is disposed to make allowance, for considerations of equity are entertained by all good men alike in their dealings with others.

All matters of moral action belong to the class of particulars, also called extremes. The practically wise man must know them; and judiciousness and gnōmē are concerned with matters of moral action, which are extremes.

Intuition also grasps extremes at both ends. The first and last terms are grasped not by reasoning but by intuition (so intuition is of two kinds): that belonging to strict demonstrative reasoning grasps immutable, necessary first terms; while that employed in practical matters grasps the extreme, the contingent, the minor premise — for minor premises are the source of the final cause, universals being made out of particulars. To grasp these, we must have perception, that is, practical intuition.

For this reason these faculties are thought to be simply gifts of nature; and while no man is thought to be wise by nature, men are thought to have gnōmē, judiciousness, and practical intuition. A proof is that we think these faculties are a consequence even of particular ages: this age has practical intuition and gnōmē, we say, as if on the notion that nature is the cause. So intuition is both beginning and end, because the proofs are based on one kind of extremes and concern the other.

Therefore one should attend to the undemonstrated dicta and opinions of skillful, old, and practically wise men, no less than to those based on strict reasoning; they see aright, having gained their moral vision from experience.

We have now stated the nature and objects of practical wisdom and philosophic wisdom, and that each belongs to a different part of the soul. But one might question their utility. "Philosophic wisdom," someone might say, "concerns itself with none of the causes of human happiness — it has nothing to do with producing anything. Practical wisdom has this recommendation, I grant; but where is the need of it? Its province is things just, noble, and good for man, which are exactly what the good man as such does. We are no more apt to do them because we know them, since the moral virtues are habits — just as we are no more apt to be healthy or in good condition merely from knowing what relates to these. (I mean things so called not from their producing health but from evidencing it in a subject.) We are not healthier or better conditioned from merely knowing medicine or athletic training.

"If it is urged that knowing what is good does not by itself make a man practically wise but becoming good does, still this wisdom will be no use either to those already good (who already have it) or to those who do not; it will make no difference to them whether they have it themselves or put themselves under the guidance of others who do. We could be content to be in respect of this as in respect of health: though we wish to be healthy, we do not set about learning medicine.

"Further, it would be strange that, though lower than philosophic wisdom, practical wisdom should be its master — which it is, since whatever produces results takes the rule and directs in each matter."
These are the points we must address.
First, being excellences of different parts of the soul, they must be choice-worthy in themselves, even on the supposition that neither produces results.

Next, they do produce results. Philosophic wisdom makes happiness — not as medicine makes health, but as healthiness does. Being a part of virtue in its most extensive sense, philosophic wisdom makes a man happy by being possessed and by being active.

Next, man's work as man is accomplished by virtue of practical wisdom and moral virtue; moral virtue gives the right aim and direction, practical wisdom the right means to its attainment. (Of the fourth part of the soul — the merely nutritive — there is no such excellence, since nothing is in its power to do or leave undone.)

As to our not being more apt to do what is noble and just because we possess practical wisdom: we must begin a little higher up, with this starting point. We say men may do things in themselves just and yet not be just men — as when they do what the laws require either against their will, or through ignorance, or for some other reason, not for the sake of the things themselves. They do what they ought, yet still to be good men one must do each act in a particular frame of mind — from moral choice and for the sake of the things themselves. Now it is virtue that makes moral choice right, but whatever is naturally required to carry out that choice belongs not to virtue but to a different faculty. We must pause and speak more clearly on these points.

There is a faculty commonly called cleverness (deinotēs), of such a nature as to be able to do and attain whatever conduces to any given purpose. If that purpose is good, the faculty is praiseworthy; if otherwise, it goes by a name which, while strictly denoting ability, implies willingness to do anything. We accordingly call the practically wise clever, and also those who can and will do anything.

Practical wisdom is not identical with cleverness, nor is it without this power of adapting means to ends. But this eye of the soul, as we may call it, does not attain its proper state without goodness, as we have said and as is quite plain. The syllogisms into which moral action may be analyzed have as their major premise, "since — is the end and the chief good" (fill in the blank with whatever you please; we are merely exhibiting the form). How this blank should be filled is seen only by the good man; vice distorts moral vision and causes men to be deceived about practical principles.
It is clear, then, that a man cannot be practically wise without being good.

We must inquire again about virtue too. It may be divided into natural virtue and matured virtue, the two bearing a relation to each other similar to that which practical wisdom bears to cleverness — not identity but resemblance. I speak of natural virtue because it is held that each moral disposition attaches to us somehow by nature. We have dispositions toward justice, self-mastery, and courage immediately from birth. But we seek goodness in its highest sense as something distinct from these, and that these dispositions should attach to us in a different way. Children and animals have these natural states, but they are plainly hurtful unless combined with the intellectual element. This much at least is a matter of experience: as a strong body, if set in motion without sight, must fall violently because it has no sight, so also in the case we are considering. If it can get the intellectual element, it then excels in acting. Just so the natural state of virtue, being like this strong body, will be virtue in the highest sense only when combined with the intellectual element.

So, just as in the case of the opinionative faculty there are two forms (cleverness and practical wisdom), so also in the moral case there are two: natural virtue and matured virtue. The latter cannot be formed without practical wisdom.

This leads some to say that all the virtues are merely intellectual practical wisdom. Socrates was partly right and partly wrong in his inquiry: wrong in thinking all the virtues were merely forms of practical wisdom, right in saying they were not independent of that faculty.

A proof is that all now add on, in defining virtue, the "state" (mentioning also the standard to which it refers — "that which is in accordance with right reason"). "Right" means in accordance with practical wisdom. All, then, seem to have an instinctive notion that the state in accordance with practical wisdom is virtue. We must slightly change their statement: virtue is not merely the state in accordance with right reason, but the state that implies the possession of right reason; which on such matters is practical wisdom. Our difference from Socrates is this: he thought the virtues were reasoning processes — all instances of scientific knowledge in its strict sense — while we say they imply the possession of reason.
From what has been said, it is clear that one cannot be strictly good without practical wisdom, nor practically wise without moral goodness.

By the distinction between natural and matured virtue, one can meet the argument that the virtues are separable, since the same man is not by nature most inclined to all of them at once, so he must have acquired one before another. We reply that this is possible with the natural virtues but not with those in virtue of which a man is simply called good; they all belong to him together with the one faculty of practical wisdom.

It is plain too that even if it were not apt to act we would have needed practical wisdom, because it is the excellence of a part of the soul; and that moral choice cannot be right independently of practical wisdom and moral goodness. Moral goodness gives the right end; practical wisdom causes the doing of those things that conduce to the end.

Practical wisdom, however, is not master of philosophic wisdom (of the superior part of the soul), just as medicine is not master of health; medicine does not make use of health but looks to how it may come to be. So practical wisdom commands for the sake of philosophic wisdom but does not command it.
The objection is about as valid as if one said political science governs the gods because it gives orders about everything in the community.
APPENDIX
From Posterior Analytics I, chapters 1–2.
(Only those parts are translated that throw light on the Ethics.)

All teaching, and all intellectual learning, proceeds on the basis of previous knowledge, as will appear on examining each case. The mathematical sciences, and every other system, draw their conclusions in this way. So too of reasoning by syllogism or by induction; both teach through what is previously known — the former assuming premises as from wise men, the latter proving universals from the self-evidence of particulars. Rhetoricians persuade similarly: through examples (which amount to induction) or through enthymemes (which amount to syllogism).
CHAPTER II

We suppose that we know a thing (in the strict and proper sense) when we suppose ourselves to know the cause by which the thing is, as the cause of it — and that this cannot be otherwise. The idea to be conveyed by the word knowing is plainly something of this kind; those who do not really know suppose themselves thus related to the matter, and those who do know really are so. Of whatever there is properly knowledge, this cannot be otherwise than it is. Whether there is another way of knowing we will say later; but we say we know through demonstration, by which I mean a syllogism apt to produce knowledge — that is, by possessing which we know.

If knowledge is such as we have described, then knowledge produced by demonstrative reasoning must be drawn from premises that are true, first, incapable of syllogistic proof, better known, prior in time, and causes of the conclusion. Thus the principles will be akin to the demonstrated conclusion.
(Syllogism there may be without such premises, but it will not be demonstration, since it will not produce knowledge.)
They must be true, since it is impossible to know what is not.

They must be first, that is, indemonstrable; for if demonstrable, one cannot be said to know them without having demonstrated them — to know such things as are demonstrable is the same as having demonstration of them.

They must be causes, better known, and prior in time. Causes, because we know when we are acquainted with the cause. Prior, if they are causes. Known beforehand — not merely comprehended in idea but known to exist. (The terms "prior" and "better known" bear two senses: prior by nature and prior relative to ourselves are not the same, nor are better known by nature and better known to us. By "prior and better known relative to ourselves" I mean things nearer to sensation; by abstractedly prior, things farther from it. Those are farthest which are most universal; those nearest are particulars, and these are mutually opposed.)

By "first" I mean principles akin to the conclusion; for principle means the same as first. The principle, or first step, in demonstration is a proposition incapable of syllogistic proof — one to which there is none prior. Of such syllogistic principles, I call a "thesis" what one cannot demonstrate and which is not necessary for learning something else. What is necessary for learning something else is an axiom.

Further, since one is to believe and know the thing by having a syllogism of the kind called demonstration, and what makes it such is the nature of the premises, it is necessary not only to know the principles beforehand but to know them better than the conclusion, either all or at least some of them; for that which is the cause of a quality inhering in something else always inheres itself more — as the cause of our loving is itself more lovable. So, since the principles are the cause of our knowing and believing, we know and believe them more, because through them we know the conclusion that follows.

Further: the man who is to have knowledge through demonstration must not only know and believe his principles better than his conclusion, but he must believe nothing more firmly than the contradictories of those principles out of which the contrary fallacy might be constructed; since he who knows is to be simply and absolutely infallible.

chapters.title: Book 7 — Continence and Pleasure
paragraphs: Next we must start from a different point and observe that there are three forms of what is to be avoided in respect of moral character: vice, imperfect self-control, and brutishness. It is plain what the contraries of the first two are; we call the one virtue, the other self-control. As answering to brutishness it will be most suitable to assign superhuman — heroic and godlike — virtue. Priam says of Hector in Homer that "he was very excellent, nor was he like the offspring of mortal man, but of a god." If, as is commonly said, men are raised to the position of gods by reason of very high excellence, the state opposed to brutishness will plainly be of this kind. For as animals are neither virtuous nor vicious, so neither are gods: the state of gods is something more precious than virtue, and the state of brutes something different in kind from vice.

As it is rare for a man to be godlike (the Spartans use the term when they admire a man exceedingly; they call him seios anēr), so the brutish man is rare too. This character is found most among barbarians; some cases are caused by disease or maiming. We also designate by this opprobrious term men who exceed in vice all ordinary measure. We will mention this disposition later; vice has been spoken of before. For the present we must speak of imperfect self-control and its kindred faults of softness and luxury, on the one hand, and of self-control and endurance on the other. We are to conceive of these not as being the same states exactly as virtue and vice, nor as differing in kind.

We should adopt the same method as before: state the phenomena, raise and discuss the difficulties, and then exhibit, if possible, all the current opinions about these affections of the moral character — or, if not all, the greater part and the most important. We may consider the matter sufficiently illustrated when the difficulties are solved and the most approved theories are left as a residue.
The chief points may be enumerated as follows. It is thought that:
I. Self-control and endurance belong to the class of things good and praiseworthy; imperfect self-control and softness belong to that of things low and blameworthy.
II. The man of self-control is identical with the man apt to abide by his resolution; the man of imperfect self-control, with him apt to depart from his resolution.

III. The man of imperfect self-control does things at the instigation of his passions, knowing them to be wrong; the man of self-control, knowing his lusts to be wrong, refuses by reason to follow their suggestions.
IV. The man of perfected self-mastery unites the qualities of self-control and endurance. Some say that everyone who unites these is a man of perfect self-mastery; others do not.
V. Some confound the two characters of the man who has no self-control and the man of imperfect self-control; others distinguish between them.
VI. It is sometimes said that the practically wise man cannot be of imperfect self-control; sometimes, that men who are practically wise and clever are of imperfect self-control.
VII. Men are said to be of imperfect self-control not simply, but with an addition: in respect of anger, of honor, of gain.
These, then, are roughly the common statements.
A question may be raised about the nature of the right conception in violation of which a man fails of self-control.

That he can fail while knowing, in the strict sense, what is right, some say is impossible. Socrates thought it strange that, while knowledge is present in the mind, something else should master it and drag it about like a slave. Socrates in general argued against the theory, maintaining that there is no such state as imperfect self-control: no one acts contrary to what is best, conceiving it to be best, except through ignorance of what is best.

With all due respect to Socrates, his account is at variance with plain facts. We must inquire, with respect to the affection, if it is caused by ignorance, what the nature of the ignorance is; for it is plain that the man so failing does not suppose his acts to be right before he is under the influence of passion.

Some partly agree with Socrates and partly not. They agree that nothing can be stronger than knowledge, but do not agree that no man acts contrary to his conviction of what is better. They say it is not knowledge but only opinion that the man in question has, while yielding to the instigation of his pleasures.

But then, if it is opinion and not knowledge, and the opposing conception is not strong but mild (as in a case of real doubt), failing to abide by it in the face of strong lusts would be excusable. But wickedness is not excusable, nor is anything deserving blame.

Is it practical wisdom, then, which in this case offers opposition — since it is the strongest principle? The supposition is absurd; we would have the same man uniting practical wisdom and imperfect self-control. No single person would maintain that it is consistent with the character of practical wisdom to do voluntarily what is very wrong. We have shown before that the very mark of such a character is aptitude to act, as distinguished from mere knowledge of what is right; he is conversant with particular details and possesses all the other virtues.

If having strong and bad lusts is necessary to the idea of the man of self-control, this character cannot be identical with the man of perfected self-mastery; strong or bad desires do not enter into the idea of the latter. Yet the man of self-control must have such lusts. For suppose them good; the moral state that would hinder him from following their suggestions must be bad, and so self-control would not always be good. Suppose them weak and not wrong; self-control would be nothing grand. Suppose them wrong but weak; nothing great.

Again, if self-control makes a man apt to abide by all opinions without exception, it may be bad (in the case of a false opinion); and if imperfect self-control makes a man apt to depart from all without exception, there will be cases where it is good. Take Neoptolemus in Sophocles' Philoctetes: he is praised for not abiding by what Odysseus persuaded him to, because he was pained at being guilty of falsehood.

Again, false sophistical reasoning presents a difficulty. Men wish to prove paradoxes, to be thought clever when they succeed, and the reasoning used becomes a difficulty; the intellect is fettered. One is unwilling to abide by the conclusion because it does not please his judgment, but unable to advance because he cannot disentangle the web of sophistry.

On this supposition it is conceivable that folly joined with imperfect self-control may turn out in a given case to be goodness: a man, by his imperfection of self-control, acts contrary to his notions; his notion is that what is really good is bad and ought not to be done, so he will eventually do what is good and not what is bad.

Again, on the same supposition, the man who by conviction pursues and chooses things because they are pleasant must be thought better than he who does so not through a quasi-rational conviction but through imperfect self-control. He is more open to cure, since he can receive a contrary conviction. To the man of imperfect self-control the proverb would apply, "When water chokes, what should a man drink?" Had he not been convinced at all, a contrary conviction might have stopped him; but though he has convictions, he acts against them.

Again, if any and every thing is the object-matter of imperfect and of perfect self-control, who is the man of imperfect self-control simply? No one unites all cases of it, and we commonly say some men are imperfect simply, without adding any particular thing in which they are so.
Such, roughly, are the difficulties. Of these theories we must remove some and leave others as established; for the solving of a difficulty is a positive act of establishing something as true.

We must examine first whether men of imperfect self-control act with knowledge of what is right or not. Next, if with such knowledge, in what sense. Next, what we are to assume is the object-matter of the man of imperfect self-control and of the man of self-control — pleasure and pain of all kinds, or certain definite ones. And as to self-control and endurance, whether these are designations of the same character or different. And likewise all the questions connected with the present inquiry.

The real starting point is whether the two characters of self-control and imperfect self-control are distinguished by their object-matter or by their respective relations to it. Is the man of imperfect self-control such simply by virtue of having such and such object-matter? Or not by that, but by his being related to it in such and such a way? Or by both? Next, are self-control and imperfect self-control unlimited in object-matter? He who is simply called a man of imperfect self-control is not unlimited in object-matter, but has exactly the same as the man who has lost all self-control. Nor is he called so merely because of his relation to this object-matter (then his character would be identical with that just mentioned, complete loss of self-control); he is called so because his relation to it is of a particular kind. The man who has lost all self-control is led on with deliberate moral choice, holding that it is his line to pursue pleasure as it arises. The man of imperfect self-control does not think he ought to pursue it, but pursues it all the same.

As to the notion that it is true opinion and not knowledge in contravention of which men fail in self-control, it makes no difference to the point in question. Some of those who hold opinions have no doubt about them but suppose themselves to have accurate knowledge. If it is urged that men holding opinions are more likely than men with knowledge to act in contravention of their conceptions, since they have only moderate belief, we reply that knowledge will not differ in this respect from opinion. Some men believe their own opinions no less firmly than others do their positive knowledge; Heraclitus is a case in point.

Rather, the following is the account. The term "knowing" has two senses. Both the man who has knowledge without using it, and he who does use it, are said to "know." There will be a difference between a man who acts wrongly though possessed of knowledge he does not call into operation, and him who has it and actively exercises it. The latter is a strange case; the mere having, if not exercising, presents no anomaly.

Since there are two kinds of propositions affecting action, universal and particular, there is no reason why a man may not act against his knowledge, having both propositions in his mind, using the universal but not the particular; for particulars are the objects of moral action.

There is a difference in universal propositions: one may relate partly to a man's self and partly to the thing in question. Take "dry food is good for every man"; this may have the two minor premises "this is a man" and "such-and-such is dry food." But whether a given substance is such, a man either has not the knowledge or does not exert it. According to these different senses there is an immense difference; for a man to know in the one sense and yet act wrongly would be nothing strange, but in any other sense it would be cause for wonder.

Men may also have knowledge in yet another way. We constantly see a man's state so differing, between having and not using knowledge, that he has it in a sense and also has not: when asleep, for instance, or mad, or drunk. Men under the actual operation of passion are in similar conditions. Anger, lust, and some other such feelings make changes even in the body, and in some even cause madness. Plainly we must say that men of imperfect self-control are in a state similar to these.

Their saying what embodies knowledge is no proof of their then exercising it. Those under the operation of these passions repeat demonstrations or verses of Empedocles, just as children learning string words together without yet knowing the meaning (since they must grow into it, and that takes time). So we must suppose men failing in self-control say these moral sayings as actors do.

Further, a man may look at the matter from the actual working of the mind. Every action may be analyzed into a syllogism: one premise is a universal maxim, the other concerns particulars of which perception (moral or physical) is cognizant. When one conclusion results from these two, it follows necessarily that, in theory, the mind must assert the conclusion, and in practical propositions the man must act accordingly.

Let the universal be "All that is sweet should be tasted"; the particular, "This is sweet." It follows that the man who is able and not hindered not only draws but puts in practice the conclusion "This is to be tasted." When there is in the mind one universal proposition forbidding tasting, and another — "All that is sweet is pleasant," with its minor "This is sweet" (which is the one really at work) — and desire is in the man, the first universal bids him avoid, but desire leads him on to taste, since desire has the power of moving the organs. So he fails in self-control, in a certain sense under the influence of reason and of an opinion not contrary in itself to reason, only accidentally so; for it is desire, not opinion, that is contrary to right reason. This is why brutes are not said to be of imperfect self-control: they have no power of conceiving universals, only of receiving and retaining particular impressions.

How the ignorance is removed and the man of imperfect self-control recovers his knowledge — this account is the same as for the drunk or asleep, and is not peculiar to this affection, so physiologists are the people to apply to. The minor premise of every practical syllogism is an opinion on matter cognizable by sense, and it determines actions. He who is under the influence of passion either has not this, or has it in such a way that his having does not amount to knowing but only to saying — as a drunk man might recite Empedocles. The minor term is not universal, nor is it thought to have the power of producing knowledge as the universal term does. So the result Socrates was seeking does come out: the affection does not take place in the presence of what is thought to be specially knowledge, nor is this dragged about by reason of the affection; it is knowledge conveyed by sense that is dragged about.
Let this stand as our account of the question whether failure in self-control is with knowledge, and the manner in which it is possible though knowledge is possessed.

Next, we must discuss whether there is a character to be designated by "imperfect self-control" simply, or whether all who are so are so only in respect of some particular thing; and if there is such a character, what its object-matter is.
That pleasures and pains are the object-matter of men of self-control and of endurance, and also of men of imperfect self-control and of softness, is plain.

Things that produce pleasure are either necessary, or objects of choice in themselves but admitting of excess. All bodily things that produce pleasure are necessary; I call such those relating to food and other gross appetites — in short, the bodily things we assumed were the object-matter of the absence of self-control and of perfected self-mastery.

The other class are not necessary, but chosen in themselves: victory, honor, wealth, and similar good or pleasant things. Those who are excessive in liking for such things, contrary to the right reason within them, we do not call men of imperfect self-control simply, but with an addition — in respect of money, gain, honor, or anger, and not simply. We consider them as different characters, having the title only by a kind of resemblance. (Similarly, when we add to a man's name "conqueror at the Olympic games," the account of him as man differs little from the account of him as the man who conquered; but it still differs.) A proof that there really is a difference between those designated with an addition and those simply so called is this: imperfect self-control is blamed not only as an error but as a vice, either wholly or partially; none of those other cases is so blamed.

But of those whose object-matter is the bodily enjoyments — which we say are also the object-matter of the man of perfected self-mastery and of the man who has lost all self-control — he who pursues excessive pleasures, and too much avoids painful things (such as hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and everything connected with touch and taste), not from moral choice but in spite of his moral choice and intellectual conviction, is simply called a man of imperfect self-control, without the addition of a particular object-matter as we do with anger.

A proof that the term is so applied is that the kindred term "soft" is used with respect to these enjoyments but not the others. For this reason we put into the same rank the man of imperfect self-control, the man who has lost it entirely, the man of self-control, and the man of perfected self-mastery — but none of those other characters. These four have the same pleasures and pains as object-matter; but though they share the object-matter, they are not related to it in the same way: two act upon moral choice, two without it. A man is more entirely given up to his passions who pursues excessive pleasures and avoids moderate pains without being urged at all, or only slightly, by desire, than the man who does so because his desire is very strong. One asks, what would the former be likely to do if he had the added stimulus of youthful lust and violent pain from lack of those pleasures we have called necessary?

Of desires and pleasures, some are in kind noble and good. (Things pleasant, as we said before, divide into: naturally objects of choice, naturally objects of avoidance, and indifferent — money, gain, honor, victory.) In respect of all these, and of those indifferent, men are blamed not for being affected by, desiring, or liking them, but for exceeding in these feelings.

So they are blamed who are mastered by, or pursue, any object, though noble and good in itself, contrary to reason: men who are more earnest than they should be about honor, or their children or parents. These are good objects, and men are praised for earnestness about them; but they admit of excess — if one should fight even against the gods, as Niobe did, or feel toward one's father as Satyrus did, who got the nickname philopatōr because he was thought to be exceedingly foolish about it.

There is no depravity in these things, for the reason given: each is naturally choice-worthy, but excess about them is wrong and blameworthy. And similarly there is no imperfect self-control about them; imperfect self-control is not only to be avoided, but blameworthy.

Because of the resemblance to imperfect self-control, the term is used with the addition in each case of the particular object-matter — just as we call a man a bad physician or bad actor whom we would not call simply bad. As in those cases we do not apply the term simply because each state is not a vice but only like a vice by analogy, so in respect of imperfect self-control and self-control we must limit the names to those states having the same object-matter as perfected self-mastery and utter loss of self-control; only by resemblance do we apply them to anger. So we designate a man of imperfect self-control in respect of anger with an addition, as we do with honor or gain.

Some things are naturally pleasant, of two kinds: those pleasant generally, and those pleasant relative to particular kinds of animals and men. Others are not naturally pleasant but become so through maimings, custom, or depraved tastes. One may observe moral states similar to those we have described, having these classes of things for their object-matter.

I mean the brutish — as in the case of the female who, they say, would rip open pregnant women and eat the fetus; or the tastes among savage tribes bordering on the Pontus, some liking raw flesh, some being cannibals, some lending one another their children for feasts; or what is said of Phalaris. These are brutish states, caused in some by disease or madness: the man who sacrificed and ate his mother, or him who devoured the liver of his fellow-servant. Others are caused by disease or by custom: plucking out one's hair, eating one's nails, eating coals and earth. Where nature is really the cause, no one would call such persons men of imperfect self-control; likewise for those in diseased states through custom.

Having any of these inclinations is foreign to what is called vice, as brutishness is. When a man has them, his mastering them is not properly self-control, nor his being mastered by them imperfection of self-control in the proper sense, but only by resemblance. Just as a man of ungovernable wrath fails of self-control in respect of anger, not simply. All excessive folly, cowardice, lack of self-control, or irritability are either brutish or morbid. The man who is naturally afraid of all things, even if a mouse stirs, is cowardly in the brutish way; there was a man who, by disease, was afraid of a cat. Of fools, those naturally destitute of reason and living only by sense are brutish, as are some tribes of far-off barbarians; those in such a state by disease, epileptic or frantic, are morbid.

A man may have one of these inclinations but not yield to it — suppose Phalaris had restrained his unnatural desire to eat a child. Or he may both have and yield. As vice belonging to human nature is simply called vice, while the other is called vice with the addition "brutish" or "morbid" and not simply vice, so manifestly there is brutish and morbid imperfection of self-control; but only the one that is of the nature of utter absence of self-control in man is entitled to the unqualified name.

The object-matter of imperfect self-control and self-control is, then, restricted to the same as that of utter absence of self-control and perfected self-mastery. The rest is the object-matter of a different species, named so metaphorically and not simply. We will now examine the claim that imperfect self-control in respect of anger is less disgraceful than in respect of lusts.

In the first place, anger does in a way listen to reason, but mishears it — like quick servants who run out before hearing the whole of what is said and then mistake the order, or like dogs barking at the slightest stir before seeing whether it is friend or foe. Anger, by its natural heat and quickness, hears reason but without hearing reason's command, rushes to its revenge. Reason or some impression suggests that there is insolence or contempt in the offender; anger reasons, as it were, that one ought to fight against what is such, and fires up immediately. Lust, on the other hand, if reason or sense merely says a thing is sweet, rushes to enjoy it. Anger thus follows reason in a manner, but lust does not, and is therefore more disgraceful. He who cannot control his anger yields in a manner to reason; the other yields to lust and not to reason at all.

Again, a man is more excusable for following natural desires, just as he is for following lusts common to all men, and to the degree they are common. Anger and irritability are more natural than lusts in excess or for unnecessary objects. This was the ground of the defense a man made who beat his father: "My father used to beat his, and his father his, and this little fellow here," pointing to his child, "will beat me when he is grown a man; it runs in the family." And the father, as he was being dragged along, told his son to leave off beating him at the door — for he himself had dragged his father only so far, no farther.
Again, characters are less unjust in proportion as they involve less insidiousness. The angry man is not insidious, nor is anger; it is open. Lust is insidious, as they say of Aphrodite,
"Cyprus-born goddess, weaver of deceits,"
or as Homer speaks of the girdle called the Cestus:
"Persuasiveness, cheating even the subtlest mind."
Since imperfect self-control of this kind is more unjust, it is also more disgraceful than that in respect of anger; it is simply imperfect self-control, and vice in a certain sense.

No man feels pain in being insolent, but everyone who acts from anger acts with pain; the insolent man acts with pleasure. If those things are most unjust with which we have most right to be angry, then imperfect self-control from lust is more unjust than from anger, because in anger there is no insolence.

So it is clear that imperfect self-control in respect of lusts is more disgraceful than in respect of anger, and that the object-matter of self-control and its imperfection is bodily lusts and pleasures. Of these we must take the differences into account: as said at the outset, some are proper to the human race and natural in kind and degree, others brutish, others caused by maimings and diseases.

Only the first of these are the object-matter of perfected self-mastery and of utter absence of self-control. That is why we never attribute either of these states to brutes (except metaphorically, and when one kind of animal differs entirely from another in insolence, mischievousness, or voracity); brutes have no moral choice or process of deliberation, but are quite different from human beings, as are madmen.
Brutishness is not as low as vice, yet it is to be regarded with more fear: in the brute, the highest principle has not been corrupted, as in the human — the subject has it not at all.

It is like comparing an inanimate with an animate being as to which is worse; the badness of what has no originative principle is always less harmful — intellect being an originative principle. A similar case: comparing injustice and an unjust man; each is worst in a different way — but a bad man would do ten thousand times more harm than a bad brute.

Now with respect to pleasures and pains coming through touch and taste, and the desiring or avoiding of them (which we said constitute the object-matter of utter absence of self-control and of perfected self-mastery), one may be so disposed as to yield to temptations most men could resist, or to resist those to which most men yield. In respect of pleasures, these two are the man of imperfect self-control and the man of self-control; in respect of pains, the man of softness and the man of endurance. The moral state of most men is between the two, though they lean somewhat to the worse characters.

Since some of the indicated pleasures are necessary and some not, others necessary up to a point but not in excess or defect (and similarly with lusts and pains), the man who pursues excessive pleasures, or such as are themselves excesses, from moral choice, for their own sake, not for anything else to result — he is utterly void of self-control. He must be incapable of remorse, and so incurable; without remorse is without cure. (He who loves pleasure too little is the opposite character; the man of perfected self-mastery is the mean.) Similar is he who avoids bodily pains not because he cannot withstand them, but because he chooses not to.

Among those who go wrong without choosing to, one is led by pleasure, the other avoids the pain of denying his lust. These are different. Everyone pronounces a man worse for doing something base without any impulse of desire, or with a very slight one, than for doing the same under a very strong desire — more base to strike a man when not angry than in wrath. One naturally asks, "What would he have done under passion?" (On this ground, by the way, the man utterly void of self-control is worse than he who has it imperfectly.) Of the two characters mentioned as included in utter absence of self-control, the one is rather softness, the other properly the man of no self-control.

To imperfect self-control is opposed self-control; to softness, endurance. Endurance is continued resistance, while self-control is actual mastery; these are as different as not being conquered from conquering. So self-control is more choice-worthy than endurance.

He who fails against temptations most men hold out against is soft and luxurious (luxury being a kind of softness): the kind of man who lets his robe drag in the dirt to save trouble of lifting it, and who apes the sick man without thinking himself wretched, though behaving like a wretched man. So too with self-control and its imperfection: if a man yields to violent and excessive pleasures or pains, it is no wonder, but rather a matter for allowance, if he made what resistance he could — Philoctetes in Theodectes' drama when wounded by the viper; Cercyon in Carcinus' Alope; or men who try to suppress laughter and burst into a loud fit, as happened to Xenophantus. But it is a matter for wonder when a man yields, and cannot contend against, the pleasures or pains the common herd can resist — unless his failure is owing to natural constitution or disease (the Scythian kings are constitutionally soft; there is a natural difference between the sexes).
The slave to amusement is commonly thought to lack self-control, but is really soft; amusement is a relaxing, being a rest, and the character in question exceeds due bounds in this.

Of imperfect self-control there are two forms, precipitancy and weakness. Those of the weakness form have made resolutions but, through passion, do not abide by them. Others are led by passion because they have never formed any resolutions at all. Some, like those who get rid of ticklishness by tickling themselves beforehand, have felt and seen the approach of temptation, have roused themselves and their resolution, and do not yield to passion whether the temptation is somewhat pleasant or somewhat painful. The precipitate form is most found in those constitutionally of a sharp or melancholy temperament; either by the swiftness or by the violence of their passions, they do not wait for reason, being disposed to follow whatever notion is impressed on their mind.

The man utterly destitute of self-control, as noted, is not given to remorse: it is part of his character that he abides by his moral choice. But the man of imperfect self-control is almost made up of remorse. So the case is not as we determined before: the former is incurable, the latter curable. Depravity is like chronic diseases (dropsy and consumption), imperfect self-control like acute disorders. The former is a continuous evil, the latter not. Imperfect self-control and confirmed vice are different in kind: the latter is imperceptible to its victim, the former not so.

Of the forms of imperfect self-control, those are better who are carried off their feet by a sudden access of temptation than those who have reason but do not abide by it; these last are overcome by less passion, and not wholly without premeditation. The man of imperfect self-control is like those soon intoxicated, on less wine than the common run of men.

That imperfect self-control is not confirmed viciousness is plain; yet perhaps it is such in a way, since in one sense it is contrary to moral choice, in another the result of it. At all events, in respect of the actions, the case is as Demodocus said of the Milesians: "The Milesians are not fools, but they do just the things fools do." So men of imperfect self-control are not unjust, but they do unjust acts.

To resume. Since the man of imperfect self-control pursues bodily pleasures in excess and in defiance of right reason, but without a deliberate conviction, while the man utterly destitute of self-control acts upon a conviction resting on his natural inclination to pursue these pleasures, the former may be easily persuaded to a different course, the latter not. Virtue and vice respectively preserve and corrupt the moral principle; the motive is the principle or starting point in moral actions, just as axioms and postulates in mathematics. In neither field is it reason that teaches the principle; it is excellence, natural or acquired by custom, that holds right notions about the principle. Who does this in morals is the man of perfected self-mastery; the contrary is the man utterly destitute of self-control.

There is also a character who can be swept off his feet in defiance of right reason through passion — whom passion so far masters as to prevent his acting in accordance with right reason, but not so far as to make him convinced that he ought to pursue such pleasures without limit. This is the man of imperfect self-control, better than he who is utterly destitute of it, and not a bad man simply; in him the highest and best part — the principle — is preserved. Opposed to him is the one who abides by his resolutions and does not depart from them, at least not at the instigation of passion.
It is evident, then, that self-control is a good state and its imperfection a bad one.

Next: is a man of self-control for abiding by his conclusions and moral choice whatever they may be, or only by the right ones? And a man of imperfect self-control for not abiding by whatever conclusions and moral choice, or for not abiding by false conclusions and wrong moral choices (to put the case as before)?

The truth is this: incidentally, the one character abides and the other does not by conclusions and moral choice of any kind; per se, by true conclusions and right moral choice. Per se and incidentally: suppose a man chooses or pursues this thing for the sake of that; he pursues and chooses that per se, and this only incidentally. For per se we commonly use the word "simply"; so in a way, it is opinion of any kind by which the two characters abide or not, but the one "simply" entitled to the designation is he who abides by, or departs from, the true opinion.

There are also people with a trick of abiding by their opinions — commonly called positive — hard to persuade, whose convictions are not easily changed. These bear some resemblance to the character of self-control, just as the prodigal resembles the liberal or the rash man the brave; but they differ in many points. The man of self-control does not change through passion or lust, yet when occasion requires will be easy to persuade. The positive man does not change at the call of reason, though many of this class take up desires and are led by pleasures. Among the positive are the opinionated, the ignorant, and the boorish. The opinionated are such from motives of pleasure and pain: the pleasurable feeling of a kind of victory in not having their convictions changed, and pain when their decrees are reversed. So in fact they rather resemble the man of imperfect self-control than the man of self-control.

Some depart from their resolutions not from imperfect self-control: take Neoptolemus in Sophocles' Philoctetes. Certainly pleasure was the motive of his departure, but it was a noble pleasure — truthfulness was noble in his eyes, and he had been persuaded by Odysseus to lie.
So it is not everyone who acts from the motive of pleasure who is utterly destitute of self-control, or base, or of imperfect self-control — only he who acts from the impulse of a base pleasure.

As there is also a character who takes less pleasure in bodily enjoyments than he ought, and who fails to abide by the conclusion of his reason, the man of self-control is the mean between him and the man of imperfect self-control. The latter fails to abide because of excess, the former because of deficiency; the self-controller abides, and never changes through anything other than such conclusions.

Since self-control is good, both the contrary states must be bad, as indeed they plainly are. But because one of them is seen in few people and but rarely, self-control comes to be viewed as opposed only to its imperfection, just as perfected self-mastery is thought opposed only to utter want of self-control.

As many terms are used by likeness, so people have come to speak of the self-control of the man of perfected self-mastery by likeness. The self-controlled and the self-mastering man have this in common: neither does anything against right reason from the impulse of bodily pleasures. But the former has bad desires, the latter not; the latter is constituted so as not even to feel pleasure contrary to his reason; the former feels it but does not yield.

Alike, too, are the man of imperfect self-control and the utterly self-indulgent, though distinct. Both follow bodily pleasures, but the latter under a notion that it is his proper line, the former without any such notion.

The same man cannot be at once practically wise and of imperfect self-control. The character of practical wisdom includes goodness of moral character, as we showed before; and practical wisdom is not merely knowledge, but aptitude for action — of which the man of imperfect self-control is destitute. There is no reason, though, why the merely clever should not be of imperfect self-control. The reason some men are sometimes thought to be practically wise and yet of imperfect self-control is this: cleverness differs from practical wisdom in the way I stated in an earlier book, being near it so far as the intellectual element is concerned, but differing in respect of moral choice.

The man of imperfect self-control is not like one who has and uses his knowledge, but like one who has it and is overpowered by sleep or wine. He acts voluntarily (knowing in a sense what he does and the result), but he is not a confirmed bad man, since his moral choice is good; so he is at any rate only half bad. Nor is he unjust, because he does not act with deliberate intent. Of the two chief forms of the character, one is not apt to abide by his deliberate resolutions; the other, the man of constitutional strength of passion, is not apt to deliberate at all.
So in fact the man of imperfect self-control is like a community that makes all proper enactments and has admirable laws, but does not act on them — verifying the taunt of Anaxandrides,
"That state did will it, which cares nothing for laws."
The bad man, by contrast, is like a state that acts on its laws, but its laws are bad.
Imperfection of self-control and self-control are both above the average state of men; the latter is more true to his reason, the former less so, than is in most men's power.

Of the two forms of imperfect self-control, that is more easily cured which men have who are constitutionally of strong passions, rather than the form of those who form resolutions and break them. And those who are imperfect by habituation are more easily cured than those naturally so — for custom is easier to change than nature, though the very likeness of custom to nature makes it difficult to change; as Evenus says,
"Practice, I say, my friend, does long endure, and at the last is even very nature."
We have said, then, what self-control is, what imperfection of self-control is, what endurance and softness are, and how these states are mutually related.

To consider the subject of pleasure and pain falls within the province of the political philosopher, since it is he who fixes the master end that guides us in dominating any object as absolutely evil or good.

There is more to be said: an inquiry into their nature is necessary. First, because we held that moral virtue and moral vice are both concerned with pains and pleasures. Next, because most men assert that happiness must include pleasure — which accounts for the Greek word for happy, makarios, chairein (to rejoice) being the root.

Some hold that no pleasure is good, either in itself or as a result, because good and pleasure are not identical. Others hold that some pleasures are good, but the greater number bad. A third view grants that every pleasure is good, but denies that the chief good can be pleasure.
In support of the first opinion (that pleasure is utterly not-good) it is urged:
1. Every pleasure is a perceptible process toward a complete state, and no such process is akin to the end to be attained; no process of building is akin to the completed house.
2. The man of perfected self-mastery avoids pleasures.
3. The practically wise man aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure.
4. Pleasures impede thought, and the more so the more keenly felt. An obvious instance will readily occur.
5. Pleasure cannot be referred to any art; yet every good is the result of some art.
6. Children and brutes pursue pleasures.
In support of the second (that not all pleasures are good): some pleasures are base and cause reproach, and some are even hurtful, since some pleasant things produce disease.
In support of the third (that pleasure is not the chief good): that it is not an end but a process toward creating an end.
This is, I think, a fair account of current views.
But the reasons alleged do not prove pleasure either not-good or the chief good, as the following considerations show.

First, good being either absolute or relative, natures and states embodying it will be so too, and therefore also movements and processes of creation. Of those thought to be bad, some will be bad absolutely but not relatively — perhaps even choice-worthy; others not even choice-worthy relative to any particular person, only at certain times or for a short time, and not choice-worthy in themselves.
Others are not even pleasures, though they produce that impression: namely, those accompanied by pain and whose purpose is cure, such as those of sick people.

Next, since good may be either an active working or a state, those processes (kinēseis or geneseis) that tend to place us in our natural state are pleasant incidentally, because of that tendency. The active working is really in the desires aroused in the remaining (sound) part of our state or nature; there are pleasures with no connection to pain or desire, such as the acts of contemplative intellect, in which case there is no deficiency in the state or nature of the one performing them.

A proof is that the same pleasant thing does not produce pleasure when the natural state is being filled up or completed as when it is already in its normal condition. In the normal state, what give pleasure are things pleasant per se; in the other state, even things contrary. People take pleasure in sharp or bitter things, none of which is naturally or per se pleasant; so neither are the pleasures from them naturally pleasant. The classification of pleasures must follow that of pleasant things.

Next, it does not follow that there must be something better than any given pleasure because (as some say) the end must be better than the process creating it. Not all pleasures are processes, nor are all attended by any process; some are active workings or even ends — they result not from our coming to be something but from our using our powers. It is not true that the end is always distinct from the process; only in the case of processes that conduce to the perfecting of the natural state.

For this reason it is wrong to say that pleasure is "a perceptible process of production." For "process etc." should be substituted "active working of the natural state," and for "perceptible" substitute "unimpeded." The reason it is thought to be a "process etc." is that pleasure is good in the highest sense; people confuse "active working" with "process," though they are distinct.

Next, that there are bad pleasures because some pleasant things are harmful to health is like saying some healthful things are bad for "business." In this sense both may be called bad, but that does not make them bad simply. Exercising pure intellect sometimes hurts a man's health; what hinders practical wisdom, or any state, is not the pleasure peculiar to it but some pleasure foreign to it. The pleasures arising from the exercise of pure intellect or from learning only promote each.

Next: "No pleasure is the work of any art." What else would you expect? No active working is the work of any art — only the faculty of so working. Still, the perfumer's art or the cook's are thought to relate to pleasure.
Next: "The man of perfected self-mastery avoids pleasures." "The practically wise man aims at escaping pain rather than at attaining pleasure."
"Children and brutes pursue pleasures."
One answer will do for all.

We have said in what sense all pleasures are good per se and in what sense not. It is the latter class children and brutes pursue, such as are accompanied by desire and pain — the bodily pleasures that answer to this description, and the excesses of them; in short, those in respect of which the utterly self-indulgent man is what he is. The practically wise man aims at the absence of the pain arising from these pleasures. So these are the pleasures the man of perfected self-mastery avoids; obviously he has pleasures peculiarly his own.

It is allowed that pain is an evil to be avoided — partly as bad per se, partly as hindering in some particular way. Now the contrary of what is to be avoided, qua to be avoided (that is, qua evil), is good. Pleasure, then, must be a good.

Speusippus' attempted answer — that pleasure may be opposed to pain but not contrary, just as the greater of a magnitude is contrary to the less but only opposed to the exact half — will not hold; he cannot say pleasure is identical with evil of any kind.
Granting that some pleasures are low, there is no reason why some particular pleasure may not be very good, just as some particular science may be although there are some that are low.

Perhaps it even follows, since each state may have an active working unimpeded (whether the active workings of all be happiness or that of some one of them), that this active working, if unimpeded, must be choice-worthy. Pleasure is exactly this. So the chief good may be pleasure of some kind, though most pleasures be (let us assume) low per se.

For this reason all men think the happy life is pleasant, and interweave pleasure with happiness. Reasonably enough: happiness is perfect, but no impeded active working is perfect. The happy man therefore needs, as additions, the goods of the body, external goods, and good fortune, so as not to be fettered on these points. Those who say the man being tortured on the wheel, or fallen into great misfortunes, is happy so long as he is good, talk nonsense, whether they mean to or not. On the other hand, because fortune is needed as an addition, some identify good fortune with happiness; but it is not, since even this in excess is a hindrance, and perhaps then has no right to be called good fortune, being good only insofar as it contributes to happiness.
The fact that all animals, brute and human, pursue pleasure is some presumption of its being in a sense the chief good;

"there must be something in what most folks say." Only, as one and the same nature or state neither is nor is thought to be the best, so not all pursue the same pleasure; yet pleasure all do pursue. Perhaps what they pursue is not what they think, nor what they would say they pursue, but really one and the same; in all there is some instinct above themselves. Bodily pleasures have received the name exclusively, because theirs is the most frequent form and is universally shared; since these alone are known to many, they believe these to be the only ones.

It is plain too that, unless pleasure and its active working are good, it will not be true that the happy man's life embodies pleasure. Why should he want it on the supposition that it is not good, and that he can live even with pain? On that assumption, pain is neither evil nor good, and so why should he avoid it?
Besides, the life of the good man is no more pleasurable than any other unless it is granted that his active workings are more pleasurable too.

Some inquiry into bodily pleasures is also necessary for those who say that some pleasures are highly choice-worthy (the good ones), but not the bodily ones — those being the object-matter of the man utterly destitute of self-control.
If so, we ask: why are the contrary pains bad? They cannot be, on their assumption, since the contrary of bad is good.

May we not say that necessary bodily pleasures are good in the sense in which what is not-bad is good? Or that they are good only up to a certain point? Such states or movements as cannot have too much of the better cannot have too much of pleasure; those that can of the former can also of the latter. Bodily pleasures do admit of excess; the low bad man is so because he pursues their excess rather than necessary pleasures. Meat, drink, and the objects of other animal appetites do give pleasure to all, but not in the right manner or degree to all. His relation to pain is the reverse: it is not excessive pain, but pain at all, that he avoids (which makes him, in this way too, a bad, low man); only in the case of him who pursues excessive pleasure is pain contrary to excessive pleasure.

It is not enough to state the truth; we should show how the false view arises, since this strengthens conviction. When we have given a probable reason why something not true impresses people as true, it gives them a stronger conviction of the truth. So we must explain why bodily pleasures appear more choice-worthy than any others.

The first obvious reason is that bodily pleasure drives out pain. Because pain is felt in excess, men pursue pleasure in excess (usually bodily pleasure) as a remedy. These remedies come to be violent ones, which is the very reason they are pursued; the impression on the mind is because they are seen side by side with their contrary.
As was said before, there are two reasons why bodily pleasure is thought to be not-good:
1. Some pleasures of this class are activities of a low nature — whether congenital (as in brutes) or acquired by custom (as in low bad men).
2. Others are in the nature of cures — cures of some deficiency; and of course it is better to have the healthy state originally than to have it accrue afterwards.
(But some pleasures result when natural states are being perfected; these are good as a result.)

The very fact of their being violent causes them to be pursued by those who can relish no others: such men create violent thirsts for themselves (if harmless, no fault is found; if harmful, it is bad and low), because they have no other things in which to take pleasure, and the neutral state is distasteful to some people constitutionally. Toil of some kind is inseparable from life, as physiologists testify, telling us that the acts of seeing or hearing are painful, only that we are used to the pain and do not notice it.

In youth, constant growth produces a state much like vinous intoxication; youth is pleasant. Men of the melancholic temperament constantly need some remedial process (because the body, from its temperament, is constantly being disturbed), and they are in a chronic state of violent desire. Pleasure drives out pain — not only pleasure directly contrary to pain, but any pleasure provided it is strong. This is how men come to be utterly destitute of self-mastery — that is, low and bad.

Pleasures unconnected with pain do not admit of excess — such as belong to objects naturally pleasant and not merely pleasant as a result. By the latter I mean the remedial; the reason these are thought pleasant is that the cure results from the action, in some way, of the sound part of the constitution that remains. By "pleasant naturally" I mean those that activate a nature that is itself pleasant.

The reason no single thing is invariably pleasant is that our nature is not simple but complex, involving something different from itself (insofar as we are corruptible beings). Suppose one part of this nature is doing something; that something is, to the other part, unnatural. If there is an equilibrium between the two natures, then whatever is done is indifferent. Obviously, if there were any being whose nature was simple and not complex, the same course of action would always be most pleasurable for such a being.

For this reason the divine feels pleasure that is always one and simple. Not only motion is an activity; so is motionlessness, and pleasure resides rather in the absence than in the presence of motion.

The reason the poet's dictum "change is of all things most pleasant" is true is "a baseness in our blood." For as a bad man is easily changeable, bad must also be the nature that craves change; it is neither simple nor good.
We have now said our piece about self-control and its opposite, and about pleasure and pain — what each is, and how one set is good, the other bad. We have yet to speak of friendship.

chapters.title: Book 8 — Friendship
paragraphs: Next, it seems, should come a discussion of friendship. First, friendship is either a virtue or connected with virtue; and it is most necessary for life. No one would choose to live without friends even if he had all other good things. Men who are rich, or possess authority and influence, are thought to have special need of friends: what is the use of such prosperity if there is no doing of kindnesses, of which friends are the most usual and most commendable objects? And how can prosperity be kept and preserved without friends? — the greater it is, the more slippery and hazardous. In poverty and all other adversities, too, men think friends their only refuge.

Friendship helps the young avoid error, the old with care and the lapses in action their weakness causes, and those in their prime to do noble deeds ("the two together," as Homer says) — they are thus more able to devise and carry out plans.

Friendship seems to be implanted in us by nature: in the parent toward the offspring, and the offspring toward the parent (not only among humans but among birds and most animals); in those of the same tribe toward one another, and especially in men of the same nation. Hence we commend those who love their fellows; and one sees in the course of travel how close of kin and how friendly man is to man.

Friendship seems also the bond of communities, and legislators seem more anxious to secure it than justice. Concord is something like friendship, and concord is what they aim at, driving out faction as hostile to it.

Where people are in friendship, justice is not required; but though they are just, they still need friendship in addition, and the principle most truly just is thought to partake of the nature of friendship.

Friendship is not only necessary but honorable. We praise those fond of friends, and having numerous friends is thought to be to a man's credit. Some go so far as to hold that "good man" and "friend" are synonymous.

The disputed points about friendship are not few. Some say it is a kind of resemblance, and that men like one another are friends — hence the sayings "like to like," "birds of a feather." Others, on the contrary, say that all such are covered by the maxim, "two of a trade never agree."
Some push the inquiry higher and reason physically, as Euripides, who says,
"The earth by drought consumed doth love the rain, and the great heaven, overcharged with rain, doth love to fall in showers upon the earth."
Heraclitus holds that "opposition is expedient, and the best agreement arises from differing things, and all things come into being by the principle of antagonism."
Empedocles, among others, directly opposes this, saying "like aims at like."

These physical questions we will set aside as foreign to the present inquiry; we will examine such questions as are proper to man and concern moral characters and feelings. For instance: does friendship arise among all indiscriminately, or is it impossible for bad men to be friends? And: is there but one species of friendship, or several? Those who hold there is but one on the ground that friendship admits of degrees hold it on insufficient proof, since things different in species also admit of degrees (we spoke about this before).

Our view will be clearer once we have ascertained what is properly the object-matter of friendship. It is thought that not everything indiscriminately, but some special matter only, is its object — namely, what is good, pleasurable, or useful. What is useful is that through which a good or a pleasure accrues; so the objects of friendship, as absolute ends, are the good and the pleasurable.

A question arises: is it the good absolutely, or that which is good to the individual, for which men feel friendship? (These two are sometimes distinct.) Similarly for the pleasurable. Each individual feels friendship toward what is good to himself; abstractedly, the real good is the object of friendship, and to each individual it is what is good to each. So each feels friendship not for what is, but for what conveys to his mind the impression of being, good to himself. This makes no real difference, since what is truly the object of friendship will also convey this impression.

There are, then, three grounds on which men feel friendship. The term is not applied to fondness for inanimate things, since there is no requital of the affection nor wish for the good of those objects. It is ridiculous to say a man fond of wine wishes well to the wine — the only sense in which he does is that he wishes it kept safe for his own use. But to a friend one should wish all good for the friend's sake. When men wish good to another without reciprocation, they are called kindly; friendship is described as kindliness between persons who reciprocate it. Must we not add that the feeling must be mutually known? Many are kindly disposed toward people they have never met but whom they conceive to be amiable or useful, and this notion amounts to the same as a real feeling between them.

These are plainly kindly disposed toward one another; but how can they be called friends while their mutual feelings are unknown to each other? To complete the idea of friendship, then, they must have kindly feelings toward one another, wish one another good from one of the causes mentioned, and these kindly feelings must be mutually known.

As the motives to friendship differ in kind, so do the respective feelings and friendships. The species of friendship are three, equal in number to the objects of it, since in each line there may be "mutual affection mutually known."

Those who have friendship for one another desire one another's good according to the motive of their friendship. So those whose motive is utility have no real friendship for one another, but only so far as some good arises to them from one another.

Those whose motive is pleasure are in the same case: they feel friendship for men of easy pleasantry not because they are of a given character but because they are pleasant to themselves. Those whose motive for friendship is utility love their friends for what is good to themselves; those whose motive is pleasure, for what is pleasurable to themselves. That is, not for what the friend is in himself, but insofar as he is useful or pleasurable. These friendships are incidental: the beloved is not loved for being the person he is but for providing advantage or pleasure.

Such friendships are very apt to dissolve if the parties do not remain alike. When one is no longer pleasurable or useful, the others cease to have friendship for him. Utility is not permanent but constantly varying; so when the motive that made them friends is gone, the friendship dissolves, since it existed only relative to those circumstances.

Friendship of this kind is thought to exist chiefly among the old (who at that age pursue not what is pleasurable but what is profitable), and among men in their prime or among the young who pursue profit. They have no intimate intercourse with one another — sometimes they are not even pleasurable to one another — nor do they desire such intercourse unless their friends are profitable to them; they are pleasurable only insofar as they raise hopes of advantage. With these friendships is commonly ranked the friendship of hospitality.

The friendship of the young is thought to be based on pleasure: they live at the beck and call of passion and pursue what is pleasurable and of the present moment. As their age changes, so too do their pleasures.
This is why the young form and dissolve friendships rapidly: the friendship changes with the pleasurable object, and such pleasure changes quickly.

The young are also much given to love, a passion largely of impulse and based on pleasure. They form friendships and quickly drop them, changing often in the same day; but they wish for society and intimate intercourse with their friends, since they thus attain the object of their friendship.

Perfect friendship, then, is that between those who are good and whose similarity is in their goodness. These men wish one another's good in like ways, insofar as they are good (and they are good in themselves); those are specially friends who wish good to their friends for their sakes, feeling this way toward them on their own account and not as a mere matter of result. So the friendship between such men continues as long as they are good — and goodness has a principle of permanence in it.

Each party is good in himself and also relative to his friend; all good men are not only good in themselves but also useful to one another. Such friends are also mutually pleasurable, since all good men are so in themselves and relatively to one another: to each individual the actions pleasurable are those that correspond to his nature, and similar ones. When men are good, these will always be the same, or at least similar.

Friendship in these conditions is permanent, as we would expect, since it combines all the qualifications of friends. Friendship of any kind is based on good or pleasure (either in themselves or relative to the one feeling friendship), and results from a resemblance of some sort; this kind contains all the requisites, since in it the parties are similar and so on. Moreover, in it there is the good and the pleasant in themselves, and as these are especially the object-matter of friendship, so the feeling and state of friendship are found most intense and excellent in men so qualified.

Such friendships will probably be rare, since men of this kind are rare. And besides all the required qualifications, time and intimacy are required; as the proverb says, men cannot know one another "till they have eaten the requisite quantity of salt together." Nor can they admit one another to intimacy, much less be friends, until each has appeared to the other and been proved a fit object of friendship. Those who quickly exchange friendly acts may be said to wish to be friends, but are not, unless they are also proper objects and mutually known to be such; a desire for friendship may arise quickly, but not friendship itself.
This friendship is perfect with respect to time and in all other points; the same and similar results accrue to each party from the other, which ought to be the case between friends.

Friendship based on the pleasurable is, so to say, a copy of this, since the good are sources of pleasure to one another. The friendship based on utility likewise — the good being also useful to one another.
