Friendships between men so connected are most permanent when the same result accrues to both from one another (pleasure, for instance), and not merely so but from the same source, as in the case of two men of easy pleasantry; and not as between a lover and his beloved, who do not derive their pleasure from the same causes — the one from seeing, the other from receiving attentions. When the bloom of youth fades, the friendship sometimes ceases, since the lover no longer takes pleasure in the sight and the beloved no longer receives the attentions. In many cases, though, such people remain friends if, being of similar tempers, they have come by custom to like each other's disposition.

Where people do not exchange pleasure for pleasure but profit for profit in matters of love, the friendship is both less intense and less permanent. Those who are friends for advantage commonly part when the advantage ceases; in reality they were never friends of one another but of the advantage.

So it appears that from motives of pleasure or profit, bad men may be friends to one another, or good to bad, or men of neutral character to any character at all. But disinterestedly, for each other's sake, plainly only the good can be friends; bad men have no pleasure even in themselves unless some advantage arises.

The friendship of the good is alone superior to slander: it is not easy to believe a third person about one whom one has long tried and proved. Between good men there is mutual confidence, the feeling that one's friend would never have done one wrong, and all other such things as are expected in friendship really worthy of the name. In the other kinds, nothing prevents all such suspicions.

I call them friendships, since men commonly give the name to those connected for profit (justified by political language — alliances between states are thought to be contracted with a view to advantage), and to those attached by pleasure (as children are). We may also be allowed to call such persons friends, and to say there are several species of friendship — primarily and specially that of the good as being good, and the rest only by resemblance. People connected otherwise are friends insofar as some good and some mutual resemblance arises (remembering that the pleasurable is good to those fond of it).

These secondary friendships do not combine very well; the same persons do not become friends both from advantage and from pleasure, since these matters of result are not often combined. Friendship having been divided into these kinds, bad men will be friends by reason of pleasure or profit, their point of resemblance; while the good are friends for one another's sake, insofar as they are good.
These last may be termed friends without qualification; the former are friends as a matter of result, called friends by resemblance to the former.

Just as with the different virtues some men are called good for a certain inward state, others for acts of working, so with friendship. Those who live together take pleasure in and impart good to one another; but those asleep or locally separated do not perform acts, but only are in a state from which they would act in friendly fashion if they did act. Distance in itself has no direct effect on friendship, but only prevents its being acted out. Yet if the absence is protracted, it is thought to cause a forgetfulness even of the friendship. Hence the saying, "many a friendship does want of intercourse destroy."

Accordingly, neither the old nor the morose are well suited for friendship, since the pleasurableness in them is small; no one can spend his days with what is positively painful, or even not pleasurable — avoiding the painful and aiming at the pleasurable being among the most obvious tendencies of human nature. Those who get on with one another fairly but are not in the habit of intimacy are more like people with kindly feelings than friends. Nothing is so characteristic of friends as living together; the needy desire help, the happy companionship, being the last to want solitary existence. But people cannot spend time together unless they are mutually pleasurable and take pleasure in the same objects, a quality thought to belong to the friendship of companionship.

The connection between the good is friendship par excellence, as has often been said. What is good or pleasant in itself is thought to be an object of friendship and choice-worthy; and to each individual whatever is such to him. The good man is such to the good man for both reasons.

(Entertaining the sentiment is like a feeling, but friendship itself is like a state: the former may have even inanimate things as its object, but the requital of friendship is attended with moral choice, which proceeds from a moral state. Men wish good to the objects of their friendship for their sakes, not in the way of a feeling but of a moral state.)

In loving their friend, the good love their own good (the good man, when brought into that relation, becomes a good to him with whom he is so connected), so each party loves his own good and repays his friend equally both in wishing well and in the pleasurable: for equality is said to be a tie of friendship. These points belong most to friendship between good men.

Between morose or elderly men friendship is less apt to arise; they are somewhat awkward-tempered and take less pleasure in intercourse and society, which are thought especially friendly and productive of friendship. The young become friends quickly, the old not so (since people do not become friends with any unless they take pleasure in them); and likewise the morose. Yet men of these classes have kindly feelings toward one another, wishing good and rendering mutual assistance in need; but they are not quite friends, since they neither spend time together nor take pleasure in one another — circumstances specially belonging to friendship.

To be a friend to many in the way of perfect friendship is not possible — just as one cannot be in love with many at once. It is a kind of excess, which naturally has but one object; besides, it is not easy for one man to be very pleased with many at once, nor perhaps to find many really good. A man needs experience and close intimacy, which are very difficult.
But it is possible to please many on the score of advantage and pleasure; many are of this kind, and the services can be rendered in a short time.

Of the two imperfect kinds, the one most resembling the perfect is the friendship based on pleasure, in which the same results accrue from both and they take pleasure in one another or in the same objects — such as the friendships of the young, generous spirit being most found there. The friendship of advantage is the link of shopkeepers.

The very happy have no need of profitable people but do of pleasant ones: they wish for companions to live intimately with. What is painful they bear briefly, but continuously no one could — not even the chief good itself, if it were painful to him individually. So they look for pleasant friends; perhaps they ought to require such to be good also, and good specifically for themselves, then they will have all the proper requisites of friendship.

Men in power are often seen to make use of several distinct friends: some are useful, some pleasurable, but the two are not often united. They do not in fact seek those who would combine pleasantness and goodness, nor such as would be useful for honorable purposes; with a view to pleasure they look out for men of easy pleasantry, and for men clever at executing business — qualifications not commonly found united.

It has been said the good man unites pleasantness and usefulness. But such a one will not be a friend to a superior unless he is also superior in goodness; otherwise, being surpassed in one point, he cannot make things equal by a proportionate degree of friendship. Characters uniting superior station and goodness are not common.

All the kinds of friendship mentioned exist on a footing of equality: either the same results accrue to both and they wish the same things for one another, or they exchange one thing against another — pleasure against profit. Such friendships, as noted, are less intense and less permanent.

Their resemblance or unlikeness to the same thing is what makes them to be thought and not to be friendships. They resemble friendships by their likeness to the virtue-based kind (having the pleasurable or the profitable, both of which belong to that kind); and they do not resemble friendships by their unlikeness to that true kind. The unlikeness is this: the virtue-based is above slander and permanent, while these change quickly and differ in many other points.

But there is another form of friendship, that of superior and inferior: between father and son, older and younger, husband and wife, ruler and ruled. These differ among themselves too. The friendship between parents and children is not the same as between ruler and ruled; nor does the father have the same feeling toward the son as the son toward the father, nor the husband toward the wife as she toward him; the work, and therefore the excellence, of each differs, and so the causes of their feeling friendship differ. Distinct, too, are their feelings and states of friendship.

The same results do not accrue to each from the other, nor in fact should they be looked for. But when children render to parents what they ought to the authors of their being, and parents to sons what they ought to their offspring, the friendship will be permanent and equitable.

The feeling of friendship should be in due proportion in all friendships between superior and inferior: the better man, or the more profitable, should be the object of a stronger feeling than he himself entertains. When friendship comes to be at a certain rate, equality of a sort is produced — which is thought a requisite of friendship.
(The equal is not, however, in the same case for justice and friendship. In strict justice, the proportionate equal ranks first, the numerically equal second; in friendship, exactly the reverse.)

That equality is required is plainly shown by great differences of goodness, badness, or prosperity. People are then no longer friends, and do not even feel that they should be. The clearest illustration is the gods, most superior in all good things. Or kings: men greatly their inferiors do not feel entitled to be friends with them, nor do very insignificant people feel entitled to be friends of those of very high excellence or wisdom. In such cases it is out of the question to define up to what point they may remain friends — you may remove many points of agreement and the friendship still lasts; but when one party is very far separated (as a god from men), it cannot continue.

This gives rise to a doubt: do friends really wish the highest goods for their friends — for example, that they become gods? If the wish were accomplished, they would no longer have them for friends, nor have those good things (since friends are good things). If it has been rightly said that a friend wishes his friend good for that friend's sake, he must wish him to remain what he now is — the greatest good of which, as a man, he is capable; yet perhaps not of all goods, since each man desires good for himself most of all.

The desire for honor makes most men wish rather to be the objects of friendship than to entertain it themselves (and so they are fond of flatterers; a flatterer is a friend inferior, or pretending to be, and rather entertains friendship toward another than is himself the object of it). Being an object of friendship is thought nearly the same as being honored, which most men desire. Yet men seem to choose honor not for its own sake but incidentally: most men delight to be honored by those in power because of the hope it raises — they think they will get whatever they want from them, so they delight in honor as an earnest of future benefit. Those who grasp at honor from good men and those really acquainted with their merits wish to confirm their own opinion of themselves; so they take pleasure in the conviction they are good, based on the judgment of those who assert it. But in being the objects of friendship, men delight for its own sake. So this may be judged higher than being honored, and friendship in itself choice-worthy. Friendship is thought to consist in feeling, rather than in being the object of the sentiment of friendship. This is proved by the delight mothers take in the feeling: some give up their children to be adopted and raised by others and, knowing them, bear this feeling toward them without ever seeking to have it returned (when both are not possible); they are content with seeing them well off and bearing this feeling toward them, even though the children, through ignorance, never render them filial regard.

Since friendship consists rather in entertaining than in being the object of the sentiment, and those who are fond of their friends are praised, entertaining the sentiment is evidently the excellence of friends. Those in whom this exists in due proportion are stable friends, and their friendship is permanent. In this way those who are unequal may best be friends, since they may thus be made equal.

Equality and similarity are a tie of friendship, especially similarity in goodness: good men, being stable in themselves, are also stable toward others, and neither ask degrading services nor render them, but rather prevent them; it is the part of the good neither to do wrong themselves nor to allow their friends in so doing.

The bad, by contrast, have no principle of stability; they do not even remain like themselves. Only for a short time do they become friends, by taking delight in one another's wickedness. Those connected by profit or pleasure hold together somewhat longer — so long, that is, as they can give pleasure or profit mutually.

The friendship based on profit is thought to be most of all formed from contrary elements: the poor man is thus a friend of the rich, the ignorant of the man of information — a man desiring what he is in want of gives something else in exchange. To this class we may refer the lover and the beloved, the beautiful and the ill-favored. For this reason lovers sometimes look ridiculous claiming to be the objects of as intense a feeling as they entertain; of course, if they are equally fit objects of friendship, they may be entitled; but if they have nothing of the kind, it is ridiculous.

Perhaps the contrary does not aim at its contrary for its own sake, but only incidentally. The mean is really what is reached for: it is good for the dry not to become wet but to attain the mean, and similarly for the hot and the rest.
Let us drop these questions; they are somewhat foreign to our purpose.

It seems, as was said at the outset, that friendship and justice have the same object-matter and subsist between the same persons. In every communion there is thought to be some principle of justice and also some friendship. Men address as friends those who are their comrades by sea or in war, and likewise those brought into communion with them in other ways. The friendship — and the justice — is coextensive with the communion. This justifies the proverb "the goods of friends are common": friendship rests on communion.

Brothers and intimate companions have everything in common, while others have their property separate, and some have more in common than others, as the friendships also differ in degree. So too the principles of justice involved: not the same between parents and children as between brothers, nor between companions as between fellow-citizens, and so on for all conceivable friendships. The principles of injustice differ likewise at these different grades, and the acts are intensified by being done to friends: it is worse to rob your companion than a mere fellow-citizen; to refuse help to a brother than to a stranger; to strike your father than anyone else. Justice naturally increases with the degree of friendship, being between the same parties and of equal extent.

All cases of communion are, so to speak, parts of the great social one; men associate for some advantage and to procure some things needful for life. The great social communion is thought to have been associated originally, and to continue, for some advantage. This is what legislators aim at, calling just what is generally expedient.

Other cases of communion aim at particular advantages: a ship's crew at what is to result from the voyage, undertaken for money or some such object; comrades in war at what is to result from the war, grasping at wealth, victory, or a political position; those of the same tribe or demos likewise.

Some are thought to be formed for pleasure's sake — bacchanals or club fellows, aiming at sacrifice or mere company. All these seem to fall under the great social communion, since that communion's aim is not merely momentary expediency but life as a whole and at all times. With that in view, members institute sacrifices and assemblies, to give honor to the gods and to procure for themselves respite from toil combined with pleasure. Sacrifices and religious assemblies in old times seem to have been a kind of first fruits after the ingathering of the crops, when they had most leisure.
So all instances of communion are parts of the great social one, and corresponding friendships follow.
Of political constitutions there are three kinds, and an equal number of deviations from them — corruptions of them, so to speak.

The proper forms are kingship, aristocracy, and what recognizes the principle of wealth, which it seems appropriate to call timocracy (I give it the name of a political constitution because people commonly do). Of these, monarchy is best, timocracy the worst.

The deviation from monarchy is despotism; both are monarchies but widely different. The despot looks to his own advantage, the king to his subjects'. He is no king who is not thoroughly independent and superior in all good things; such a man has no further wants, and so will not look to his own advantage but to his subjects'. One not in such a position is a mere king elected by lot for the time.

Despotism is the contrary of such kingship, since the despot pursues his own good; its inferiority is most evident, and what is worse is contrary to what is best. The transition to despotism is from kingship, despotism being a corrupt form of monarchy: the bad king becomes a despot.

From aristocracy the transition to oligarchy is made through the fault of the rulers in distributing the public property contrary to right proportion, giving either all that is good, or the greatest share, to themselves, and keeping offices in the same hands always, making wealth their idol. So a few bear rule, and they bad men instead of the best.

From timocracy the transition is to democracy, the two being contiguous: it is the nature of timocracy to be in the hands of a multitude, and all in the same grade of property are equal. Democracy is the least vicious, since its form of constitution undergoes least change.
These, then, are the changes the constitutions usually undergo, being least in degree and easiest to make.

One may find likenesses and, as it were, models of these even in domestic life. The communion between a father and his sons presents the figure of kingship, since the children are the father's care; hence Homer calls Zeus "Father," kingship being intended as paternal rule. Among the Persians, however, paternal rule is despotic: they treat their sons as slaves. (The relation of master to slaves is of the nature of despotism, since what is regarded is the master's interest.) The first seems to be as it should be; the Persian custom seems wrong, since different persons need different rules.

Between husband and wife the relation takes the form of aristocracy: he rules by right, and in such points only as the husband should, giving to the wife all that befits her. Where the husband lords it in everything, he changes the relation into oligarchy; he does so contrary to right, not as being the better of the two. In some cases wives take the reins, being heiresses; then rule is carried on not by goodness but by wealth and power, as in oligarchies.

Timocracy finds its type in the relation of brothers: they are equal except for such differences as age introduces; if they are very different in age, the friendship comes to be no longer a fraternal one. Democracy is represented especially by families with no head (all being there equal), or where the head is weak, and every member does what is right in his own eyes.

Corresponding to each political constitution, then, is a friendship coextensive with its principle of justice. That between king and subjects is in the relation of superiority of benefit: the king benefits his subjects (supposing him a good king who cares for their welfare, as a shepherd tends his flock — hence Homer, to quote him again, calls Agamemnon "shepherd of the people"). Of this kind too is paternal friendship, only it exceeds the kingly in the greatness of benefits done; the father is the author of being (esteemed the greatest benefit), and of maintenance and education (things also ascribed, by the way, to ancestors generally). By the law of nature the father has the right of rule over his sons, ancestors over their descendants, and the king over his subjects.

These friendships are between superiors and inferiors, for which reason parents are not only loved but also honored. The principle of justice between these parties is not exactly equal but proportionate — since so is the friendship.

Between husband and wife there is the same friendship as in aristocracy: the relation is determined by relative excellence, the better person has the greater good, and each has what befits. So too the principle of justice between them.

The fraternal friendship is like that of companions: brothers are equal and much of an age, and such persons generally have like feelings and dispositions. Like to this also is the friendship of a timocracy, since the citizens are intended to be equal and equitable; rule passes from hand to hand and is distributed on equal terms. The friendship is accordingly so.

In the deviations from the constitutional forms, just as the principle of justice is small, so is the friendship; and least of all in the most perverted form. In despotism there is little or no friendship. Generally, where ruler and ruled have nothing in common, there is no friendship, since there is no justice; the case is as between an artisan and his tool, or body and soul, or master and slave. All these are benefited by those who use them, but toward inanimate things there is neither friendship nor justice — nor even toward a horse or an ox, or a slave qua slave, since there is nothing in common. A slave as such is an animate tool, a tool an inanimate slave. Qua slave, then, there is no friendship toward him — only qua man. It is thought there is some principle of justice between every man and every other who can share in law and be a party to an agreement; and so some friendship, insofar as he is a man. In despotisms, then, friendships and the principle of justice are inconsiderable; in democracies they are most considerable, since equals have much in common.

All friendship, of course, is based on communion, as said. But one would be inclined to separate off from the rest the friendship of kindred, and that of companions. Those of men of the same city, tribe, or crew, and all such, are more peculiarly based on communion, since they plainly exist by some agreement, express or implied. Among these one may also rank the friendship of hospitality.

The friendship of kindred is of many kinds, all of which appear to depend on the parental. Parents love their children as being a part of themselves; children love their parents as being themselves somewhat derived from them. Parents know their offspring better than the children know they are from the parents, and the source is more closely bound to what is produced than what is produced is to what formed it. Whatever is derived from oneself is proper to that from which it is so derived (a tooth, a hair, or any other thing to him who has it); but the source to it is in no degree proper, or in an inferior degree.

There is also the greater length of time: parents love their offspring from the first moment of their being, but their offspring love them only after a lapse of time when they have attained intelligence or instinct. These considerations also show why mothers have stronger affection than fathers.

Parents love their children as themselves (what is derived from themselves becomes, by separation, a kind of other self), and children love their parents as being sprung from them. Brothers love one another as being sprung from the same; their sameness with the common stock creates a sameness with one another. Hence the phrases "same blood," "root," and so on. They are in a sense the same, even in the separate distinct individuals.

Being brought up together, and the nearness of age, are a great help to friendship: a man likes one of his own age, and persons used to one another are companions. Hence the resemblance between the friendship of brothers and that of companions.
Cousins and all other relatives derive their bond of union from these — from their community of origin. The strength of this bond varies with their respective distances from the common ancestor.

The friendship felt by children toward parents, and by men toward the gods, is as toward something good and above them; these have conferred the greatest possible benefits — being the causes of their being, their nourishment, and their having been educated after they were brought into being.

Such friendship also has the pleasurable and the profitable in greater measure than friendship between persons unrelated by blood, in proportion as their life is more shared in common. Fraternal friendship has all that friendship of companions has, and more in the good and generally in those who are alike: they are more closely tied, have a feeling of affection for one another from birth to begin with, and are more like in disposition, being from the same stock and having grown up together and been educated alike. Besides this they have the greatest opportunities of time for testing one another, and can therefore depend most securely on the trial.

Between husband and wife there is thought to be friendship by a law of nature: man is by nature more disposed to pair than to associate in communities, in proportion as the family is prior in time and more absolutely necessary than the community. Procreation is more common to man with the other animals; all the other animals have communion thus far. But humans cohabit not merely to procreate, but also with a view to life in general: in this connection the works are immediately divided, some belonging to the man, others to the woman. Thus they help one another, putting what is peculiar to each into the common stock.

For these reasons this friendship is thought to combine the profitable and the pleasurable. It will also be based on virtue if they are good people; each has goodness and they may take delight in this quality in each other. Children too are thought to be a tie — hence the childless sooner separate; children are a good common to both, and anything in common is a bond of union.

The question how a man is to live with his wife, or more generally how one friend is to live with another, seems no different from this: how it is just that they should. The principle of justice between friend and friend is not the same as between strangers, or companions, or mere chance fellow travelers.

There are then, as stated at the outset of this book, three kinds of friendship; and in each there may be friends on a footing of equality and friends in the relation of superior and inferior. People alike in goodness, and better with worse, and likewise pleasant people, become friends. Again, because of advantage, people are friends — either exactly balancing their mutual profitableness or differing from one another. Those who are equal should by that equality be equalized in the degree of their friendship and the other points; those on a footing of inequality, by rendering friendship in proportion to the other party's superiority.

Fault-finding and blame arise, either solely or most naturally, in friendship whose motive is utility. Those who are friends by reason of goodness are eager to do kindnesses to one another — a natural result of goodness and friendship; and when men are vying for this end, there can be no fault-finding or contention. No one is annoyed at one who entertains friendship for him and does kindnesses; a refined man requites them with kind actions. Even if one of the two exceeds the other, since he is attaining his object he will not find fault, since good is the object of each.

Nor can there well be quarrels between men who are friends for pleasure. If they delight in living together, both attain their desire; a man would be in a ridiculous position if he found fault with another for not pleasing him, since it is in his power to avoid the company. But friendship from advantage is very liable to fault-finding. Since the parties use one another with a view to advantage, the requirements are continually enlarging; they think they have less than they are entitled to, and find fault when, justly entitled, they do not get as much as they want; while those doing the kindnesses can never come up to the requirements of those receiving them.

As the just is of two kinds, unwritten and legal, so friendship because of advantage is of two kinds, the moral and the legal; and the most fruitful source of complaints is that parties contract obligations in one line of friendship and discharge them in another. The legal kind rests on specified conditions, either purely business from hand to hand, or somewhat more gentlemanly as regards time, but still by agreement a quid pro quo.

In this legal kind the obligation is clear and admits of no dispute; the friendly element is the delay in requiring its discharge. For this reason in some countries no actions can be maintained at law to recover such debts — it is held that those who have dealt on credit must be content to abide the issue.

The moral kind is not on specified conditions: a man gives as to his friend, and so on; but still he expects to receive an equivalent or more, as if he had not given but lent. He also finds fault, because he does not get the obligation discharged in the way it was contracted.

This results from the fact that all men, or most, wish for what is honorable but, when tested, choose what is profitable. Doing kindnesses disinterestedly is honorable; receiving benefits is profitable. In such cases one should, if able, make a return proportionate to the good received, and do so willingly — one ought not to make a disinterested friend of a man against his inclination. One should act, that is, as having made a mistake originally in receiving kindness from someone one ought not to have — he being not a friend nor doing the act disinterestedly. So one should discharge oneself of the obligation as having received a kindness on specified terms. If able, one would undertake to repay the kindness; if unable, even the doer would not expect it. So, if able, one ought to repay it. But one should at the outset ascertain from whom one is receiving kindness, and on what understanding, so that one may accept on that understanding or not.
A disputed question: should one measure a kindness by the good done to the receiver, and make this the standard for requital, or by the kind intention of the doer?

Those who have received kindnesses frequently plead in depreciation that they received from their benefactors things that were small for them to give, or such as they themselves could have gotten from others. The doers of the kindnesses affirm that they gave the best they had, and what could not have been gotten from others, under danger or in similar straits.

May we not say: since utility is the motive, the advantage conferred on the receiver must be the standard? He it is who requests the kindness, and the other serves him in his need on the understanding he will get an equivalent; the assistance rendered is exactly proportionate to the advantage the receiver has obtained, so he should repay as much as he gained by it, or even more, this being more creditable.
In friendships based on goodness this question of course is never raised; here the doer's motive seems to be the proper standard, since virtue and moral character depend principally on motive.
Quarrels also arise in unequal friendships, because each party thinks himself entitled to the greater share; when this happens, the friendship is broken up.

The better man thinks the greater share pertains to him of right, since more is always awarded the good. Similarly the one more profitable to another than that other is to him: "one who is useless," they say, "ought not to share equally, for then it comes to a tax, not a friendship, unless the fruits are reaped in proportion to the works done." Their notion: as in a money partnership those who contribute more receive more, so should it be in friendship.

The needy man and the less virtuous advance the opposite claim: they say "it is the very business of a good friend to help those in need, else what is the use of a good or powerful friend, if one is not to reap the advantage at all?"

Each seems to advance a right claim and to be entitled to more out of the connection than the other — only not more of the same thing. The superior man should receive more respect, the needy man more profit: respect being the reward of goodness and beneficence, profit the relief of need.

This is plainly the principle acted on in political communities. No one receives honor who gives no good to the common stock; the property of the public is given to him who does good to the public, and honor is the property of the public. One cannot both make money out of the public and receive honor likewise, since no one will put up with the less in every respect. So to him who suffers loss as regards money they award honor, and money to him who can be paid by gifts; as said before, observing due proportion equalizes and preserves friendship.

Like rules should be observed in the intercourse of unequal friends: to him who advantages another in money or goodness, that other should repay honor, making return according to his power; friendship requires what is possible, not what is strictly due, this being not possible in all cases — as with honors paid to the gods and to parents. No man could ever make the due return in these cases; he is thought good who pays respect according to his ability.

For this reason it may be judged that it is never allowable for a son to disown his father, though a father may his son. He who owes is bound to pay; a son can never, by anything he has done, fully requite the benefits first conferred on him by his father, and so is always a debtor. But those to whom anything is owed may cast off their debtors: therefore the father may his son. Yet it must perhaps be admitted that no father would sever himself utterly from a son except in a case of exceeding depravity, since, apart from the natural friendship, it is like human nature not to put away from oneself the assistance a son might render. But to the son, if depraved, assisting his father is a thing to be avoided, or at least one which he will not be very anxious to do — most men being willing to receive kindness but averse to doing it as unprofitable.
Let this suffice on these points.

chapters.title: Book 9 — Friendship (continued)
paragraphs: In all friendships between dissimilar parties, the proportionate is what equalizes and preserves the friendship, as said already. In social friendship the cobbler, for instance, gets an equivalent for his shoes at a certain rate; and the weaver and all others likewise. Here a common measure has been provided in money, and to this all things are referred and by it measured. But in the friendship of love the complaint is sometimes from the lover that, though he loves exceedingly, his love is not requited — perhaps while he has nothing that can be an object of friendship. Often, again, from the beloved, that he who as a suitor promised anything and everything now performs nothing. These cases occur because the lover's friendship for the beloved is based on pleasure, the other's for him on utility, and in one of the parties the requisite quality is not found. As these are respectively the grounds of the friendship, the friendship breaks up when the motives cease. The parties loved not each other, but qualities in each other that are not permanent, and so neither are the friendships. Friendship based on the moral character of the parties, being independent and disinterested, is permanent, as said already.

Quarrels also arise when the parties realize different results and not those they desire; failing to attain one's particular object is, in this case, the same as getting nothing at all. Take the well-known case: a man made promises to a musician, rising in proportion to the excellence of his music; but the next morning, when the musician claimed fulfillment, he said he had given him pleasure for pleasure. If each party had intended this, it would have been fair; but if one desires amusement and the other gain, and one gets his object while the other does not, the dealing cannot be fair. A man fixes his mind on what he happens to want, and will give so and so for that specific thing.

The question then arises: who is to fix the rate — the giver or the receiver? At first sight, the giver seems to leave the rate to be fixed by the other. They say this was the practice of Protagoras: when he taught a man anything, he would bid the learner estimate the worth of the knowledge gained by his own private opinion, and he would take so much from him. In such cases some adopt the rule,
"With specified reward a friend should be content."

Those are fairly criticized who take money in advance and then do nothing of what they said they would, their promises having been so far beyond their ability — for they do not perform what they agreed. The Sophists, perhaps, are obliged to take this course because no one would give a penny for their knowledge. These, I say, are fairly criticized, since they do not do what they have already been paid for.

Where no stipulation is made about the respective services, those who do the first service disinterestedly will not raise the question (as we have said), because it is the nature of friendship based on mutual goodness to look to the other's intention — intention being characteristic of the true friend and of goodness.

The same rule should apply to those connected with each other as teachers and learners of philosophy. Here the value of the commodity cannot be measured in money, and in fact an exactly equivalent price cannot be set on it; perhaps it is sufficient to do what one can, as in the case of the gods or one's parents.

But where the original giving is not on these terms but avowedly for some return, the most proper course is for the requital to be such as both shall allow is proportionate. Where this cannot be, for the receiver to fix the value would seem not only necessary but also fair. When the first giver gets what is equivalent to the advantage received by the other (or to what the other would have given to secure the pleasure he has had), then he has the value from him. This is the course adopted in buying and selling, and in some places the law does not allow actions on voluntary dealings, on the principle that when one man has trusted another he must be content to have the obligation discharged in the same spirit as he originally contracted it. That is, it is thought fairer for the trusted than for the trusting party to fix the value. Generally, those who have and those who wish to get a thing do not set the same value on it: what is their own, and what they give in each case, seems to them worth a great deal. Still, the return is made according to the receiver's estimate — and perhaps the receiver should estimate what he has received not by the value he sets on it now that he has it, but by the value he set on it before he obtained it.

Questions also arise on such points as these: Has one's father an unlimited claim on one's services and obedience, or is the sick man to obey his physician? In electing a general, should the candidates' warlike qualities alone be regarded?
Likewise, should one do a service for a friend rather than a good man? Should one requite a benefactor or give to one's companion, supposing both are not within one's power?

Is not the true answer that it is no easy task to determine all such questions accurately, since they involve numerous differences of amount, honor, and necessity? It is obvious that no one person can unite all claims in himself. Generally, the requital of benefits is a higher duty than doing unsolicited kindnesses to a companion — the discharging of a debt is more obligatory than the giving. Yet this rule admits exceptions. Which is the higher duty for one who has been ransomed from robbers: to ransom his ransomer in return, whoever he is; to repay him on his demand though he has not been captured; or to ransom his own father? A man ought to ransom his father even in preference to himself.

So as a general rule the debt should be discharged; but if in a particular case the giving greatly preponderates as being honorable or necessary, we must be swayed by these considerations. In some cases the requital may not be equal — suppose the original benefactor conferred a kindness on a good man, knowing him such, while the good man has to repay one he believes a scoundrel.

In certain cases no obligation lies to lend to one who has lent: suppose a bad man lent thinking one was a good man and would repay, while the said good man has no hope of repayment, knowing the lender to be bad. Either the case is really so and the claim is not equal, or it is not so but supposed to be. Still, acting so is not to act wrongly. As oftentimes said before, all statements about feelings and actions can be definite only so far as their object-matter is; it is obvious that all people do not have the same claim on one, and one's father's claims are not unlimited — just as Zeus does not claim all kinds of sacrifice indiscriminately. Since the claims of parents, brothers, companions, and benefactors are all different, we must give to each what belongs to and befits each.

This is seen to be the course commonly pursued. To marriages men commonly invite their relatives, since they come from a common stock and therefore all the actions pertaining to it are common. To funerals men think relatives ought to assemble in preference to others, for the same reason.

In respect of maintenance, it is our duty to assist our parents in preference to all others, as being their debtors, and because it is more honorable to assist in these respects the authors of our existence than ourselves. Honor we ought to pay to parents as to the gods — but not all kinds; not the same to a father as to a mother; nor to a father the honor due to a scientific man or a general, but the honor that is a father's due; and likewise to a mother what is a mother's.

To all our elders we owe the honor befitting their age: rising in their presence, turning out of the way for them, and similar marks of respect. To companions and brothers, frankness and full sharing in all we have. To those of the same family, tribe, or city, and all similarly connected, we should constantly try to render their due, discriminating what belongs to each by nearness of connection, goodness, or intimacy. Among those of the same class the discrimination is easier; among those in different classes it requires more trouble. This should not make us give up the attempt, though; we must observe the distinctions as far as practicable.
The question is also raised whether to dissolve friendships whose parties do not remain what they were when the connection was formed.

With those whose motive is utility or pleasure, there is nothing wrong in breaking off when they no longer have those qualities, since they were friends not of each other but of those qualities; when these have failed, it is reasonable to expect that they should cease to feel the sentiment.

But a man has reason to complain if the other, really attached to him for advantage or pleasure, pretended to be so for his moral character. As we said at the outset, the most common source of quarrels between friends is their not being friends on the same grounds as they suppose themselves to be.

When a man has been deceived into supposing he excited friendship on the ground of his moral character, the other doing nothing to indicate the true ground, he has only himself to blame. But when deceived by the pretense of the other, he has a right to find fault with the deceiver — even more than with utterers of false coin, in proportion to the greater preciousness of the object of the villainy.

Suppose a man takes up another as good, who turns out to be a scoundrel; is he still bound to feel friendship? May we not say at once: it is impossible? Not everything is the object-matter of friendship, only what is good; there is no obligation to be a bad man's friend, and in fact one should not be — one should not be a lover of evil, nor assimilated to what is base, since, as we said, like is friendly to like.

Are we to break with him instantly? Not in every case; only when the friend is incurably depraved. When there is a chance of amendment, we are bound to aid in repairing our friends' moral character even more than their substance, in proportion as character is better and more closely related to friendship. Still, he who breaks off is not judged to act wrongly: he was never a friend to such a character as this man now is, and since the man is changed and cannot be restored, he withdraws from the connection.

Another case: suppose one party remains what he was when the friendship was formed, while the other becomes morally improved and widely different in goodness. Is the improved to treat the other as a friend?

May we not say this is impossible? The case is clearest when the difference is great, as in friendships of boys. Suppose of two boyhood friends one still remains a boy in mind and the other becomes a man of the highest character — how can they be friends? They are not pleased with the same objects, nor like and dislike the same things; these points will not belong to them in relation to each other, and without them, as said, they cannot be friends, since they cannot live in intimacy. We spoke earlier of the case of those who cannot do so.
Is the improved party to bear himself toward his former friend no differently than if the connection had never existed?

Surely he should bear in mind the intimacy of past times, and just as we feel bound to do favors for friends in preference to strangers, so to those who have been friends and are no longer we should make allowance on the score of former friendship, unless the cause of severance is excessive depravity.
The friendly feelings exhibited toward our friends, and by which friendships are characterized, seem to have sprung from those we entertain toward ourselves.

People define a friend as "one who intends and does what is good, or what he believes to be good, to another for that other's sake," or "one who wishes his friend to be and to live for that friend's own sake" (which is the mothers' feeling toward their children, and the feeling of friends who have quarreled). Others: "one who lives with another and chooses the same objects," or "one who sympathizes with his friend in his sorrows and in his joys" (this too especially of mothers).

By some one of these marks people generally characterize friendship. Each of these the good man has toward himself, and all others have them insofar as they suppose themselves to be good. (As said before, goodness — that is, the good man — seems to be the measure for everyone else.)

For the good man is at unity in himself and with every part of his soul desires the same things. He wishes for himself both what is, and what he believes to be, good; and he does it (it being characteristic of the good to work at the good); and he does it for his own sake, insofar as he does it for the sake of his intellectual principle, which is generally thought to be a man's self. He wishes himself (and especially this principle by which he is an intelligent being) to live and be preserved, since existence is a good to the good man.

It is to himself that each individual wishes what is good; no man, conceiving the possibility of becoming other than he now is, chooses that that new self should have all things indiscriminately. A god, for instance, at this moment has the chief good, but he has it by being whatever he actually now is. The intelligent principle must be judged to be each man's self, or at least eminently so (though other principles also help to constitute him the man he is).

Furthermore, the good man wishes to continue to live with himself; he can do so with pleasure, since his memories of past actions are full of delight and his anticipations of the future are good, and such are pleasurable. Then, too, he has good store of matter for his intellect to contemplate, and he especially sympathizes with his self in its griefs and joys, because the objects that give him pain and pleasure are always the same, not one thing today and another tomorrow — he is not given to repentance, so to speak. Since each of these feelings is entertained by the good man toward his own self, and since a friend feels toward a friend as toward himself (a friend being, in fact, another self), friendship is thought to be some one of these things, and they are accounted friends in whom they are found. Whether there can really be friendship between a man and his self we will not discuss now; there may be thought to be, insofar as there are two or more of the aforesaid requisites, and because the highest degree of friendship, in the usual acceptation, resembles a man's feeling toward himself.
It may be urged that the aforesaid requisites are found to all appearances in the common run of men, though they are of a low stamp.

May it not be answered that they share in them only so far as they please themselves and conceive themselves to be good? These requisites are certainly not found, really or even apparently, in anyone very depraved and villainous; we may almost say not even in bad men at all. They are at variance with themselves and lust after different things from those which, in cool reason, they wish for, just like men who fail in self-control: they choose what is hurtful but pleasurable over what in their own minds they believe to be good. Others, from cowardice and indolence, decline to do what they are yet convinced is best for them. Those who, from depravity, have actually done many dreadful things hate and avoid life, and accordingly kill themselves. The wicked seek others in whose company to spend their time, but flee themselves because they have many unpleasant memories and can only look forward to others like them when in solitude; they drown their remorse in the company of others. Having nothing to raise the sentiment of friendship, they never feel it toward themselves.

Nor in fact can those of this character sympathize with their selves in their joys and sorrows, because their soul is, as it were, rent by faction; one principle, by reason of the depravity in them, is grieved at abstaining from certain things, while the other and better principle is pleased at abstaining; and one drags them this way and the other that, as though actually tearing them asunder. And though it is impossible actually to have pain and pleasure at the same time, yet after a little time the man is sorry for having been pleased, and would wish those objects had not pleased him; the wicked are full of remorse.

It is plain, then, that the wicked man cannot be in the position of a friend even to himself, because he has in himself nothing that can excite the sentiment of friendship. If to be thus is exceedingly wretched, a man's duty is to flee from wickedness with all his might and to strive to be good, so that he may be a friend to himself and come to be a friend to another.

Kindly feeling, though resembling friendship, is not identical with it: it may exist toward those we do not know, and without the object being aware of it, which friendship cannot. (This, by the way, has been said before.) Further, it is not even affection, since it does not imply intensity or yearning, both consequences of affection. Affection requires intimacy, but kindly feeling may arise quite suddenly — as sometimes happens toward men we see matched against others in some contest; we come to be kindly disposed to them and sympathize in their wishes, but would not join them in any action, since we conceive this feeling of kindness suddenly and so have but a superficial liking.

Kindly feeling seems to be the starting point of a friendship, as pleasure received through sight is the beginning of love. No one falls in love without being first pleased with the beloved's appearance; yet one who takes pleasure in it does not therefore necessarily love, but only when he longs for the object in its absence and desires its presence. Likewise, men cannot be friends without passing through the stage of kindly feeling; yet those in that stage do not necessarily advance to friendship. They merely have an inert wish for the good of those toward whom they feel it, but would not join them in action nor put themselves out for them. Metaphorically one might say kindly feeling is dormant friendship; when it has endured and ripened into intimacy, it comes to be real friendship — but not the friendship whose object is advantage or pleasure, since such motives cannot produce even kindly feeling.

One who has received a kindness requites it by kindly feeling toward his benefactor, and is right to do so. But one who wishes another well because he has hope of advantage through him is not kindly disposed to that person but rather to himself — just as he is not his friend if he pays court to him for an interested purpose.

Kindly feeling always arises by reason of goodness and a certain amiability, when one man gives another the notion of being a fine fellow, or brave man, or the like — as we said sometimes happens with those matched against one another.
Unity of sentiment (concord) is also connected with friendship, and so is not the same as unity of opinion, which might exist between people unacquainted with one another.

Nor do people usually say men have unity of sentiment merely because they agree in opinion on any point — astronomical science, for instance — unity of sentiment about this having no connection with friendship. But they say communities have unity of sentiment when they agree about expedient things, take the same line, and carry out what has been determined in common consultation.

So unity of sentiment has for its object-matter matters of action, those of importance, and of mutual interest (or, in the case of a single state, common interest): as when all agree in the choice of magistrates, or forming alliance with the Spartans, or appointing Pittacus ruler (assuming he himself was willing). But when each wishes himself to be in power (as the brothers in the Phoenissae), they quarrel and form parties; plainly, unity of sentiment does not merely imply that each entertains the same idea, whatever it may be, but that they do so in respect of the same object. When both the populace and the sensible men of a state wish the best men to be in office, all attain their object.
Unity of sentiment, then, is plainly a social friendship, as it is also said to be; its object-matter is things expedient and relating to life.

This unity exists among the good; they have it toward themselves and toward one another, being (if the expression is allowed) in the same position. The wishes of such men are steady and do not ebb and flow like the Euripus; they wish what is just and expedient, and aim at these in common.

The bad, on the contrary, can as little have unity of sentiment as they can be real friends, except to a slight extent, desiring as they do unfair advantage in profitable things while shirking labor and service for the common good. Each wishes these things for himself and is jealous of and hinders his neighbor; not watching over the common good, they lose it. The result is that they quarrel while compelling each other to work, but are unwilling to perform their own just share.

Benefactors are commonly held to have more friendship for the objects of their kindness than these have for them. The fact is made a subject of discussion, as being contrary to reasonable expectation.

The account that satisfies most is that the one are debtors, the others creditors; and as in actual loans debtors wish creditors out of the way while creditors are anxious for the preservation of debtors, so those who have done kindnesses desire the continued existence of those they have helped, under the notion of getting a return of their good offices; while these are not particularly anxious about requital.

Epicharmus, I suspect, would probably say those who give this solution judge from their own baseness. Yet it is certainly like human nature; most men have short memories on these points and aim rather at receiving than conferring benefits.

The real cause seems to rest in nature, and the case is not parallel to that of creditors. In that case there is no affection for the persons, only a wish for their preservation with a view to the return; whereas those who have done kindnesses feel friendship and love for those they have helped, even if they neither are nor could be in a position to serve their benefactors.

This is also true of artisans; everyone feels more affection for his own work than that work would for him if it were animate. It is perhaps specially the case with poets; they have very great affection for their poems, loving them as their own children. To this kind of thing I should compare the case of benefactors: the object of their kindness is their own work, and so they love it more than it loves its creator.

The account of this is that existence is to all a thing choice-worthy and an object of affection; we exist by acts of working, that is, by living and acting. He then who has created a given work exists, so to say, by his act of working; therefore he loves his work because he loves existence. This is natural, for the work produced displays in actuality what existed before potentially.

Then again, the benefactor has a sense of honor in right of his action, so that he may well take pleasure in the person in whom this resides. But to the one who has received the benefit, there is nothing honorable with respect to his benefactor — only something advantageous, which is both less pleasant and less an object of friendship.

Pleasure is derived from the actual working out of a present action, from anticipation of a future one, and from recollection of a past one; but the highest pleasure and special object of affection is that which attends on the actual working. The benefactor's work abides (what is honorable is enduring), but the advantage received passes away.
There is pleasure in recollecting honorable actions, but in recollecting advantageous ones there is none, or much less. (By the way, the contrary is true of the expectation of advantage.)
Further, entertaining the feeling of friendship is like acting on another; being the object of the feeling is like being acted on.
So entertaining the sentiment of friendship, and all feelings connected with it, attend on those who, in any case of benefaction, are the superior party.

Once more: all people value most what has cost them much labor. Those who have themselves made their money are fonder of it than those who have inherited it; receiving kindness is unlaborious, but doing it is laborious. This is also why mothers are fondest of their offspring; their part in producing them is attended with most labor, and they know most certainly that the children are theirs. This feeling seems to belong to benefactors too.

A question is also raised whether it is right to love oneself best, or someone else. Men find fault with those who love themselves best, and call them in a disparaging way lovers of self. The bad man is thought to do everything he does for his own sake merely, and the more so the more depraved he is; so men reproach him with never doing anything unselfish. The good man, on the contrary, acts from a sense of honor (and the more so the better he is), and for his friend's sake, careless of his own interest.

But facts are at variance with these theories, and not unnaturally. It is also said that a man is to love most him who is most his friend, and he is most a friend who wishes good to him to whom he wishes it for that man's sake even if no one knows. Now these conditions — and in fact all the rest by which a friend is characterized — belong specially to each individual in relation to his self: we said all friendly feelings are derived to others from those which primarily have self as object. All the current proverbs support this: "one soul," "the goods of friends are common," "equality is a tie of friendship," "the knee is nearer than the shin." All these exist specially with reference to a man's own self; he is specially a friend to himself and so bound to love himself the most.

It is reasonably questioned which of the two we should follow, both having plausibility. Perhaps in theories of this kind the proper course is to distinguish and define how far each is true, and in what way. If we could ascertain the sense in which each uses "self-loving," this might be cleared up.

Those who use it disparagingly give the name to those who in wealth, honors, and bodily pleasures give themselves the larger share; for most men grasp at these and are earnest about them as the best things — which is why they are matters of contention. Those covetous of these gratify their lusts and passions generally, that is, the irrational part of their soul. Most men are so disposed, and the name has taken its rise from the mass, which is low and bad. Those self-loving in this sense are justly reproached.

That men generally use the term to denote those who give such things to themselves is plain. Suppose a man were anxious beyond others to do just acts, or acts of self-mastery, or any other virtuous acts, and in general to secure for himself what is in itself noble and honorable; no one would call him self-loving or blame him.

Yet such a one might be judged more truly self-loving: he gives himself what is most noble and most good, and gratifies that principle of his nature which is most rightfully authoritative, obeying it in everything. Just as what possesses the highest authority is thought to constitute a community or any other system, so in the case of man. He is most truly self-loving who loves and gratifies this principle.

Again, men are said to have, or to fail of, self-control according as the intellect controls or not — plainly implying that this principle constitutes each individual. People are thought to have done of themselves, and voluntarily, those things especially that are done with reason.

It is plain, then, that this principle either entirely or specially constitutes the individual man, and that the good man specially loves this. So he must be specially self-loving in a kind other than that which is reproached, and as far superior to it as living according to reason is to living at the beck and call of passion, and aiming at the truly noble to aiming at apparent advantage.

All approve and commend those who are eminently earnest about honorable actions. If all would vie with one another in respect of the noble (kalon) and be intent on doing what is most truly noble, society at large would have all that is proper, while each individual would have the greatest of goods — virtue being assumed to be such.

So the good man ought to be self-loving; by doing what is noble he will advantage himself and also do good to others. But the bad man ought not to be, since he will harm himself and his neighbors by following low and evil passions. In the bad man's case, what he ought to do and what he does are at variance; but the good man does what he ought, because all intellect chooses what is best for itself, and the good man puts himself under the direction of intellect.

Of the good man it is also true that he does many things for his friends' and country's sake, even to dying for them if need be. Money, honors, and in short all the good things others fight for, he will throw away while eager to secure to himself the noble; he will prefer a brief and great joy to a tame and enduring one, and to live nobly for one year rather than ordinarily for many, and one great and noble action to many trifling ones. This is perhaps what befalls men who die for country or friends: they choose great glory for themselves. They will lavish their own money so that friends may receive more; the friend gets the money, but the man himself gets the noble — so in fact he gives himself the greater good. Similarly with honors and offices: he will give all these to his friend, since this reflects honor and praise on himself. With good reason, then, is he esteemed a fine character, since he chooses the honorable before all things. It is possible even to give up opportunities of action to a friend; to have caused a friend's doing a thing may be more noble than having done it oneself.
In short, in all praiseworthy things the good man plainly gives himself a larger share of the honorable. In this sense it is right to be self-loving; in the vulgar sense it is not.
A question is raised also about the happy man: will he want friends or not?

Some say the blessed and independent have no need of friends, since they already have all that is good, and being independent, want nothing further; a friend's office is to be a second self and procure for a man what he cannot get by himself — hence the saying,
"When fortune gives us good, what need we friends?"
But it looks absurd, while we assign the happy man all other good things, not to give him friends — which are, after all, thought the greatest of external goods.

If it is more characteristic of a friend to confer than to receive kindnesses, if being beneficent belongs to the good man and to virtue, and if it is more noble to confer kindnesses on friends than on strangers, the good man will need objects for his benefactions. From this last arises a question: is the need of friends greater in prosperity or in adversity? The unfortunate man wants people to do him kindnesses, while the fortunate want objects for their kind acts.

It is perhaps absurd to make our happy man a solitary; no man would choose the possession of all goods in the world on condition of solitude, man being a social animal and formed by nature for living with others. The happy man has this qualification, since he has all things good by nature. Obviously the society of friends and good men must be preferable to that of strangers and ordinary people. So the happy man does need friends.

What, then, do those quoted first mean, and how are they right? Is it not that the mass of mankind mean by friends those useful? The happy man will not need such, since he has all good things already. Nor will he need such as are friends for the pleasurable — or only slightly — because his life, being already pleasurable, needs no pleasure imported from without. Since the happy man does not need friends of these kinds, he is thought not to need any.

But this is probably not true. It was stated at the outset that happiness is a kind of working; working plainly is something that must come into being, not already there like a mere piece of property.

If being happy consists in living and working, and the good man's working is in itself excellent and pleasurable (as said at the beginning of the treatise), and if what is our own ranks among things pleasurable, and if we can view our neighbors better than ourselves and their actions better than our own — then the actions of friends who are good are pleasurable to the good, since they have both the naturally pleasant requisites. So the man in the highest state of happiness will need friends of this kind, since he desires to contemplate good actions, and actions that are his own — and those of his friend, a good man, are such.

Again, common opinion requires the happy man to live with pleasure to himself. Life is burdensome in solitude; it is not easy to work continuously by oneself, but in company and in relation to others it is easier, and so the working, being pleasurable in itself, will be more continuous (a thing required in the happy man's life). The good man, being good, takes pleasure in actions according to virtue and is annoyed at those springing from vice, just as a musical man is pleased with beautiful music and annoyed by bad. Besides, as Theognis says, virtue itself may be improved by practice, from living with the good.

On more purely metaphysical grounds, it will probably appear that the good friend is naturally choice-worthy to the good man. We have said that whatever is naturally good is also in itself good and pleasant to the good man. The fact of living, so far as animals are concerned, is characterized generally by the power of sensation; in man, by the power of sensation or of rationality (the faculty being referred to its actual operation; the main point being the actual operation). Living, then, seems mainly to consist in the act of sensing or exerting rationality. The fact of living is itself one of the good and pleasant things (a definite totality, and whatever is such belongs to the nature of good). What is naturally good is good to the good man, for which reason it seems pleasant to all. (Of course one should not suppose a depraved and corrupted life, or one spent in pain — such a life is indefinite, as are its inherent qualities; however, what is to be said of pain will be clearer later.)

If the fact of living is in itself good and pleasant — evident from the fact that all desire it, especially the good and supremely happy, whose course of life and existence are most choice-worthy — then also he who sees perceives that he sees; he who hears perceives that he hears; he who walks perceives that he walks; and similarly there is a faculty reflecting upon and perceiving that we are working. So we can perceive that we perceive and intellectually know that we intellectually know; but to perceive that we perceive or intellectually know is to perceive that we exist, since existence was defined as perceiving or intellectually knowing. To perceive that one lives is a thing pleasant in itself, life being naturally good, and the perceiving in ourselves of things naturally good being pleasant.
So the fact of living is choice-worthy, especially to the good, since existence is good and pleasant to them; they receive pleasure from the internal consciousness of what is in itself good.

But the good man is to his friend as to himself, "friend" being but a name for a second self; therefore, as his own existence is choice-worthy to each, so too, or similarly, is his friend's existence. The ground of one's own existence being choice-worthy is the perception of oneself being good, any such perception being in itself pleasant. Therefore one ought to be thoroughly conscious of one's friend's existence, which results from living with him — sharing in his words and thoughts. For this is what "living together" means as applied to the human species, not mere feeding together as among animals.

If, then, to the man in a high state of happiness existence is in itself choice-worthy, being naturally good and pleasant, and so too is a friend's existence, then the friend also must be among things choice-worthy. But whatever is choice-worthy to a man he should have, or else he will be in this point deficient. So the man who is to come up to our notion of "happy" will need good friends.

Are we, then, to make our friends as numerous as possible? Or, as it is thought well said of acquaintance — "have not many acquaintances, yet be not without" — should we adopt the same precept for friendship and say a man should not be without friends, yet also not have exceedingly many?

For friends intended for use, the quoted maxim will, it seems, fit exceedingly well: to requite the services of many is a labor, and a whole life would not be long enough to do this for them. If more numerous than what will suffice for one's own life, they become officious and hindrances to living well, and so we do not want them. Of those for pleasure, a few are quite enough, like seasoning in our food.

But of the good, are we to make as many friends as we can, or is there a measure to the number, as there is to what constitutes a political community? You cannot make one out of ten men, and if you increase the number to a hundred thousand, it is no longer a community. The number is perhaps not some one definite number, but any between certain extreme limits.

Of friends likewise there is a limited number — perhaps the greatest number with whom it would be possible to keep up intimacy; this being thought one of the greatest marks of friendship, and it being quite obvious that it is not possible to be intimate with many — that is, to divide oneself among many. Besides, they must also be friends to one another if they are all to live together, and it is hard to find this in many men at once.
It also becomes difficult to take home to oneself the joys and sorrows of many; in all probability one would have to sympathize at the same time with the joys of one and the sorrows of another.

Perhaps, then, it is well not to strive to have very many friends, but only enough for intimacy; it seems impossible to be very much a friend to many at the same time, and for the same reason, not to be in love with many objects at once — love being a kind of excessive friendship which implies but one object. All strong emotions must be limited in the number toward whom they are felt.

If we look at the facts, this seems to be so: not many at a time become friends in the way of companionship; the famous friendships of this kind are between two persons. Those who have many friends and meet everybody on an intimate footing seem to be friends really to no one except in the way of general society — the overly obliging characters we described.

In mere society a man may be a friend to many without being overly obliging, by being truly good; but one cannot be a friend to many because of their virtue and for their own sake — it is a matter for satisfaction to find even a few such.

Are friends most needed in prosperity or adversity? They are required in both. The unfortunate need help, and the prosperous want people to live with and to do kindnesses to; they desire to act kindly to someone.

To have friends is more necessary in adversity, and so in this case useful friends are wanted; to have them in prosperity is more honorable, and so the prosperous want good men for friends, it being preferable to confer benefits on, and to live with, these. The very presence of friends is pleasant even in adversity: men when grieved are comforted by the sympathy of friends.

Hence the question may be raised: do friends in a manner take part of the weight of calamities, or does their presence, being pleasurable, and the consciousness of their sympathy, make the sufferer's pain less?
We will not further discuss whether these suggested causes or others produce the relief; at least the effect is a matter of plain fact.

But their presence probably has a mixed effect. The very seeing of friends is pleasant, especially to one in misfortune; actual help toward lessening the grief is afforded — the natural tendency of a friend, if he has tact, being to comfort by look and word, since he knows the sufferer's temper and disposition and so knows what gives him pleasure and pain. But also, perceiving a friend to be grieved at his misfortunes causes the sufferer pain, since everyone avoids being the cause of pain to his friends. For this reason men of a manly nature are cautious not to implicate their friends in their pain; unless a man is exceedingly callous to others' pain, he cannot bear the pain thus caused to his friends. He does not admit men to wail with him, not being given to wailing at all. Women and men who resemble women like to have others groan with them, and love such as friends and sympathizers. But plainly it is our duty in all things to imitate the higher character.
The advantages of friends in our prosperity are the pleasant intercourse and the consciousness that they are pleased at our good fortune.

We ought, then, to call in friends readily on the occasion of good fortune, since it is noble to be ready to do good to others; but on the occasion of bad fortune, we should do so with reluctance, making others share our ills as little as possible; hence the saying, "I am unfortunate, let that suffice." The most proper occasion for calling them in is when with small trouble to themselves they can be of very great use.

On the contrary, it is perhaps fitting to go to one's friends in their misfortunes unasked and with alacrity, since kindness is the friend's office, especially toward those in need who do not demand it as a right — this being more creditable and pleasant to both. On occasion of their good fortune we should go readily if we can forward it in any way (men need their friends for this likewise), but be backward in sharing it, since any great eagerness to receive advantage is not creditable.
One should perhaps be cautious not to present an appearance of sullenness in declining the sympathy or help of friends, as happens occasionally.
It appears, then, that the presence of friends is, in all circumstances, choice-worthy.
May we not say, then, that as seeing the beloved is most prized by lovers, who choose this sense rather than any other because love
"is engendered in the eyes, with gazing fed,"

so intimacy is to friends most choice-worthy, friendship being communion? As a man is to himself, so he is to his friend; with respect to himself, the perception of his own existence is choice-worthy, and so it is in respect of his friend.

Besides, their friendship is acted out in intimacy, so with good reason they desire this. Whatever in each man's opinion constitutes existence, or whatever it is for the sake of which they choose life, in this they wish their friends to join them. Hence some men drink together, others gamble, others do gymnastic exercises or hunt together, others study philosophy together — in each case spending their days together in what they like best in life; since they wish to be intimate with their friends, they do and partake in those things whereby they think to attain this.

So the friendship of the wicked becomes depraved; being unstable, they share in what is bad and become depraved by being made like one another.
