But the friendship of the good is good, growing with their intercourse; they improve by repeated acts and by mutual correction, taking an impress from one another in the points that please them. Whence the poet,
"From the good shalt thou surely learn good things."
Here let us end our discourse on friendship. The next subject is pleasure.

chapters.title: Book 10 — Pleasure and Happiness
paragraphs: Next comes a discussion of pleasure, which is thought to be most closely bound up with our kind. Men train the young by steering them with the rudders of pleasure and pain. To like and dislike what one ought is judged most important for forming good moral character, since these feelings extend throughout life, exerting an influence and giving a bias toward virtue and happiness; men choose what is pleasant and avoid what is painful.

We should by no means pass over such subjects, especially since they involve much difference of opinion. Some call pleasure the chief good; others, on the contrary, maintain that it is exceedingly bad — some from a real conviction, others from the notion that it is better, with a view to life and conduct, to show pleasure up as bad even if it is not so really, arguing that the mass of men are biased toward it and are slaves to their pleasures, and so should be drawn the other way to possibly arrive at the mean.

I suspect this policy is unsound. In matters of human feelings and actions, theories are less convincing than facts; when found conflicting with actual experience, they are not only despised but drag the truth down with them. He who deprecates pleasure, if once seen to aim at it, gets the credit of backsliding to it as being universally such as he said it was — the mass of men being incapable of nice distinctions.

Real accounts of such matters, then, seem most expedient, not for knowledge merely but for life and conduct. They are believed as being in harmony with facts, and so they prevail with the wise to live in accordance with them.
But of such considerations enough. Let us proceed to the current maxims about pleasure.

Eudoxus thought pleasure was the chief good, since he saw all, rational and irrational alike, aiming at it. He argued that, since what is the object of choice must be good and what most so the best, the fact of all being drawn to the same thing proved this thing to be the best for all. "Each," he said, "finds what is good for itself just as it does its proper nourishment, and so what is good for all and the object of aim for all is their chief good."

(His theories were received not so much for their own sake as because of his excellent moral character; he was thought eminently to possess perfect self-mastery, and so it was not thought that he said these things because he was a lover of pleasure, but that he really was convinced.)
He thought his position no less proved by the argument from the contrary: since pain is in itself an object of avoidance to all, its contrary must likewise be an object of choice.

Again he urged that what is most choice-worthy is what we choose not for the sake of, or with a view to, anything further; pleasure is confessedly of this kind, since no one ever asks to what purpose he is pleased, feeling that pleasure is in itself choice-worthy.
Again, when added to any other good, it makes that good more choice-worthy — as, for instance, just actions or acts of self-mastery; and good can only be increased by itself.

But this argument at least seems to prove only that pleasure belongs to the class of goods, not that it does so more than anything else. Every good is more choice-worthy in combination with another than taken alone. In fact, it is by just such an argument that Plato proves pleasure is not the chief good: "the life of pleasure is more choice-worthy in combination with practical wisdom than apart from it; if the compound is better, then simple pleasure cannot be the chief good, since the chief good cannot by any addition become more choice-worthy than it is already." Obviously nothing else can be the chief good which by combination with things in themselves good becomes more choice-worthy.
What is there, then, of such a nature? (Meaning, of course, what we can partake of, since what we are looking for must be such.)

As for those who object that "what all aim at is not necessarily good," I cannot see much in what they say. What all think, we say, is. He who would cut away this ground from under us will bring forward nothing more dependable. If the argument had rested on the desires of irrational creatures, there might have been something in the objection; but since the rational also desire pleasure, how can the objection hold weight? It may be that even in the lower animals there is some natural good principle above themselves, aiming at the good peculiar to them.

Nor does that seem sound which is urged about the argument from the contrary. Some say, "it does not follow that pleasure must be good because pain is evil, since evil may be opposed to evil, and both evil and good to what is indifferent." What they say is right enough in itself, but does not hold in the present instance. If both pleasure and pain were bad, both would be objects of avoidance; if neither, neither would be — at all events both would fare alike. But now men plainly avoid one as bad and choose the other as good, so there is a complete opposition.
Nor is pleasure excluded from being good because it does not belong to the class of qualities: the acts of virtue are not qualities either, nor is happiness — yet both are goods.
They say the chief good is limited but pleasure unlimited, since it admits of degrees.

If they judge this from the act of feeling pleasure, then the same applies to justice and the other virtues; men are said to be more or less of such characters (according to the different virtues), more just or more brave; and one may practice justice and self-mastery more or less.

If, on the other hand, they judge from the pleasures themselves, they may miss the true cause, namely, that some are unmixed and others mixed. Just as health, being in itself limited, still admits of degrees, why should not pleasure do so and yet be limited? In the former case we account for it by the fact that there is not the same adjustment of parts in all men, nor one and the same in the same individual; but health, though relaxed, remains up to a certain point, and differs in degrees. The same may be the case with pleasure.
Again, assuming the chief good to be perfect and all movements and generations imperfect, they try to show pleasure is a movement and a generation.

Yet they do not seem warranted even in calling it a movement. To every movement swiftness and slowness are thought to belong — if not in itself (as the motion of the universe), then relatively. But neither belongs to pleasure. Though one may have gotten quickly into the state of pleasure (as into that of anger), one cannot be in the state quickly, nor relatively to the state of any other person. But we can walk or grow, and so on, quickly or slowly.
Of course one can change into the state of pleasure quickly or slowly, but to act in the state (that is, have the perception of pleasure) quickly is not possible.

How can it be a generation? According to common views, not anything is generated from anything, but a thing resolves itself into that out of which it was generated; whereas, of that of which pleasure is supposed to be a generation, pain is a destruction.
Again, they say pain is a lack of something suitable to nature, and pleasure a supply of it.

But these are affections of the body. If pleasure really is a supplying of what is suitable to nature, that which the supply occurs in must feel the pleasure — that is, the body; yet this is not thought to be so. So pleasure is not a supplying; only a person, of course, will be pleased when a supply takes place, just as he will be pained when cut short.

This notion seems to have arisen from the pains and pleasures connected with natural nourishment; when people feel a lack and so have pain first, they are, of course, pleased with the supply of their lack.

But this is not the case with all pleasures. Those attending mathematical studies are unconnected with any pain; among the senses, those from the sense of smell; and many sounds, sights, memories, and hopes. Of what can these be generations? Here there has been no lack of anything to be later supplied.

To those who bring forward disgraceful pleasures, we may reply that these are not really pleasant. It does not follow that because they are pleasant to the ill-disposed we must admit them to be pleasant except to those persons — just as we should not say those things are really wholesome, sweet, or bitter which are so only to the sick, or those objects really white which seem so to people with ophthalmia.

Or we might say pleasures are choice-worthy but not as derived from these sources — just as wealth is, but not as the price of treason; or health, but not on the terms of eating anything however loathsome.

Or we may say pleasures differ in kind. Those derived from honorable objects, for instance, differ from those arising from disgraceful ones; it is not possible to experience the pleasure of the just man without being just, or of the musical man without being musical; and so on.

The commonly drawn distinction between the friend and the flatterer would seem to show clearly either that pleasure is not a good, or that there are different kinds of pleasure. The friend is thought to have good as the object of his intercourse, the flatterer pleasure only; the latter is reproached, while the former men praise as having different objects.

Again, no one would choose to live his whole life through with a child's intellect, though receiving the highest possible pleasure from such objects as children receive it from; or to take pleasure in doing any of the most disgraceful things, though sure never to be pained.

There are many things about which we should be diligent even though they brought no pleasure — seeing, remembering, knowing, possessing the various excellences. That pleasures do follow on these naturally makes no difference; we should certainly choose them even if no pleasure resulted.

It seems plain, then, that pleasure is not the chief good, nor is every kind of it choice-worthy; and that there are some choice-worthy in themselves, differing in kind — that is, in their sources. Let this suffice as an account of current maxims about pleasure and pain.
What pleasure is and how characterized will be plainer if we take up the subject afresh.
An act of sight is thought to be complete at any moment; it lacks nothing the later accession of which would complete its whole nature.

Pleasure resembles this; it is a whole, so to speak, and one could not at any moment take a pleasure whose whole nature would be completed by lasting longer. For this reason it is not a movement; all movement takes place in time of a certain duration and has a certain end to accomplish. The movement of house-building, for instance, is complete only when the builder has produced what he intended — either in the whole time required for the whole design, or in a given portion. All subordinate movements are incomplete in the parts of the time, and differ in kind from the whole movement and from one another (the fitting of stones together is a movement different from the fluting of a column, and both from the construction of the temple as a whole; this last is complete as lacking nothing in the proposed result, while those of the basement or the triglyph are incomplete, each being a movement of a part).
As I said, they differ in kind; you cannot at any moment you choose find a movement complete in its whole nature — only, if at all, in the whole time required.

So too with the movement of walking and all others. If motion is a movement from one place to another, it has different kinds: flying, walking, leaping, and such. Not only so, but there are different kinds even in walking. The "where-from" and "where-to" are not the same in the whole course as in a portion, nor in one portion as in another; nor is crossing this line the same as crossing that, since a man is not merely crossing a line but a line in a given place, and this is in a different place from that.

Of movement I have discoursed exactly in another treatise. Here I will only say it seems not to be complete at any given moment, and that most movements are incomplete and specifically different, since the whence and whither constitute different species.

But the whole nature of pleasure is complete at any given moment. Plainly, then, pleasure and movement must differ, and pleasure must belong to the class of things whole and complete. This might also appear from the impossibility of moving except in a definite time, whereas there is no such restriction on the sensation of pleasure: what exists at the very present moment is a kind of "whole."

From these considerations, then, it is plain that people are not warranted in saying pleasure is a movement or a generation. These terms are not applicable to all things, only to what is divisible and not wholes. Of an act of sight there is no generation, nor of a point, nor of a monad; nor is any of these a movement or a generation. Neither, then, of pleasure is there movement or generation, since it is, so to speak, a whole.

Every perceptive faculty works upon the object corresponding to it, and perfectly when the faculty is in a good state and works on the most excellent object within its range (perfect working being much what I have described; let us not quibble about saying "the faculty" works instead of "the subject in which the faculty resides"). In each case the best working is that of the faculty in its best state upon the best of its objects. This will further be the most perfect and most pleasant; pleasure attends every perceptive faculty, every intellectual operation and speculation; and what is most pleasant is what is most perfect, which is the working of the best faculty upon the most excellent of its objects.

Pleasure perfects the working. But pleasure does not perfect it in the same way as the faculty and the object of perception do, being good; just as health and the physician are not in similar senses causes of a healthy state.

That pleasure does arise upon the exercise of every perceptive faculty is evident; we commonly say sights and sounds are pleasant. It is especially so when the faculty is most excellent and works upon an object of the same quality; when both the object and faculty are such, pleasure will always exist — supposing, of course, an agent and a patient.

Pleasure perfects the act of working not as an inherent state but as a supervening finish — such as bloom in people at their prime. So long as the object of intellectual or sensitive perception is as it should be, and the faculty discerning or realizing the object is such, there will be pleasure in the working; when what has the capacity of being acted on and what is apt to act are alike and similarly related, the same result follows naturally.

How is it, then, that no one feels pleasure continuously? Is it not that he grows weary, since all human faculties are incapable of unintermitting exertion? So pleasure does not arise either, since it follows upon the act of working. Some things please when new but afterwards not in the same way, for exactly the same reason: at first the mind is roused and works on these objects at full tension, like people gazing steadily at something; afterwards the working is not what it was at first but careless, and so the pleasure too is dulled.

One might conclude that all men grasp at pleasure, since all aim at life, and life is an act of working; every man works at and with those things he best likes. The musical man works with his hearing at music; the studious man with his intellect at speculative questions; and so on. Pleasure perfects the acts of working, and so perfects life, which men grasp at. No wonder, then, that they aim at pleasure too: to each it perfects life, which is itself choice-worthy. (We may leave aside the question whether we choose life for pleasure's sake or pleasure for life's sake; the two are closely connected and admit of no separation, since pleasure does not come into being without working, and every working pleasure perfects.)

This is one reason why pleasures are thought to differ in kind: we suppose that things differing in kind must be perfected by things so differing. This is plainly so with the productions of nature and art — animals, trees, pictures, statues, houses, furniture; so also acts of working different in kind must be perfected by things differing in kind. Intellectual workings differ specifically from those of the senses, and these from one another; so do the pleasures that perfect them.

This may also be shown from the intimate connection between each pleasure and the working it perfects. The pleasure proper to any working increases that working; those who work with pleasure judge more closely and carry out things to a greater degree of nicety. For instance, those who take pleasure in geometry become geometricians and apprehend particular points more completely; likewise those fond of music, architecture, or anything else improve in their pursuit, since they feel pleasure in it. The pleasures aid in increasing the workings; what aids is proper and peculiar; and what is proper and peculiar to things specifically different is itself specifically different.

This may be shown even more clearly by the fact that pleasures arising from one kind of working hinder other workings. People fond of flute music cannot keep attention to conversation when they catch the sound of a flute, since they take more pleasure in flute-playing than in the working at hand; the pleasure attending flute-playing destroys the working of conversation.

Much the same happens when a person is engaged in two different workings at once: the pleasanter pushes out the other, and if the disparity is great, then more and more, till the man ceases altogether to work at the other.

This is why, when we are very much pleased with something, we do nothing else; and only when we are moderately pleased do we vary our occupation with another. In the theater, people who eat sweetmeats do so most when the performance is indifferent.

Since the proper and peculiar pleasure gives accuracy to workings and makes them more enduring and better of their kind, while foreign pleasures mar them, the difference between them is plainly wide. In fact, foreign pleasures have pretty much the same effect as the pains proper to a working, which destroy it. If a man dislikes writing, or calculation, one does not write, the other does not calculate; the working is attended with some pain. So contrary effects are produced upon the workings by the pleasures and pains proper to them, by which I mean those arising upon the working itself, independently of anything else. As for foreign pleasures, we have said they produce a similar effect to the pain proper to the working — they destroy the working, only not in the same way.

As workings differ in goodness and badness, some being fit objects of choice, others of avoidance, others in nature indifferent, so with pleasures: each working has its own proper pleasure attending it. The one proper to a good working is good; the one proper to a bad, bad. Even the desires for what is noble are praiseworthy, and for what is base blameworthy.

The pleasures attending workings are more closely connected with them than the desires for them; desires are separate both in time and nature, while pleasures are close to the workings and so indivisible from them as to raise the question whether the working and the pleasure are identical. But pleasure does not seem to be an intellectual operation or a faculty of perception — that is absurd. It gives the impression of being the same from not being separated from them.

As the workings differ, so their pleasures. Sight differs from touch in purity, and hearing and smelling from taste; so too do their pleasures. Intellectual pleasures differ from sensual, and different kinds of intellectual and sensual differ from one another.

It is thought, moreover, that each animal has a pleasure proper to itself, as it has a proper work — namely, that pleasure which attends the working. The soundness of this will appear on particular inspection: horse, dog, and man have different pleasures. As Heraclitus says, an ass would sooner have hay than gold — provender is pleasanter to asses than gold. So the pleasures of animals specifically different are also specifically different, but those of the same, we may reasonably suppose, are without difference.

Yet in human creatures they differ not a little; the same things please some and pain others, and what are painful and hateful to some are pleasant to others. So with sweet things: the same will not seem so to the man in a fever as to him in health; nor will the invalid and the person in robust health have the same notion of warmth. The same goes for other things.

In all such cases, what "is" is what impresses the good man with the notion of being so. If this is a sound maxim (as it is usually held), and virtue — the good man as such — is the measure of everything, then those must be real pleasures that gave him the impression of being so, and those things pleasant in which he takes pleasure. It is not at all astonishing that what is unpleasant to him should give another person the impression of being pleasant; men are liable to many corruptions and marrings. The things in question are not pleasant really, but only to these particular persons, and to them only as being thus disposed.

It is plain we must assert those pleasures confessedly disgraceful to be real pleasures only to depraved tastes. Of those thought to be good, what kind, or which, must we say is the pleasure of man? Is not the answer plain from considering the workings, since the pleasures follow on these?

If there is one or several workings belonging to the perfect and blessed man, the pleasures that perfect these workings must be said to be specially and properly the pleasures of man; all the rest in a secondary sense, and in various degrees according as the workings are related to those highest and best.

Now that we have spoken of the excellences of both kinds, of friendship in its varieties, and of pleasures, it remains to sketch happiness, since we assume that to be the one end of all human things. We shall save time by recapitulating what was said before.

We said happiness is not a mere state; if it were, it might belong to one who slept his whole life through and merely vegetated, or to one fallen into very great calamities. If these possibilities displease us and we would rather place happiness among some kind of working (as was said), and workings are of different kinds — some necessary and choice-worthy with a view to other things, others in themselves — we must plainly rank happiness among those choice-worthy for their own sakes, not among those choice-worthy for the sake of something further; happiness has no lack of anything but is self-sufficient.

By choice-worthy in themselves are meant those from which nothing is sought beyond the act of working. Such are thought to be actions according to virtue, since doing what is noble and excellent is one of the things choice-worthy for their own sake.

Such amusements as are pleasant are also choice-worthy in themselves; people do not choose them with any further purpose, and in fact receive more harm than profit, neglecting their persons and property. Still, most of those judged happy take refuge in such pastimes — which is why those with varied talent in them are highly esteemed among tyrants, since they make themselves pleasant in the things those aim at, and tyrants accordingly want such men.

These things are thought to be appurtenances of happiness because men in power spend their leisure in them; yet we cannot argue from such men's example. Neither virtue nor intellect is necessarily involved in having power, and yet these are the only sources of good workings. Nor does it follow that because these men, never having tasted pure and generous pleasure, take refuge in bodily ones, those are therefore more choice-worthy; for children also believe that those things are most excellent which are precious in their eyes.

As children and men have different ideas of what is precious, so too have the bad and the good. As we have many times said, those things are really precious and pleasant which seem so to the good man. To each individual that working is most choice-worthy which is in accordance with his own state; to the good man that is so which is in accordance with virtue.

Happiness, then, is not in amusement. It is absurd to make the end amusement, and to toil and endure hardship all one's life for the sake of amusement. We choose nearly everything with some further end in view — except happiness, for happiness is the end comprehending all others. To take pains and labor for the sake of amusement is foolish and childish. But to amuse oneself with a view to steady work afterwards, as Anacharsis says, is thought right; amusement is like rest, and men want rest because unable to labor continuously.
Rest, therefore, is not an end, since it is adopted with a view to working afterwards.

It is held that the happy life must be one according to excellence, which is accompanied by earnestness and does not stand in amusement. Things done in earnest are better than things merely ludicrous and joined with amusement. The working of the better part, or the better man, we say is more earnest; and the working of the better is better and more capable of happiness.

As for bodily pleasures, any ordinary person — even a slave — might enjoy them just as well as the best man living; but no one supposes a slave to share happiness except so far as it is implied in life. Happiness stands not in such pastimes but in the workings according to excellence, as has also been said.

If happiness is a working according to excellence, it must be according to the highest excellence — the excellence of the best principle. Whether this best principle is intellect or some other thought naturally to rule and lead and to conceive of noble and divine things — whether it is in its own nature divine, or the most divine of our internal principles — the working of this in accordance with its own proper excellence must be the perfect happiness.

That this is contemplative has been stated already, and seems consistent with what was said before and with truth. First, this working is of the highest kind, since intellect is the highest of our internal principles, and the subjects it is conversant with are the highest that fall within our knowledge.
Next, it is also the most continuous; we are better able to contemplate than to do anything else whatever continuously.

Again, we think pleasure must in some way be an ingredient of happiness, and of all workings according to excellence, the one in the way of philosophic wisdom is confessedly most pleasant. The pursuit of wisdom is thought to contain pleasures admirable for purity and permanence; and it is reasonable that the occupation is more pleasant to those who have mastered than to those still seeking it.

Self-sufficiency, too, will attach chiefly to the contemplative working. The actual necessaries of life are needed alike by the man of science, the just man, and all other characters. But supposing all are sufficiently supplied, the just man needs people toward whom, and together with whom, to practice justice — and so with the self-masterer, the brave man, and the rest. The man of science can contemplate and speculate even when alone, and the more entirely he deserves the name, the more able he is to do so. Perhaps he will do better for having fellow workers, but he is certainly most self-sufficient.

Again, this alone would seem to be rested in for its own sake, since nothing results from it beyond the fact of having contemplated; whereas from all things objects of moral action we mean to get something besides the doing them, be it more or less.

Happiness is thought to stand in perfect rest: we toil that we may rest, and go to war that we may be at peace. All the practical virtues require either society or war for their working, and the actions in these are thought to exclude rest — those of war entirely, since no one chooses war or prepares for it for its own sake; he would be a bloodthirsty villain who made enemies of his friends to secure the existence of fighting. The working of the statesman also excludes rest, and besides the actual work of government seeks for power and dignities, or at least happiness for himself and his fellow citizens — a happiness distinct from the national happiness, which we evidently seek as different.

If of all actions according to the various virtues those of politics and war are preeminent in honor and greatness, yet are restless, aim at some further end, and are not choice-worthy for their own sakes; but the working of the intellect, being apt for contemplation, is thought to excel in earnestness, aim at no end beyond itself, and have a pleasure of its own that helps to increase the working; and if the attributes of self-sufficiency, capacity for rest, and unweariedness (so far as compatible with human infirmity) and all other attributes of the highest happiness plainly belong to this working — this must be perfect happiness, attaining a complete duration of life. (Duration is added because none of the points of happiness is incomplete.)

Such a life will be higher than mere human nature, because a man will live thus not insofar as he is man but insofar as there is a divine principle in him. In proportion as this principle excels his composite nature, so too will its working excel that in accordance with any other kind of excellence. If pure intellect, compared with human nature, is divine, then the life in accordance with it is divine compared with man's ordinary life.

We must not give ear to those who bid a man, as man, to mind only man's affairs, or as mortal only mortal things. As far as we can, we must make ourselves like immortals and do all with a view to living in accordance with the highest principle in us; small as it may be in bulk, in power and preciousness it far excels all the others.
This principle would seem to constitute each man's "self," since it is supreme and above all others in goodness; it would be absurd for a man not to choose his own life but the life of another.

Here the earlier observation applies: what is proper to each is naturally best and pleasantest to him. To man, then, the life in accordance with pure intellect (since this principle most truly is the man) is the happiest.

Second in degree of happiness will be the life according to the other kind of excellence; workings in accordance with this are proper to man. We do acts of justice, courage, and the other virtues toward one another, in contracts, services, and in all kinds of actions and feelings, by observing what is befitting for each; and all these are plainly proper to man. Excellence of moral character is thought to result in some points from physical circumstances, and to be, in many, closely connected with the passions.

Practical wisdom and excellence of moral character are closely united, since the principles of practical wisdom accord with the moral virtues, and the moral virtues are right when they accord with practical wisdom.

These, being bound up with the passions, must belong to the composite nature; and the excellences of the composite nature are proper to man. So too, then, is the life and happiness in accordance with them. But the happiness of pure intellect is separate and distinct. Let this suffice on the subject, since great exactness is beyond our purpose.

The contemplative life would also seem to require only a small supply of external goods, certainly less than the moral. As far as necessaries are concerned, we may suppose both equally need them (though in fact the man who lives in society takes more trouble about his person and such things; there will be some little difference). But when we come to their workings, a great difference appears.

The liberal man must have money to do his liberal actions with; the just man, to meet his engagements (mere intentions are uncertain, and even unjust men pretend to wish to do justly). The brave man must have power, if he is to perform any of the actions proper to his virtue; and the man of perfected self-mastery must have opportunity for temptation — else how can he or any of the others display his real character?

(A question is sometimes raised: whether moral choice or the actions have most to do with virtue, since it consists in both? Plainly the perfection of virtuous action requires both; but for the actions many things are required, and the greater and more numerous the actions, the more.) As for the man engaged in contemplative speculation, not only are such things unnecessary for his working, but are even hindrances to the contemplation itself; of course, insofar as he is a man and lives in society, he chooses to do what virtue requires, and so he will need such things for maintaining his character as a man, though not as a speculative philosopher.

That perfect happiness must be a kind of contemplative working may also appear from this. Our conception of the gods is that they are above all blessed and happy. What kind of moral actions are we to attribute to them? Those of justice? Will they not look ridiculous forming contracts, restoring deposits, and the like? Well then, shall we picture them performing brave actions, withstanding objects of fear and meeting dangers because it is noble to do so? Or liberal ones? But to whom would they be giving? Besides, it is absurd to think they have money or anything of the kind. As for actions of perfected self-mastery, what would theirs be? Would it not be a degrading praise that they have no bad desires? In short, if one followed the subject into details, all the circumstances connected with moral actions would appear trivial and unworthy of gods.

Still, everyone believes they live, and therefore they work; it is not supposed they sleep their time away like Endymion. If from a living being you take away action, still more if creation, what remains but contemplation? So the working of the gods, eminent in blessedness, must be apt for contemplative speculation; and of all human workings, that is the one most capable of happiness which is nearest akin to this.
A corroboration is that other animals do not share in happiness, being completely shut out from any such working.
To the gods, then, all life is blessed; to men, insofar as there is in it some copy of such working; but to other animals none is happy, since none shares in contemplative speculation.

Happiness, then, is coextensive with this contemplative speculation, and in proportion as people have the act of contemplation, they have the being happy — not incidentally, but in the way of contemplative speculation itself, which is in itself precious.

Happiness must, then, be a kind of contemplative speculation. But since it is man we are speaking of, he will also need external prosperity, since his nature is not by itself sufficient for speculation; he must have health of body, nourishment, and tendance of all kinds.

Still, because without external goods a man cannot enjoy high happiness, we must not think he will need many and great goods to be happy. Neither self-sufficiency nor action stands in excess, and one may act nobly without being ruler of sea and land; with moderate means a man may act in accordance with virtue.

This may be seen clearly: men in private stations are thought to act justly, not merely no less than men in power but even more. It will be quite enough that just so much belongs to a man as is necessary, for his life will be happy who works in accordance with virtue.

Solon perhaps drew a fair picture of the happy, when he said they are men moderately supplied with external goods, who have achieved the most noble deeds (as he thought) and lived with perfect self-mastery; for men of moderate means may act as they ought.

Anaxagoras also seems to have conceived the happy man as neither rich nor powerful, saying he should not wonder if he were accounted strange by the multitude; they judge by outward circumstances, of which alone they have any perception.

So the opinions of the wise seem to accord with our account. Such things carry some weight, but truth in matters of moral action is judged from facts and actual life, for herein rests the decision. We should examine the preceding statements by referring them to facts and actual life; when they harmonize, accept them; when they are at variance, treat them as mere theories.

He who works in accordance with, and pays observance to, pure intellect, and tends this, seems likely to be both in the best frame of mind and dearest to the gods. If, as is thought, any care is bestowed on human things by the gods, it is reasonable to think they take pleasure in what is best and most akin to themselves (which must be pure intellect), and that they requite with kindness those who love and honor this most, as paying observance to what is dear to them, and as acting rightly and nobly. Plainly the man of wisdom chiefly combines all these; he is therefore dearest to the gods, and probably also most happy.
On this view also the man of science will be most happy.

Now that we have said enough, in our sketchy way, on the virtues, on friendship, and on pleasure, are we to suppose our original purpose complete? Or must we not acknowledge, as is commonly said, that in matters of moral action mere speculation and knowledge is not the real end, but rather practice? If so, then in respect of virtue, knowledge is not enough: we must further strive to have and exert it, and take whatever other means there are of becoming good.

If talking and writing were of themselves sufficient to make men good, they would justly, as Theognis observes, reap numerous and great rewards, and the thing to do would be to provide them. But in fact, while talking and writing plainly have the power to guide and stimulate the generous among the young and to base on true virtuous principle any noble and truly high-minded disposition, they are powerless to guide the mass of men to virtue and goodness. It is not in their nature to be amenable to a sense of shame but only to fear, nor to abstain from what is low because it is disgraceful but because of the punishment attached to it. They live at the beck and call of passion, pursue their proper pleasures and the means of securing them, and avoid the contrary pains; but of what is noble and truly pleasurable they have no idea, since they have never tasted it.

What mere words can transform such men? It is either actually impossible, or a task of no mean difficulty, to alter by words what has been of old taken into men's very dispositions. It may be ground for contentment if with all the means and appliances for goodness in our hands we can attain to virtue.

The formation of a virtuous character is ascribed by some to nature, some to custom, some to teaching. Nature's part, whatever it may be, obviously does not rest with us but belongs to those who in the truest sense are fortunate, by reason of some divine agency.

As for words and precept, they will, it is to be feared, not avail with all; it may be necessary that the mind of the disciple have been previously prepared for liking and disliking as he ought — just as the soil must be, to nourish the seed sown. He who lives in obedience to passion cannot hear any advice that would dissuade him, nor, if he heard, understand; how can one reform such a one? In general, passion is not thought to yield to reason but to brute force. So there must be, to begin with, a kind of affinity to virtue in the disposition — which must cleave to what is honorable and loathe what is disgraceful. But to get right guidance toward virtue from the earliest youth is not easy unless one is brought up under such laws. Living with self-mastery and endurance is not pleasant to the mass of men, and especially not to the young. So their food, and manner of living generally, ought to be the subject of legal regulation, since things will not be disagreeable when become habitual.

Yet perhaps it is not sufficient that men while young get right food and tendance. They will have to practice and become accustomed to certain things even after they have attained manhood; so we shall need laws on these points too, and, in short, on the whole of life. The mass of men are amenable to compulsion rather than reason, and to punishment rather than a sense of honor.

Some therefore hold that while lawgivers should employ the sense of honor to exhort and guide men to virtue (expecting that those well trained in habits will obey), they should impose chastisement and penalties on the disobedient and of less promising nature, and expel the incurable entirely. The good man, living under a sense of honor, will obey reason; the baser sort, who grasp at pleasure, will be kept in check like beasts of burden by pain. They say, accordingly, that pains should be such as are most contrary to the pleasures they like.

As said already, he who is to be good must have been brought up and habituated well, then live accordingly under good institutions, and never do what is low and mean, either against or with his will. These objects can be attained only by men living under some guiding intellect and right order, with power to back them.

Paternal rule has neither strength nor compulsory power, nor in fact has the rule of any one man, unless he is a king or in like position. But law has power to compel, since it is a declaration emanating from practical wisdom and intellect. Men feel enmity toward fellow men who oppose their impulses, even when they rightly do so; the law, by contrast, is not an object of hatred, even while enforcing right rules.

Sparta is nearly the only state where the framer of the constitution has made any provision, it would seem, about the food and manner of living of the people. In most states these matters are entirely neglected, and each man lives just as he likes, ruling his wife and children Cyclops-fashion.

Of course the best would be that there should be a right public system and that we should be able to carry it out. But since these points are neglected as a public matter, the duty would seem to devolve on each individual to contribute to the cause of virtue with his own children and friends, or at least to make this his aim and purpose. This, it seems, from what has been said, he will be best able to do by making a legislator of himself; all public systems are plainly formed through laws, and good ones through good laws. Whether the laws are written or unwritten, whether applied to the training of one or many, will make no difference, just as it does not in music, gymnastics, or any such pursuits acquired by practice.

As in communities laws and customs prevail, so in families the express commands of the head, and customs also; and even more in families, because of blood relationship and benefits conferred — in families you have to begin with people who have affection and are naturally obedient to controlling authority.

Further, private training has advantages over public, as in the case of medicine. As a general rule, a man in a fever should keep quiet and starve; but in a particular case this may not hold. Or, to take another illustration, the boxer will not use the same way of fighting with all antagonists.

The individual, then, will be most exactly attended to under private care, since each will more likely obtain what is expedient for him. Of course in medicine, gymnastics, or any other art, a man will treat individual cases the better for being acquainted with general rules ("so and so is good for all," or "for men in such and such cases"); for general maxims are and are called the object-matter of sciences. Still, this is no reason against the possibility of a man's taking excellent care of some one case though he possesses no scientific knowledge but, from experience, is exactly acquainted with what happens in each point — just as some people doctor themselves best, though they would be wholly unable to help others. Yet for one who wishes to become a real artist and to know the theory of his profession, it is necessary to have recourse to general principles and ascertain all their capacities; for we have said these are the object-matter of sciences.

If we may become good through laws, then whoever wishes to make men better by a system of care and training must try to make a legislator of himself. To treat skillfully just anyone is not what any ordinary person can do, but, if anyone, he who has knowledge, as in medicine and all arts involving careful practice and skill.

Our next business, then, will be to inquire from what sources, or how, one may acquire this faculty of legislation. Or shall we say that, as in similar cases, statesmen are the people to learn from, since this faculty was thought to be a part of political science? But political science plainly does not stand on the same footing as other sciences and faculties. In all other cases, those who impart the faculties and themselves exert them are the same (physicians, painters); but political matters the sophists profess to teach — while not one of them practices them, this being left to those actually engaged in politics. These might very well be thought to do it by some singular knack and by mere practice rather than by any intellectual process; they neither write nor speak on these matters (though this might be more to their credit than composing speeches for courts or the assembly), nor have they made statesmen of their own sons or their friends.

One can hardly suppose but that they would have done so if they could, seeing that they could have bequeathed no more precious legacy to their communities, nor would they have preferred, for themselves or their dearest friends, the possession of any faculty rather than this.

Practice, however, seems to contribute not a little to acquiring it; merely breathing the atmosphere of politics would never have made statesmen of them. We may conclude that those who would acquire a knowledge of statesmanship must, in addition to theory, have practice.

The sophists who profess to teach it are plainly a long way from doing so; they have no knowledge at all of its nature and objects. If they did, they would never have put it on the same footing with rhetoric, or even on a lower one; nor would they have thought it easy to legislate by simply collecting the famous laws and selecting the best — as if selection were not a matter of skill, and judging aright a very great matter, as in music. Only those with practical knowledge of a thing can judge performances rightly, or understand the means and way by which they are accomplished, and what harmonizes with what; the unlearned must be content to discover whether the result is good or bad, as in painting.

Laws may be called the performances or tangible results of political science. How, then, can a man acquire from these the faculty of legislation, or choose the best? We do not see men made physicians by compilations; yet in medical treatises men try to give not only the cases but how they may be cured and the proper treatment in each, dividing the various bodily habits. These are thought useful to professional men but useless to the unprofessional. So too, collections of laws and constitutions would be exceedingly useful to those able to speculate on them and judge what is well, what ill, and what kind of things fit with what. But those who go through such matters without this qualification cannot have right judgment, unless they have it by instinct — though they may become more intelligent in such matters.

Since our predecessors have left the subject of legislation uninvestigated, it will be better perhaps to investigate it ourselves — and in fact the whole subject of polity, so that what we may call human philosophy may be completed as far as lies in us.

First, then, let us endeavor to get whatever fragments of good there may be in our predecessors' statements; next, from the polities we have collected, ascertain what kinds of things preserve or destroy communities, what particular constitutions, and why some are well and others ill managed. After such inquiry we shall be the better able to take a concentrated view as to what kind of constitution is best, what regulations are best for each, and what laws and customs.
